The views, conclusions and recommendations expressed herein are those of the authors and not necessarily those of the Department.

364 This report provides a summary of the progress to date of research and monitoring studies on contaminants in northern Canada, and related education, communications and policy activities that were conducted in 2000~200 I under the auspices of the Northern Contaminants Program (NCP). The projects cover all aspects of northern contaminants issues, as outlined in the NCP blueprints, including human health, monitoring the health of Arctic peoples and ecosystems, and the effectiveness of inter~ national controls (abiotic monitoring and modelling, biotic monitoring, local contaminants concerns), education and communications, international policy and program management.

These projects were evaluated, as proposals, by external peer reviewers, technical review teams, a social/cultural review team, territorial/regional contaminants committees and the NCP Management Committee to ensure that they support the overall NCP objectives.
Further information about the NCP is available on the NCP Web site at www.inac.gc.ca/ncp.

The Northern Contaminants Program (NCP) was established in 1991 in response to concerns about human exposure to elevated levels of contaminants in fish and wildlife species that are important to the traditional diets of northern Aboriginal peoples. Early studies indicated that there was a wide spectrum of substances - persistent organic pollutants, heavy metals, and radionuclides - many of which had no Arctic or Canadian sources, but which were, nevertheless, reaching unexpectedly high levels in the Arctic ecosystem. The Program's key objective is to reduce and, where possible, eliminate contaminants in northern traditionally harvested (country) foods while providing information that assists informed decision making by individuals and communities in their food use.

Under the first phase of the NCP (NCP-1), research was focussed on gathering the data required to determine the levels, geographic extent and source of contaminants in the northern atmosphere, environment and its people, and the probable duration of the problem. The data enabled us to understand the spatial patterns and temporal trends of contaminants in the North, and confirmed our suspicions that the major sources of contaminants were other countries. The data, which included information on the benefits from continued consumption of traditional/ country foods, was also used to carry out assessments of human health risks resulting from contaminants in those foods. Results generated through NCP-I are synthesized in the Canadian Arctic Contaminants Assessment Report.

Extensive consultations were conducted in 1997-1 998 to find the common elements between the concerns and priorities of northern communities and the scientific needs identified as critical for addressing the issue of contamination in Canada's North. As a result, priorities for current and future research are based on an understanding of the species that are most relevant for human exposure to contaminants in the North, and geographic locations and populations that are most at risk.

In 1998-1999, the NCP began its second phase (NCP-II), which will continue until 2002-2003. NCP-II supports research designed to answer questions about the impacts and risks to human health that may result from current levels of contamination in key Arctic food species. To ensure a balanced assessment of the risks, an emphasis is placed on characterizing and quantifying the benefits associated with traditional diets. Communications activities are also emphasized and supported under NCP-II. Under the leadership of the northern Aboriginal organizations, the dialogue between northerners and the scientific community, which was initiated in NCP-I, continues to build awareness and an understanding of contaminants issues, and helps to support the ability to deal with specific contaminant issues at the local level.

In addition, the NCP effort to achieve international controls of contaminants remains strong in NCP-II. The legally binding POPs protocol, under the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UN ECE) Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution, has been successfully negotiated and was signed by 34 countries (including Canada) at the UN ECE Ministerial Conference in Aarhus, Denmark, in June 1998. Canada ratified this agreement in December 1998. Negotiations for a legally binding global instrument on POPs under the United Nations Environment Programme have now also been completed with the signing of the POPs Convention in Stockholm, Sweden, May 23 , 2001. The Convention has been signed by more than 100 countries; Canada has signed and ratified the Convention. Cooperative actions under the Arctic Council, including the circumpolar Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme (AMAP) and the Arctic Council Action Plan (formally launched in October 2000), are continuing. NCP-II continues to generate the data that allows Canada to play a leading role in these initiatives.

The NCP is directed by a management committee that is chaired by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and which includes representatives from four northern Aboriginal organizations (Council of Yukon First Nations, Dene Nation, Inuit Tapirisat of Canada and Inuit Circumpolar Conference), the Yukon, Northwest Territories and Nunavut Territorial Governments, Nunavik, and four federal departments (Environment, Fisheries and Oceans, Health, and Indian Affairs and Northern Development). The management committee is responsible for establishing NCP policy and research priorities and for final decisions on the allocation of funds. Three territorial contaminants committees in the Yukon, Northwest Territories and Nunavut (established in May 2000), and a regional contaminants committee in Nunavik support this national committee. Funding for the NCP-II's $5.4 million annual research budget comes from the Treasury Board and the four participating federal departments.

The NCP Operational Management Guide, developed in 2000-200 I, and available on the NCP Web site (www.inac.gc.ca/ncp), provides a summary of the management structures and review processes used to effectively implement the NCP. The Guide explains the overall management structures currently used, the proposal review process and outlines a protocol to be used to publicly disseminate health and harvest information generated by the NCP. Background information on all NCP committees and review teams is also provided.
In 1998, the NCP Management Committee redesigned the NCP-Phase II for application under the 1999-2000 funding year. The two main initiatives undertaken were:

1) the development of blueprints that represent the long-term vision and strategic direction for NCP-11; and 2) the implementation of a more open and transparent proposal review process. This new management structure is designed to ensure that the NCP remains scientifically defensible and socio-culturally aware, while at the same time, achieving real progress in terms of the NCP's broad policy objectives.

Blueprints were developed for each of the four main NCP subprograms: i) Human Health, ii) Monitoring the Health of Arctic People and Ecosystems and the Effectiveness of International Controls, iii) International Policy, and iv) Education and Communications. The blueprints are used to provide the necessary guidance to project proponents for the development of proposals, as well as to peer reviewers, review teams and the NCP Management Committee for evaluating proposals. They are evolving documents that are reviewed at least annually.

Under a revamped proposal review process, the NCP Technical Committee was replaced with an external peer review process facilitated by review teams. The review of proposals is a two-pronged approach involving a scientific review by external peer reviewers, facilitated by technical review teams, and a socio-cultural review facilitated by a review team and the regional and Territorial Contaminants Committees (TCCs). Both sets of recommendations are considered by the Management Committee in making final funding decisions. Proposals submitted under the Education and Communications subprogram are evaluated by a review team and the TCCs. All peer reviewers, review teams and TCCs use evaluation criteria and the blueprints to review and rate proposals. Written consent from the appropriate northern community authority or national-level Aboriginal organization is required for all projects involving field work in the North and/or analyses of samples as a condition of approval for funding. The Social/Cultural Review Team ensures that each applicable proposal has a written consent form attached and sign by the applicable authority.

This report provides a summary of the progress to date of research and activities funded by the NCP in 2000-200 I, the third year of NCP-II. It is a compilation of reports submitted by project teams, emphasizing the results of research and related activities that took place during the 2000-200 I fiscal year. The report is divided into chapters that reflect the broad scope of the NCP: Human Health; Monitoring the Health of Arctic Peoples and Ecosystems and the Effectiveness of International Controls (including abiotic monitoring and modelling, biotic monitoring and local contaminants concerns); Education and Communications; International Policy; and Program Management. Projects that are reported upon in this Synopsis of Research will be presented at the I 1 th Annual Northern Contaminants Program Results Workshop, to be held in Calgary, Alberta, September 25-27, 200 I.

Time-Related Changes in trans-Nonachlor, trans-Chlordane and Oxychlordane Levels in Rat Tissues Genevieve Bondy, Toxicology Research Division, Postal Locator 220402, Bureau of Chemical Safety, Food Directorate, Health Canada, Ottawa, ON KIA OL2; Phone:(613) 957-2051; Fax: (613) 941-6959; E-mail: Genevieve_ Bondy@hc-sc.gc.ca Michael Barker, Gerard Cooke, Ivan Curran, Josee Doucet, Santokh Gill, Eric Lok, Rekha Mehta, Olga Pulido, Patrick Robertson and Paul Rowsell, Bureau of Chemical Safety, Health Canada, Ottawa, ON; Ross Norstrom and John Moisey, Environment Canada, Hull, QC Oxychlordane and trans-nonachlor are bioaccumulative contaminants related to the pesticide chlordane that have been detected in the Arctic marine food chain. Recent studies indicate that trans-nonachlor and its major metabolite oxychlordane are among the most toxic chlordanerelated contaminants, and that they are more toxic to female rats than male rats. The present study was designed to examine changes in trans-nonachlor and oxychlordane residue levels in male and female rats over time to clarify the relationships between residue accumulation, total body fat and changes in biomarkers for organ and cellular toxicity. Rats were exposed to either trans-nonachlor, oxychlordane or trans-chlordane by gavage for 28 consecutive days and necropsied 1, 28 and 56 days after the final dose. With the exception of a single female rat that died of oxychlordane toxicity at the end of the dosing period, no overt toxicity was observed in any treatment group. No visible lesions were observed in treated rats at necropsy, including the affected female. Analyses are in progress to measure changes in tissue residue levels and functional biomarkers in control and treated rats.
Although tissue and data analyses are still in progress, this study will address the following questions to provide key messages in the future:
Why is trans-nonachlor more toxic to female rats than to male rats?

How stable is trans-nonachlor in fat and other tissues? Oxychlordane is the primary metabolite of transnonachlor. Do oxychlordane levels in fat gradually increase and trans-nonachlor levels decline after exposure?

To examine changes in tissue oxychlordane and trans-chlordane enantiomer ratios over time in male Chlordane-related contaminants are present in traditional/ country foods in the Arctic (Kuhnlein et al. 1995, Muir et al. 1988, O'Hara et al. 1999, Wade et al. 1997), and in human adipose tissue and breast milk (Dearth and Hites 1991 a, Dewailly et al. 2000, Newsome et al. 1995, Newsome and Ryan 1999). The original pesticide was a mixture of many structurally related organochlorines (Dearth and Hites 1991 b) . The existing literature provides extensive toxicological data on the parent chlordane mixture (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 1994). Recent studies have focussed on the toxicity of the individual chlordane contaminants present at the highest levels in foods and in human tissues and breast milk: the chlor- dane constituents trans-nonachlor and cis-nonachlor (Bondy et al. 2000) and the metabolite oxychlordane (Bondy et al. in progress). These studies indicate that trans-nonachlor and its major metabolite oxychlordane are the most toxic chlordane-related contaminants, and that trans-nonachlor is more toxic to female rats than male rats. As expected from the literature on chlordane, liver microsomal enzymes are induced by trans-nonachlor, cis-nonachlor and oxychlordane. Biomarkers indicative of changes in kidney function were altered in male rats but not in female rats treated with trans-nonachlor and cisnonachlor. The present study was designed to address the following data gaps based on completed research :
Do trans-nonachlor levels in tissues gradually decline after exposure?
Do oxychlordane levels in tissues gradually increase if trans-nonachlor declines (indicating that transnonachlor is transformed to oxychlordane over time)?

Do differences in total body fat in female versus male rats account for higher levels of trans-nonachlor and 4. What are the levels of trans-nonachlor and oxychlor- dane in kidneys, and are functional changes in male rat kidneys related to tissue residue levels?

This study also offers the opportunity to investigate the relationship between oxychlordane and trans-chlordane chirality and their toxicological properties. When a chiral chemical is synthesized a racemic mixture, or 1: 1 ratio, of enantiomers is formed. However, there is some evidence that relative accumulation in animal tissues may differ for the ( +) and (-) enantiomers of trans-chlordane and oxychlordane. Studies have shown that there are apparent trans-chlordane enantiomers accumulating in tissues of fish from the Baltic, and that tissues from pigs given cis- or trans-chlordane have higher levels of ( + )-oxychlordane (MUiier and Buser 1994). To address questions about the relative accumulation of trans-chlordane and oxychlordane enantiomers, adipose tissues from rats treated with oxychlordane, trans-nonachlor and trans-chlordane will be analyzed for oxychlordane enantiomers. In addition, adipose from rats treated with trans-chlordane will be analyzed for trans-chlordane enantiomer residues. These analyses will provide information on the following: potential changes in enantiomer residue levels in rat adipose tissues over time; potential sex-related differences in enantiomer accumulation in adipose tissues.

The animal phase of this study was initiated in September 2000 and was completed in December 2000. Briefly, groups of male and female Sprague-Dawley rats were exposed to either trans-nonachlor, oxychlordane or trans- chlordane by gavage for 28 consecutive days (Table I). Trans-chlordane, which is a major component of the parent chlordane mixture, was included for comparison to published studies. At the end of the exposure period one-third of each group were necropsied, as indicated in Table 1. Summary of test groups for each necropsy (1 day, 28 days and 56 days after dosing} a Total rats required, including eight quality controls: 204. b Groups will be composed of eight males and eight females, except where designatedc. c Ten control and oxychlordane-treated female rats will be required for the first necropsy because data from these rats will also be used to supplement previous oxychlordane studies. We have previously exposed female rats to 1 and 10 mg·kg·1 oxychlordane.
These rats will be given a full toxicological evaluation, which requires a minimum of 10 rats per sex.

The remaining rats were necropsied 28 and 56 days after the final dose, according to the time line in Figure I. Tissue and data analyses will proceed throughout 200 I . The following endpoints will be measured: liver, kidney and adipose tissue residue levels of trans-nonachlor, oxychlordane or trans-chlordane; oxychlordane and transchlordane enantiomer ratios in tissues from treated rats; total body fat; renal function (clinical biomarkers, organic ion transport in kidney slices); and liver function (clinical biomarkers).

Time line for dosing and necropsies of trans-nonachlor, oxychlordane and transchlordane-treated rats - 28d- - 28d- - No visible lesions were seen at necropsy in any group. There was one death due to oxychlordane toxicity. A female rat was euthanised after her last dose of oxychlordane (2.5 mg·kg-1) but prior to her scheduled necropsy when she lost > I 5 g body weight in a 24-hour period. This is consistent with large weight losses seen in previous studies in female rats receiving I 0 mg·kg-1 oxychlordane. There were no visible lesions at necropsy in the affected rat.

Previous oxychlordane studies indicated that I 0 mg oxychlordane·kg body weight-1.day-1 was toxic to female rats after three consecutive oral doses, but that I mg oxychlordane·kg bw-1-d-1 was not toxic after 28 consecutive oral doses (G. Bondy, unpublished observations). The dose used in this study was 2.5 mg oxychlordane·kg bw-1.d-1 with which there was one fatality (in 30 female rats) after 28 consecutive doses. Taken together, the data indicate that the dose response curve for oxychlordane is steep in rats, with only a small difference between a fatal and a non-toxic dose. Further conclusions based on this study await the completion of tissue and data analyses.

Laurie Chan, Centre for Indigenous Peoples' Nutrition and Environment, Macdonald Campus, McGill University, 21,111 Lakeshore Road, Ste-Anne-de-Bellevue, QC H9X 3V9; Phone: (514) 398-7765; Fax: (514) 398-1020; E-mail: laurie.chan@mcgill.ca Stan Kubow, School of Dietetics and Human Nutrition, McGill University, Ste-Anne-de-Bellevue, QC; Rekha Mehta and Eric Lok, Health Protection Branch, Health Canada, Ottawa, ON This ongoing project is designed to study the possible effects of dietary modulations on mercury toxicity. Mercury accumulates in fish and marine mammals. Therefore, Inuit who consume a traditional diet may be exposed to higher levels of mercury. However, the traditional diet also contains rich sources of beneficial nutrients such as protein, oil, vitamins and minerals. There is some evidence that these nutrients may protect against mercury toxicity. This project will study effects of these nutrients on mercury toxicity by feeding rats diets containing different nutrient compositions. Results will be useful for characterization of the health risk of mercury in the Inuit diet.
There is some evidence that nutrients in the traditional Inuit diet such as protein, oil, vitamins and minerals may protect against mercury (Hg) toxicity.
This project is studying the effects of these nutrients on Hg toxicity by feeding rats diets containing different nutrient compositions.
3. Results from this project are not yet available.
• To study the effects of dietary factors on methylmercury (MeHg) toxicity. l. To study the effects of fish proteins on MeHg kinetics and toxicity.
2. To study the effects of omega~3 fatty acid, particularly fish oil and seal oil on MeHg kinetics and toxicity.

Elevated levels of Hg have been reported in terrestrial, freshwater and marine biota in the Canadian North (Jensen et al. 1997). Ringed seal (Phoca hispida), the most abundant marine mammal species in the Canadian Arctic, is a major component and the major source of Hg in the Inuit traditional diet (Chan et al. 1995). Elevated levels of Hg, i.e. exceeding the Health Canada consumer guideline (for fish flesh) of 0.5 μg·g-1 wet wt, are commonly found in ringed seal meat (Chan 1998). Results of the Broughton Island study in 1 988 showed that the Hg intake levels of 83% of the respondents exceeded the provisional tolerable weekly intake of 5 μg·kg-1-week- 1 (Chan et al. 1997). The Inuit diet also contains high concentrations of selenium and omega-3 fatty acids.

Dietary factors influence the whole-body retention of orally administered MeHg and mercuric Hg. In mice, Landry et al. ( 1979) concluded that milk increased MeHg absorption from the gastro-intestinal tract. This could have resulted from an effect of milk on the enterohepatic circulation and/or de- and re-methylation of Hg in the intestine since the absorption rate of MeHg was close to 100% in all cases. Wheat bran added to semi-synthetic diets decreased, whereas cellulose increased the retention of orally administered MeHg chloride in mice (Rowland 1986). A high-protein, low-fat diet decreased the retention of orally administered MeHg in mice (Rowland 1984). Diets containing fish protein, a good source of both selenium and sulphur amino acids, decreased the toxicity of MeHg in mice compared with diets containing casein (Ohi et al. 1976). ( 1992) found that the whole-body retention was significantly reduced when mice were fed with a diet containing 50% cod liver oil compared with mice fed with 50% coconut oil. However, the relative deposition of Hg was significantly higher in all organs of mice fed a diet containing 20% energy from cod liver oil compared with mice fed a diet containing 20% energy from soya oil.
Two animal feeding experiments have been completed.

Eighteen male Sprague-Dawley rats ( initial body weights: 150 to 170 g) were fed one of three isocaloric, starchbased, semi-purified diets containing 20% wt of either (a) fish protein, (b) whey protein, or (c) casein for 4 weeks before the dosing experiment. MeHg was administered for 14 days by gavage at three dose levels: ( 1) control, (2) 1 mg·kg-1.day-1 or (3) 3 mg·kg-1.day-1• Thirty male rats were fed one of five isocaloric, starchbased, semi-purified diets containing 20% wt of either (a) seal oil, (b) fish oil, (c) DHA oil, (d) soya oil, or (e) lard, for 4 weeks before the dosing experiment. MeHg was administered for 14 days by gavage at three dose levels: (I) control, (2) I mg·kg-1.day-1 or (3) 3 mg·kg-1.day-1• For both Experiments 1 and 2, rats were housed in pairs in plastic cages under conditions meeting the requirements of the Canadian Council for Animal Care. During the course of dosing, the rats remained on the three semipurified diets and the general metabolic indices were monitored. Faeces and urine were collected on Day 0, 6 and 13 for analysis of Hg levels and urinary constituents as markers of kidney damage, repectively.

Animals were sacrificed, necropsied, and parts of liver, kidney and brain tissues were excised and stored at -80 °C until analyzed for Hg levels and various toxicological parameters including gene transcription analysis. Fresh kidney slices were used to determine organic ion transport as an index of MeHg induced nephrotoxicity. Tissues were stored in formalin for histopathological and immunohistochemical assessment.

The following data have been collected and are currently being analyzed: body weights, organ weights, food consumption, serum biochemistry, hematology parameters and various nephrotoxicity related parameters. Hg analysis and the following specific tests for oxidative stress are being conducted:

• in vitro mitochondria superoxide radical generation in brain mitochondria, • plasma and tissue (brain, kidney and liver) lipid peroxide concentrations, • brain, kidney and liver oxidized and reduced glutathione concentrations, and • analysis of the oxidative DNA damage related 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine DNA adduct.

Tissues are being processed for routine histopathology, and immunohistochemical and transcriptional analysis to assess expression of protein products and transcripts of a variety of toxicity and stress related genes.
The analysis is in progress and there are no results to report at this time.

Estimation of Site-Specific Dietary Exposure to Contaminants in Two Inuit Communities Laurie H.M. Chan, Centre for Indigenous Peoples' Nutrition and Environment, Macdonald Campus, McGill University, 21,111 Lakeshore Road, Ste-Anne-de-Bellevue, QC H9X 3V9; Phone: (514) 398-7765; Fax: (514) 398-1020; E-mail: laurie.chan@mcgill.ca Peter Berti, PATH Canada, Ottawa, ON; Eric Loring, Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, Ottawa, ON The Centre for Indigenous Peoples' Nutrition and Environment conducted a dietary survey for l 8 Inuit communities in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut in l 998 to 2000. A preliminary contaminant exposure assessment was conducted using contaminant data from an existing database. A more site-specific exposure assessment was conducted for two communities - Chesterfield Inlet and Igloolik - that had among the highest risks of exposure according to the preliminary estimate. A total of 64 samples of traditional/country food that are either the major contaminant contributors or were missing from the database were collected and their contaminant concentrations were measured. The new estimates for organochlorine intake are lower than the previous estimates. The mean intakes for chlordane and toxaphene are still higher than the provisional tolerable daily intake (PTDI) and the revised 95th centile intake levels exceed the PTDI by about I 0-fold. The revised mean daily heavy metal intake levels are similar to the previous estimate. The revised mean mercury intake is higher than the PTDI in both communities. The intake of chlordane, toxaphene and mercury in these two communities remains a concern.
The organochlorine (OC) intake levels in Chesterfield Inlet and lgloolik are lower than previously estimated.
The intake of chlordane, toxaphene and mercury in these two communities remains a concern .

• To ascertain the results of a preliminary exposure assessment conducted based on the Centre for Indigenous Peoples' Nutrition and Environment (CINE) dietary survey. This is to be achieved by collecting and analyzing food samples from two Inuit communities that have been identified as having among the highest risks of exposure and by conducting a site-specific quantitative estimation of contaminant exposure.
I. To identify two Inuit communities that show the highest risk of contaminant exposure according to a L. Chan preliminary exposure assessment based on the CINE dietary survey.
To collect food samples that are the major contributors to contaminant intake from these two communities.
To analyze the contaminant concentrations (heavy metals and/or organics) in these food samples.
To estimate the contaminant intake in these two communities by combining the food contaminant concentration and the food intake data.
To communicate the risk of exposure to these two communities.
To validate results of the preliminary exposure assessment using results of this detailed study.

CINE has collected dietary information from 18 Inuit communities and has completed a project titled "Assessment of Dietary Benefit:Risk in Inuit Communities" (Kuhnlein et al. 2000). One of the objectives of this project is to define the levels of dietary exposure to contaminants. A typical daily contaminant intake level can be calculated by multiplying the food intake data (g·day-1) by the mean concentration of the food group (μg·g-1). To do that, we have to obtain data for contaminant concentrations in all the food items that have been mentioned in the dietary recalls in each of the 18 communities. It is not possible logistically to collect so many samples or to cover the laboratory expenses. Instead, we have used the contam~ inant data from our database as described in Chan ( 1998). The data are average values of the levels of contaminants in fish and wildlife collected from different regions in northern and Arctic Canada over the last 10 years. However, since the contaminant data used for this estimation are not collected specifically from any of these communities, the generated data are only estimates of potential intake but not actual intake. It is important to estimate the actual intake, particularly in those communities that show potentially high intake levels.

We discussed the details of this study with representatives from all the communities that participated in the dietary study, the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, and the Department of Health and Social Services of the Government of Nunavut. Igloolik and Chesterfield Inlet, two communities with estimated contaminant intakes among the highest, were invited to participate in this study. Local assistants were hired in each of the two communities with help from the Hunters and Trappers Associations. A total of 64 traditional/country food samples that are either the major contaminant contributors or samples for which we did not have data were collected and their contaminant concentrations were measured. Exposure assessment was recalculated using the new information.

Concentrations of the seven major groups of OCs including chlordane (CHL), chlorobenzene (CBZ), DDT, hexachlorocyclohexane (HCH), mirex (MIR), total poly~ chlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) (the sum of 51 congeners), and toxaphene (TOX) in the collected samples are shown in Table 1. Highest concentrations are found in marine mammal blubbers. Concentrations of the four heavy metals (arsenic [As], cadmium [Cd], lead [Pb], mercury [Hg]) and selenium (Se) are shown in Table 2. Walrus blubber and Arctic char had the highest As concentrations. Highest concentrations of Cd and Hg were found in marine mammal livers, and marine mammal muktak are richest in Se.

The revised mean daily intake and the 95th centile intake of OCs are compared to the previous estimate and the provisional tolerable daily intake (PTDI) levels in Table 3. The new estimates are all lower than the previous estimates, particularly for toxaphene. The mean intakes for CHL in Chesterfield Inlet and CHL and TOX in Igloolik are still higher than the PTDI, but the magnitude has decreased from four to 20 times to about two to five times. The previous 95th centile exceeded the PTDI by 1 00 ~fold, however, the revised intake levels exceed the PTDI by about 1 0~fold.

The revised mean daily heavy metal intake levels are very similar to the previous estimates (Table 4) . The revised mean Hg intake has increased in Chesterfield Inlet but the revised Pb intake has decreased in Igloolik. The revised Hg intake is higher than the PTDI in both communities. Effects of Prenatal Exposure to Organochlorines and Mercury on the Immune System of Inuit Infants Eric Dewailly, Public Health Research Unit, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Quebec (CHUQ), (CHUU, 2400 rue d'Estimauville, Beauport, QC GlE 7G9; Phone: (418) 666-7000 (ext 222); Fax: (418) 666-2776; E-mail; Eric.Dewailly@crchul.ulaval.ca Frederic Dallaire, Carole Vezina, Gina Muckle, Public Health Research Unit-CHUQ (CHUU and Laval University, Beauport, QC; Houda Bilrha, Raynald Roy, Rhumatology-lmmunology Research Unit-CHUQ (CHUU, Ste-Foy, QC; Pierre Ayotte, Gaston de Serres, Public Health Research UnitCHUQ (CHUL) and Laval University, Beauport, QC; Jean Philippe Weber, Quebec Toxicology Center-CHUO (CHUU, Ste-Foy, QC; Claire Infante-Rivard, McGill University, Montreal, QC; Joseph Jacobson, Wayne State University, Detroit, Ml; Marthe Belles-lies, Rhumatology-lmmunology Research Unit-CHUQ (CHUU, Ste-Foy, QC This project is nested in the ongoing PCBs and Infant Development Study. The objective is to examine the effects of prenatal and postnatal exposure to organochlorines and mercury on the incidence of infection and immune system parameters during the first year of life. A total of 244 mothers have agreed to participate in the study and 190 infant medical charts should be available for review. Of these, a subgroup of 115 infants were selected for the immunological analysis. So far, 130 charts have been reviewed and biological analyses (cytokines [IL.r 10 and TNF~a] and Hib antibodies) were performed on 60 samples. In preliminary statistical analysis, there seems to be an association between prenatal exposure to polychlorinated biphenyls and incidence of infections. However, only crude analyses were performed and no conclusion can yet be drawn since potential confounders were not considered. Data collection will continue until September 2002 and the project will be completed in March 2003 .

This study investigates possible detrimental effects on the immune system of Inuit infants which may be induced by prenatal and postnatal exposure to persistent environmental contaminants such as organochlorine (OC) compounds and heavy metals.

A total of 190 infant medical charts will be reviewed. Of them, a subgroup of 115 infants were selected for the assessment of immune system functions. So far, 17 l 30 charts have been reviewed and biological analyses were performed on 60 samples.
3. Data collection is still ongoing. Only preliminary statistical analyses have been performed and no definitive results are available yet. The project will be completed in March 2003.
• To examine the effects of prenatal and postnatal exposure to OCs and mercury (Hg) on the immune system of Inuit infants from birth to 12 months of age.
To assess prenatal and postnatal exposure to OCs and Hg.
To measure some immunological parameters (humoral and cellular immunity).

Substantial information concerning the contamination of northern marine food by persistent organic pollutants (POPs) and heavy metals is now available (Barrie et al. 1992, Braune et al. 1999, Bright et al. 1995, Burkow and Kallenborn 2000, Lockhart et al. 1992, Muir et al. 1999, Muir et al. 1992, Thomas et al. 1992). Chemicals such as pesticides (dieldrin, mirex, toxaphene), industrial compounds and by-products of industrial processes (hexachlorobenzene, polychlorinated biphenyls [PCBs], polychlorodibenzo-p-dioxins [PCCDs], polychlorodibenzofurans [PCDFs), as well as heavy metals (inorganic and organic Hg, lead, cadmium), have been emitted throughout the world for years. Many regu latory actions have been taken since the late 1970s to limit their emission but they are still released due to improper storage and ongoing use in certain parts of the world.

Prenatal and postnatal exposures to OCs, in particular dioxin-like compounds, produce a wide variety of toxic effects in animals and humans. Alterations of T-cell subsets, of serum immunoglobulin A (lgA) and IgM concentrations, of delayed-type hypersensibility and of complement activation have all been documented in rodents, primates and human (Chang et al. 1982, Esser and Welzel 1993, Hoffman et al. 1986, Holsapple et al. 1984, Lu and Wu 1985, Neubert et al. 1992, Thomas and Hinsdill 1979, Tryphonas et al. 199 1 a, Tryphonas et al.

1991 b, White et al. 1986). The development of the immune system in utero and during infancy is particularly sensitive to immunotoxic products such as OCs. High exposure during early life could lead to permanent defects of the immune system and thus decrease resistance to infectious agents (Badesha et al. 1995) .

Organic and inorganic Hg possess cytotoxic activities for cellular components of the immune system in several species of rodents. Methylmercury (MeHg), a form of organic Hg, can alter non-specific defense mechanisms, such as the inhibition of natural killer cell activity in rats and mice. It also decreases the expression of certain activation markers of T cells (HLA-Dr, IL-2R) (Moszczynski I 997). Moreover, it has been well demonstrated that MeHg can affect the functions of B cells and therefore reduce the humoral mediated response (Moszczynski 1997). Exposure to inorganic Hg induces allergies and autoimmune problems in hypersensitive individuals (Bagenstose et al. 1999).

The high incidence of infectious diseases (in particular meningitis, broncho-pulmonary and middle ear infections) in infants and children from Nunavik has been known for many years (Dufour 1988, Proulx 1988). Middle ear infections are of special concern since approximately 25% of school age Inuit children suffer some kind of hearing loss (Julien et al. 1987). Because of the immunotoxic effects of OCs and MeHg, particularly after perinatal exposure, we hypothesized that part of the high infection incidence among Inuit infants could be related to the high maternal body burden of these contaminants.

This study is nested in the ongoing PCBs and Infant Development Study and will involve approximately 190 Inuit mothers and their newborns. It investigates possible detrimental effects on the immune system of Inuit infants that may be induced by prenatal and postnatal (breast feeding) exposure to OCs and Immune system function is evaluated using several immunological markers including the level of antibody produced by the infant following Haemopnilus influenza immunization, the level and function of the complement system and its components, and the level of some Th 1 and Th2 cytokines. Vitamin A concentration is also evaluated in the mother and the infant since striking similarities exist between symptoms of high dioxin-like compound exposure and vitamin A deficiency. Finally, infectious episodes are recorded over the first 12 months of life and the possible relationship between recurrent infections and high OC burdens will be analyzed. Results of this research could be used by intervening institutions for the purpose of risk prevention and management, by other researchers and by the public.

The recruitment of participants ended in April 2001. A total of 244 mothers have agreed to participate in the study. Considering potential miscarriages, mortality and withdrawal from the study, we expect to review 190 infant medical charts. A subgroup of 115 infants were selected for the immunological analysis (cytokines, complement and antibody titer) .

Two trips (October 2000 and April 2001) to Puvirnituq, Inukjuaq and Kujjuuarapik were done to coordinate the collection and shipping of biological samples as well as to review the medical charts of the participants. So far, 130 medical charts have been reviewed .
A second fieldworker in Inukjuaq was recruited and trained. She will be helping as well as replacing the other field worker whenever it is needed.
Laboratory analyses have begun. Cytokines (Ilr 10 and TNF-a) and Hib antibodies were analyzed in 60 blood samples.
The construction of the database and the data entry and coding have begun and will continue throughout 2001-2002.

We could only perform crude preliminary analyses on some of the available data. Concerning the immunological analysis, only IL.r 1 0 and Hib results for infants at 6 months were available in the database. Table I shows the mean levels of IL.r I O concentration and Hib titer at 6 months of age according to the maternal blood level of the PCB congener 153 (the most frequent) on a lipid basis. The maternal PCB level was dichotomized; the mothers with PCB levels below the median were put in the category "low PCB exposure" and the ones with concentrations above the median were put in the category "high PCB exposure." There was no difference for the mean IL.r I 0 concentration. Hib titers were higher in the exposed group.

Eighty-nine infant medical charts that have been reviewed were partially summarized in the database. Table 2 shows the mean number of reported infectious disease episodes for the first year of life according to the prenatal PCB exposure (maternal PCB congener 153 on a lipid basis). With the exception of otitis and tonsillitis, the mean number of infections was higher in the exposed group.

We then computed the relative risk of the various infection types during the first year of life according to the prenatal PCB exposure (Table 3). Again, with the exception of otitis and tonsillitis, the risk of experiencing frequent infectious episodes was higher in the exposed group. The association between PCB exposure and the risk of having at least one episode of pneumonia was significant (p = 0.025).

The results presented in this synopsis of research are preliminary. Only crude associations are presented and we did not yet adjust for potential confounding factors. We shall be cautious when interpreting the results since many factors can influence the immune system. Our hypothesis is that prenatal PCB exposure impairs the development of the immune system. This impairment should be reflected by a weaker production of antibodies following the vaccination (and thus a lower titer in the infants blood). The higher Hib titer in the high PCBexposure group is puzzling, but this association can be due to many factors. The number of vaccine shots received, the age of the baby, and the period between the last shot and the blood sampling are critical factors to control for before speculating on the significance of this association.

The infants in the high PCB-exposure group tend to experience more infectious episodes in the first year of life compared to the ones in the low PCB-exposure group. It will be interesting to investigate the implication of breast-feeding, vitamin A status and omega-3 levels in this association.

It is too early to draw any conclusions on the effects of PCBs on the immune system. Nevertheless, there seems to be a crude association with prenatal PCB exposure and the incidence of infections. It is not known whether this association is due to the PCB exposure itself or to covariables such as nutrition and lifestyle. Exhaustive statistical analysis (in which many of the potential confounders will be evaluated) will begin in September 200 1.

By September 2001 , all the infants will be born and they will all be at least one-year old in September 2002. The last trip for the collection of the biological samples and the review the medical charts is planned for October 2002.

The construction of the final database began in March 200 I . Data entry should be complete by December 2002. The final data analysis, the writing of the report and of the publications will take place between January 2003 and March 2003 . The project will be completed in March 2003 .

Mercury in Salluit: Effects of Mercury on Oxidative Status and Sensorimotor Functions Eric Dewailly, Public Health Research Unit, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Quebec (CHUO), (CHUL), 2400 rue d'Estimauville, Beauport, QC GlE 7G9; Phone: (418) 666-7000; Fax: (418) 666-2776; E-mail: eric.dewailly@crchul.ulaval.ca Anne Beuter, Cognitive Neuroscience Centre, University of Quebec at Montreal, Montreal, QC; Pierre Ayotte and Suzanne Bruneau, Public Health Research Unit-CHUO (CHUL), Beauport, QC; Marc-Edouard Mirault, Health and Environment Research Unit-CHUO (CHUL); Minnie Grey, Nunavik Nutrition and Health Committee, Kuujjuaq, QC; Jean-Philippe Weber, Quebec Toxicology Centre, Quebec National Institute of Public Health, Ste-Foy, QC Among all contaminants present in different aquatic ecosystems in Canada, methylmercury is a major source of concern for public health. Some studies (Grandjean et al. 1994) suggest that methylmercury toxicity can be detected at levels far below the lowest observed adverse effect level proposed by the World Health Organization ( I Oto I 5 ppm in maternal hair). Thus, it seems important to determine with precision the minimal dose at which oxidative stress and neurotoxic effects can be identified. The main goal of this project is to investigate the effects of mercury on sensorimotor functions and on markers of oxidative stress in the population of Salluit, Nunavik (northern Quebec). A total of 11 3 individuals were tested for neuromotor performances and also agreed to give a sample of urine, blood and hair for analysis of mercury and persistent organic pollutants. Results are not available at this time.
This study aims at studying subtle effects mercury (Hg) can have on brain functions.
2. Measurements done in the blood will tell us more about early signs of Hg toxicity, particularly concerning cardiovascular disease.
To evaluate the oxidative status of Sallumiut exposed to Hg.
To quantify the effects of Hg on sensorimotor functions with highly sensitive measures.

In 1998- 1999, at the request of the Municipal Council of Salluit, Hg exposure of 140 Salluit, Quebec residents was E. Dewailly reassessed. Health Canada had tested residents of this community for Hg in the late l 970s and they were tested again in l 992 during the Sante Quebec Health survey. Results showed that hair Hg concentrations decreased from the end of the l 970s to l 999. However, further analysis revealed that only levels measured in 1978 were higher than those measured in 1999. Beluga harvest was particularly abundant in l 977 and returned to normal in l 978. That year ( l 977) was also exceptional for the harvest of other species such as lake trout and seal. This could explain why high Hg concentrations were found in the blood of residents who provided samples of blood in the spring of l 978. Mercury is mainly present as methylmercury (MeHg) in fish and marine mammals and their consumption constitutes an important source of exposure especially in sustenance population such as the Inuit (Dewailly et al. 2001) . Results of a food survey carried out in the community of Salluit in 1979 indicated that the main~ source of Hg exposure was the consumption of beluga, lake trout and seal liver (Wheatley and Wheatley 1981 ).

According to recommendations formulated by the World Health Organization, hair Hg concentrations should not exceed 50 ppm in adults and l 5 ppm in pregnant women (World Health Organization 1 990). The highest concentration noted in 1999 was 30 ppm and no women of childbearing age exhibited concentrations higher than 1 5 ppm (maximum = 14 ppm) .

In order to assess oxidative damage due to MeHg exposure, glutathione peroxidase and glutathione reductase activities were also measured in blood samples and were compared to activities measured in blood of healthy donors from Quebec City. Interestingly, data indicated a trend toward higher antioxidant activities in the Sallumiut group. Glutathione determinations were performed as well, but abnormally low values were obtained likely due to glutathione instability during blood processing or shipment.

Methylmercury is a highly toxic environmental neurotoxin that can cause irreparable damage to the central nervous system (Choi I 989, Clarkson 1993, Clarkson 1997). Chronic exposure to MeHg may cause a wide variety of neurological impairments including prickling, paresthesia, impaired peripheral vision, impaired hearing, impaired taste and smell, slurred speech, paraplegia, muscle weakness, irritability, memory loss, depression, sleeping difficulties, cerebella ataxia, and tremors (Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry I 994). Other studies have suggested that low level exposure to MeHg was associated with changes in sensorimotor functions (Beuter and de Geoffroy l 996, Beuter et al.

Although the underlying biochemical and molecular mechanisms that lead to impaired cell function and nerve cell degeneration are not well understood, there is abundant evidence supporting the hypothesis that a major mechanism of MeHg neurotoxicity involves an oxidative stress (Sarafian and Verity l 99 l, Yee and Choi l 996). Mercury increases production of reactive oxygen species via deregulation of mitochondrial electron transport as well as through glutathione depletion (Lund et al. The oxidative stress hypothesis is clearly supported by the finding that MeHg neurotoxicity can be inhibited by various antioxidants including selenium (Se) (Park et al. l 996) and N-acetyl-L-cysteine, a precursor of glutathione (Ornaghi et al.

In collaboration with the Municipal Council of Salluit, a new study was set up for 2000-200 l to evaluate the oxidative status of Sallumiut exposed to Hg and to quantify the effects of Hg on sensorimotor functions using highly sensitive measures.

From April to December 2Q00, the activities related to this research project centered on the development of protocols for blood sampling and manipulation. Optimal conditions of storage, shipping and processing of collected samples were determined to avoid the degradation of gluthatione. Specific testing conditions were also determined for glutathione peroxidase and glutathione reductase activity measurements in whole blood and plasma. Finally, a field nurse, previously hired and trained, prepared all material needed for sample collection, and worked on the elaboration of the consent form and a questionnaire documenting current health status, lifestyle and past medical history.

Researchers from the Cognitive Neuroscience Centre, Movement Disorders Laboratory, have developed, during the last years, neuromotor tests based on sophisticated technologies (laser, infrared, optical encoder system, CCD sensors, etc.). A Ph.D. student was trained to administer these tests to the Salluit participants. All material needed for neuromotor tests was also prepared and tested. A document was prepared to demonstrate and explain in a simple way the assessment to be administered to participants.
Fieldwork was carried out in Salluit from February 5 to March 31 , 2001 . A total of l 2 5 Salluit residents signed the consent form and participated in the present study.
Of these, 85 (68%) participants had taken part in the 1999 study on temporal trends; the others (n = 40) were recruited from the Salluit population list.

Three local research assistants were hired and trained to assist the field workers. Their tasks included communication to the local population, translation and assisting the field workers in their respective tasks (blood and hair sampling, administering the questionnaire, conducting neuromotor tests). To recruit participants, the first step was to meet with the local health committee and prepare a radio show to inform the population about the research project and spark their interest. Furthermore, posters informing the population about the study, public meetings and personal invitation letters were also used as recruiting tools.

Data collection was performed in four steps. During the initial meeting between each participant and field workers and their assistants, participants were informed about the objectives of the previous and present research, signed a consent form, provided a hair sample, and were interviewed to fill in the questionnaire. For participants of the 1999 study, individual Hg results in biological samples were presented again and discussed if needed.

2) Participants were then asked to come back the next morning for urine and blood sampling. 3) Participants returned for another appointment for the neuromotor testing measures of tremors, postural sway, simple and multiple reaction time tasks, eye-hand coordination in different pointing tasks, rapid alternating movements and rhythmic hand movements. The total duration of the tests was about 90 minutes. 4) The nurse reviewed medical files to obtain more information on medical history and actual medication.

To insure proper conservation of blood samples during the research project, 25 to 50 kg of dry ice was sent to Salluit once a week. Samples were sent to the Quebec Toxicology Laboratory and to Dr. M.-E. Mirault's laboratory for analysis.

Hg and Se were measured in blood and hair. Blood and air samples were respectively used to assess short- and long-term exposure to Hg. Blood and hair Hg analyses were performed by cold vapour atomic absorption after nitric acid digestion. Blood Se analysis was carried out by graphite furnace atomic absorption after nitric acid digestion. Because of potential confounding effects on sensorimotor endpoints, PCBs and pesticides were measured in plasma samples using high resolution gas chromatography.

Biochemical assessment of the antioxidant status included glutathione and glutathione peroxidase activity levels in blood, and plasmatic levels of oxidized and reduced coenzyme O 10, vitamin C and glutathione, measured by HPLC-coupled electrochemical detection. The oxidized/reduced CoO 10 ratio will provide a redox index, which is used to assess possible oxidative stress effects associated with Hg exposure. Measurements of urinary F2-isoprostanes, which result from in vivo lipid peroxidation, will provide an additional index of oxidative stress. The formation of F2-isoprostanes is currently recognized as the most sensitive and reliable noninvasive assay of oxidative stress in vivo. Since we found that quantification of F2-isoprostanes by commercially available ELISA kits was not reliable, we are currently setting up measurements of iPGF2a-III and iPGF2a-VI by HPLC/ESI/MS/MS, in collaboration with Dr. P. Borgeat. The lipids and lipoproteins profiles are measured by micro-ultracentrifugation, and the fatty acid profiles by gas chromatography. The cholesterol and apolipoprotein B analyses are performed at the Centre de recherche des maladies lipidiques (CHUL-CHUO) .
The measurements are still being processed; therefore, no results are available at this time. Table 1 shows the number of participants who completed the various tests according to gender.

Sociodemographic Factors Influencing Nutrition and Contaminant Exposure in Nunavik Eric Dewailly, Public Health Research Unit, Laval University Medical Research Centre, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Quebec (CHUQ), 2400 rue d'Estimauville Beauport, QC GlE 7G9; Phone: (418) 666-7000 (ext 222); Fax: (418) 666-2776; E-mail: eric.dewailly@crchul.ulaval.ca Carole Blanchet, Suzanne Gingras, Christopher Furgal and Suzanne Bruneau, Public Health Research Unit-CHUQ, Beauport, QC This study examined contaminant and nutrient intake through traditional/country foods among the Inuit population of Nunavik according to various sociodemographic factors. Results showed that the median traditional/ country food intake was higher among Inuit 40 years of age and older than among Inuit 18 to 39 years old. Mean age adjusted traditional/country food intake decreased as the level of formal education increased. Inuit living in couples appeared to have a higher level of traditional/ country food intake than single, divorced or widowed Inuit. Results also showed that the median contaminant intake increased with age and the geometric mean age adjusted contaminant intake was higher among Inuit receiving less formal education, among those living in couples and among Inuit living in households of six or more persons. For several nutrients, mean age adjusted intake was higher among residents living in Ungava coast communities as compared with residents of Hudson coast communities. Results showed that with an increase in the level of formal education completed by an individual, the more their diet was comprised of some nutrients that are commonly deficient in Inuit diets. Similar nutrient intakes were observed among Inuit living in couples, notably among one-family households. Inuit who did not have a job had a lower mean intake of nutrients as compared to Inuit having one or more jobs. These results may be helpful in identifying which segments of the population (as defined by some traditional sociodemographic variables) are "at risk" for certain contaminant exposures and nutrient deficiencies, as related to traditional/country food consumption. This information will help public health authorities in Nunavik to target and design effective food protection and promotion strategies for the consumption of traditional/country foods for specific groups within the Nunavik population.

Some sociodemographic characteristics (age, education, employment, marital status, etc.) are similar among Nunavimmiut with a higher level of traditional/ country food consumption, higher contaminant E. Dewailly exposures, and more frequently having certain nutritional deficiencies.
Differences in contaminant and nutrient intake can be related to such things as availability of and access to certain traditional/country food species and market food items.

The identification of the relationships between sociodemographic factors and traditional/country food consumption, nutrient intake and contaminant exposure can be used by public health authorities to identify specific "at risk" groups in Nunavik and better understand the potential factors related to their levels of contaminant exposure and nutritional status.
The main objective of this research project was to examine sociodemographic factors affecting contaminant exposure and nutritional status of Inuit in Nunavik. The specific objectives were to:
1. Examine traditional/country food, contaminant and nutrient intake among the Inuit in the context of their socio-economic status and reported status of individual food availability.
2. Examine the relationships among the structure of Inuit households and the intake of traditional/country foods, contaminants and nutrients.

3. Establish the link between contaminant intake, the quantity, quality and source of Inuit food consumed and a number of sociodemographic factors, considering the potential interactive effect of age on some factors.

Traditional/country foods are the primary source of Inuit exposure to most persistent environmental contaminants. Over the past decade, various studies and programs in Nunavik have been conducted to reduce contaminant intake while still maintaining nutritional benefits in the diet (e.g. Dewaillyetal. 1989, 199 1, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1996, Blanchet et al. 2000). To document and protect the dietary benefits of a traditional Inuit diet, while considering the health risks associated with the presence of contaminants in these foods, dietary surveys have been conducted among various Inuit populations to examine the quality and the quantity of traditional/country foods consumed. In most dietary studies, food intakes are only estimated by age and gender and very few studies verify the relationships between other sociodemographic factors and traditional/country food consumption . For health officials to more accurately identify groups within the population potentially "at risk" for contaminant exposure and nutritional deficiencies, and to better understand the potential factors attributed to these dietrelated circumstances, a more thorough investigation of the relationships between traditional sociodemographic variables, traditional/country food consumption, and consequent contaminant and nutrient intake is required. This data would then be used to more accurately develop and orient health protection and promotion strategies related to these issues. The Sante Quebec Nutrition Survey database is a potential source for this type of information and analysis since food intake and sociodemographic data are readily available and representative of the entire region of Nunavik (Sante Quebec 1995).

Activities in 2000-2001 consisted of a detailed analysis of the existing data on food intake among the Inuit of Nunavik collected in 1992 during the Sante Quebec Health Survey (Sante Quebec 1994, 1995) with an extension of our analysis to contaminant intakes by using contaminant databases previously developed at the Public Health Research Unit-CHUL. The target population of the Sante Quebec Health Survey was comprised of all permanent residents of private households living within the borders of Nunavik, excluding households consisting of only nonInuit people and people not related to any Inuit and institutionalized individuals. Food consumption data was obtained using a 24-hour dietary recall administered during the Sante Quebec Health Survey. The 24-hour recall was completed by 433 Inuit ranging from 18 to 74 years of age (197 men and 236 women). Accompanied by an Inuit interpreter, nurses went to respondents' homes and conducted dietary interviews to obtain a detailed and precise description of foods consumed in the previous 24 hours (Sante Quebec 1995). Food contaminant data was drawn from the database elaborated in 1994-1996 through work conducted for the project Health Risk Assessment and Elaboration of Public Health Advice Concerning Contaminants in Nunavik, supported by the Northern Contaminants Program (Dewailly et al. 1996).

The following contaminants were included in the present study analyses: lead, mercury, p,p'-DDE and PCB as expressed as Aroclor 1254: 1260 ( 1: 1 ). Nutrient data were drawn from the Canadian Nutrient Data File (Health Canada 1991), and the following nutrients were included in this study: energy, protein, lipid, carbohydrate, vitamins A, C and D, carotene, folic acid, dietary fibre, iron, calcium, magnesium, and the sum of eicosapentanoic acid (EPA) and of docosahexanoic acid (DHA). The following sociodemographic variables were obtained from the Sante Quebec database (Sante Quebec 1994) were also included in the analyses: sex; age; sector of residence (sector A corresponding to sectors llI and IV of the collective agreement and are characterized as communities having greater ease of access to the south, i.e. greater number of regular flights to the regional centre and south, and sector B corresponding to sector V of the collective agreement and being characterized as communities having less ease of access to the south [Collective Agreement 1989- 199 1 ]); coastal region (Ungava and Hudson coasts); level of forma l education completed; occupation; type of work; number of jobs; marital status; number of persons per household; and structure of households (family or non-family household, multiple fami ly or one-family household, single-parent family or couple). Contaminant intake was calculated by multiplying the daily traditional/ country food intake in grams by the corresponding concentration of the contaminant in specific food items. Median intake and geometric mean age adjusted intake of traditional/country foods, nutrients and contaminants were calculated according to sociodemographic variables and the structure of households. For statistical comparisons of medians between categories, the Kruskal-Wallis test was used. Geometric age adjusted means were calculated using analysis of covariance. Statistical analyses were conducted with the Statistical Analysis System (SAS) software and statistical significance was set at = 0.05 (Statistical Analysis System Institute Inc. 1996). The partial non-response, which consists of the non-response on each question or variable, could have resulted in some biased estimates in the present study and thus caution should be used in interpreting the results.

On the day before the survey, 73% of the Inuit population reported having eaten traditional/country foods. Among the consumers, the median intake of traditional/country foods was 209 .0 The most popular traditional/country foods consumed during this day were (in decreasing order): caribou, Arctic char, muktuk, seal meat, seal fat and lake whitefish. When estimating the traditional/country food consumption for the Inuit population as a whole, a median intake of 140.0 g was obtained. The median intake of traditional/country foods was significantly higher among Inuit 40 years of age and over than among Inuit between 18 to 39 years of age (Table 1 ). Mean age adjusted traditional/country food intake did not vary significantly according to sex, sector of residence or coastal region of residence. However, mean intake of traditional/country food among Inuit with a secondary school education was significantly lower than Inuit completing less formal education. Traditional/country food intake did not vary significantly according to individuals' occupation, the type of work they did or the number of jobs they held. However, traditional/country food intake appeared to be related to marital status, with Inuit who were divorced, separated or widowed showing the lowest mean intake of traditional/country foods. Traditional/country food consumption did not vary significantly according to the number of persons per household and the structure of households.

As previously mentioned, contaminant intake was based on the traditional/country food intake of Inuit participants the day before the interview (a total of 24 hours) and not on other days. On the day before the survey, the median contaminant intake among Inuit 40 years of age and over was significantly higher than that among Inuit between 18 to 39 years of age (data not shown) . The geometric age adjusted mean contaminant intake did not vary significantly according to sex or coastal region of residence. However, mean PCB, p,p'-DDE, mercury and lead intake was higher among Inuit in sector B (those communities having less regular access to the south) than Inuit in sector A (those communities having greater access to the south). With the exception of p,p'-DDE intake, which was not related to the level of education, mean age adjusted PCB, mercury and lead intake was significantly higher among Inuit with a lower level of formal education as compared to Inuit having completed secondary school. The mean contaminant intake did not vary significantly according to occupation, type of work or the number of jobs an individual held. However, mean age adjusted intake of p,p'-DDE and mercury was significantly higher among Inuit who were married or declared having a common-law spouse than among single, divorced or widowed Inuit. Finally, contaminant intake did not vary according to the structure of households (e.g. single parent, family, multiple family) .

Median intake of carbohydrates, vitamins A and C, carotene, dietary fibre and calcium was significantly lower among Inuit 40 years of age and over than among Inuit between 18 to 39 years (data not shown). Age adjusted geometric mean intake of energy, protein, lipid, carbohydrate, folic acid, iron, calcium and magnesium was significantly higher among men than women.
