Comparison of nutrient intake with recommended nutrient intake Median intake of protein, vitamins A and C, folic acid, iron, calcium and magnesium were compared with daily recommended nutrient intake (RN!) levels based on Health Canada's nutrition recommendations (Health Canada I 990). Protein intake exceeded the RN! regardless of sociodemographic factors. In contrast, vitamin A intake fell below the RN! Similarly, vitamin C and folic acid intake also did not meet the RN! for any sociodemographic variables. With respect to minerals, median iron intake appeared to meet the RN! regardless of the sociodemographic factor while calcium and magnesium intake was deemed insufficient (did not meet RN!) for Inuit in all categories.

Among the Inuit who answered the question concerning the lack of food in their house during the month prior to the survey (n = 210), 24% declared that they were lacking food or did not have enough to eat during this period.

However, the comparisons presented here should be approached with caution due to the small sample sizes in each category. The reporting of a lack of food did not vary according to sex, age or sector of residence. However, a greater proportion of Inuit living in Hudson coast communities reported having lacked food as compared with Inuit residing in Ungava coast communities. The lack of food did not vary according to the reported level of education. A greater proportion of Inuit who declared housework as their occupation appeared to have lacked food in the month prior to the survey. This lack of food was not related to the type of work but Inuit who reported having no job during the year before the survey more frequently declared having lacked food the previous month as compared to Inuit who had one or more jobs. The lack of food did not vary according to the number of people living in a household, however a greater proportion of separated, divorced or widowed Inuit stated having lacked food during the month prior to the survey. Further, this lack of food did not vary according to the structure of households. When verifying nutrient intake, taking into consideration food availability, the median intake of protein, carbohydrate, carotene, vitamin C, folic acid, dietary fibre and magnesium appeared to be lower among Inuit lacking food as compared with Inuit who had enough food in the month prior to the survey; this difference was only statistically significant for dietary fibre and magnesium. Contaminant intake did not vary significantly according to the reported availability of food .

This study has identified some sociodemographic factors which may influence Inuit traditional/country food consumption. Traditional/country foods are the primary source of exposure to environmental contaminants for Inuit and also provide several nutrients to the Inuit diet. Therefore, the sociodemographic factors identified in this study also may indirectly influence individual contaminant exposure and nutrient intake. In this study, we used a 24-hour dietary recall to verify the statistical relationships between traditional/country food, contaminant and nutrient intake, and sociodemographic factors. The value of the 24-hour dietary recall method in assessing the intake of groups is well established (Willett 1998). It can provide a fair estimate of a population 's average intake. However, 24-hour dietary recalls are rarely representative of long-term intake and do not allow the identification of the proportion of individuals "at risk" for contaminant exposure and nutrient deficiencies. Hence, results obtained here do not permit us to infer a causeeffect relationship between sociodemographic factors and contaminant exposure or nutrient deficiencies.

The present study shows that although traditional/country foods are of the utmost importance for Inuit, more traditional/country foods were consumed by older than younger Inuit adults. Results from the Sante Quebec survey ( 1995) indicated that traditional/country foods contributed more to the Inuit diet among older aged individuals than among younger Inuit, whereas market foods contributed more to the diet of younger Inuit. Kuhnlein ( 1994) made similar observations among Baffin Inuit women and Dene/Metis women. In the Keewatin Health Survey, Moffat and Young ( 1994) found that food consumption patterns were changing among the Inuit population in that region. Although most Inuit of the Keewatin region consumed considerable amounts of traditional/country foods, young people appeared to depend more heavily on market foods. Among Inuit of Aklavik, Northwest Territories, Wein and Freeman ( 1992) reported that children liked traditional/country foods just as much as adults, however, children rated most market foods higher in preference than adults, likely reflecting the greater availability of market foods in recent years.

Our results show that on the day prior to the survey, no geographical differences in traditional/country food consumption existed in Nunavik. However, data from the food frequency questionnaire revealed that daily traditional/country food intake of Inuit women, on an annual basis, was significantly higher among women residing in Hudson coast communities as compared with women living in Ungava coast communities. Results of Sante Quebec survey ( 1995) also revealed that residents along the Hudson coast seem to depend more on traditional/country foods than on market foods. Hence, we can conclude that traditional/country food consumption (on an annual basis) may be higher among residents in Hudson coast than in Ungava coast communities. This reflects the fact that Ungava coast communities (especially in Kuujjuaq which is the administrative capital of Nunavik) are better supplied in market foods than their Hudson coast neighbours, probably because this area was exposed earlier and more rapidly to southern Quebec influence. Similar differences in traditional/country food consumption according to the degree of urbanization of Inuit communities is reported by others (Schaefer and Steckle 1980, Kuhnlein 1992, Wein 1995, Egeland et al. 1998, Pars et al. According to Kuhnlein ( 1992), the use of traditional/ country foods in the North depends on the remoteness of the community from urban centres among other things. The variation in traditional food consumption according to region may be also attributed to the territorial availability of wildlife species. Effectively, the variation in abundance and availability of different species regionally, seasonally, and from year to year are natural sources of variation in traditional/country food consumption (Van Oostdam et al. 1999).

( 1992) found that the level of formal education was negatively related to the consumption of traditional/country foods. It was suggested that increased formal education and employment by Inuit can limit, but not necessarily eliminate, involvement in harvesting activities and therefore consumption of traditional/country foods (Van Oostdam et al. In our study, the mean age adjusted traditional/country food intake was significantly lower among Inuit reporting a higher level of formal education . Wage employment and household income also appear to have an influence on traditional/country food consumption (Chabot 1998, Rasmussen 1998, Lawn et al. 1998, Kuhnlein 1995). However, our results did not show significant differences in traditional/country food intake for variables relating to working status and occupation. Moreover, the traditional/country food consumption was not analyzed according to the income in this study since 5 2% of Inuit respondents did not answer the question measuring income in the Sante Quebec survey. Thus we can not reject the possibility that traditional/country food consumption may be related to individual income among Nunavimmiut.

Traditional/country food consumption did appear to be related to marital status in this study. The analyses showed that Inuit living in couples were more likely to consume traditional/country foods, possibly suggesting that single, separated or widowed Inuit may have less access to traditional food resources or the resources to attain these foods (equipment, etc.). Recently, Duhaime et al. (200 I) reported that the presence of a male as the head of a household and, to a lesser extent, access to a wage income raised the proportion of traditional/country foods in the total diet among Nunavik women. ( 1991 , l 988) also reported that the availability of traditional/ country foods depended greatly upon having a hunter in the family who was equipped with adequate resources (including means of transportation) and skills. A recent study conducted among Nunavik women of childbearing age revealed that frequent fish eaters were likely to be less educated, to share their house with more adults, and to live in more crowded conditions (Muckle et al. 200 l ). The authors attributed these associations to the fact that fish, which is usually caught by a family member and is available at no cost in a community freezer, is less expensive than many market foods. Our study did not reveal significant differences for traditional/country food consumption according to the structure of Inuit households. It is possible that the low number of individuals in some categories may have hidden these relationships or they simply did not exist among this data set. However, 31 it appeared that more male respondents than female respondents lived as a couple and, among single-parent families, 80% of women were at the head of the family.

This study permitted the examination of contaminants intake according to various sociodemographic factors among the Inuit population of Nunavik. However, as mentioned above, results do not permit us to establish causal relationships even though significant statistical associations were observed between the study variables. The combined results from several studies are needed to support causal relationships between such factors as sociodemographic elements and contaminant exposures. In this study, the main differences in contaminant intake observed according to sociodemographic factors can be explained by the quantity and items of traditional/country food consumed on the day before the survey. These factors depend on the availability and accessibility of traditional/country foods at this time, and the concentration of contaminants in specific traditional/country food items, which vary greatly between species. Hence, our results showed that contaminant intake was higher among older Inuit, probably reflecting their higher level of traditional/country food consumption when compared to younger individuals.

Results also showed that contaminant intake was higher among Inuit living in more isolated villages (referred to as sector B by Sante Quebec ( l 994)) than in villages with greater ease of access to the south or the regional centre (referred to as sector A in Sante Quebec ( 1994)), even though traditional/country food intake did not vary significantly according to sectors of residence. This difference may be explained by the source of contaminants consumed. Additional analyses showed that on the day before the survey, Inuit living in sector B communities had eaten a greater amount of marine mammal meat and blubber, which generally contain higher concentrations of contaminants than terrestrial meat or fish, than Inuit living in sector A communities. Our results showed that the daily mean intake of PCB, mercury and lead was higher among Inuit with a lower level of formal education, probably reflecting their higher overall consumption of traditional/country foods. Additionally, Inuit who reported having no formal education appeared to consume more caribou previous to the survey whereas Inuit with an elementary level education appeared to consume more fish. Inuit living in couples showed higher p,p'-DDE and mercury intake than divorced/separated, widowed or single Inuit. This may be explained by a higher marine mammal intake among these individuals. While total traditional/country food intake did not vary significantly according to the number of persons per household, the mean intake of PCB, p,p'-DDE and lead was significantly higher in households of 6 persons or more. This relationship can be explained by further analyses conducted in this study which showed that the consumption of marine mammals among Inuit living in households of 6 persons or more was higher than in households with fewer individuals.

Differences in nutrient intake according to sociodemographic factors observed here may be explained by such things as the high price and the lack of availability of some food items (such as fruits and vegetables), the low income of some Inuit households, the general decrease in traditional/country food consumption among some segments of the population and the lack of general nutritional education in the population. Additionally, fear of contaminants may play a role in Inuit food choice behaviour (Dewailly et al. l 994); the potential influence of this information on individual choice is currently being studied (Furgal et al. Moreover, our results on food availability show that a greater proportion of Inuit in Hudson coast communities, jobless Inuit and separated/divorced or widowed Inuit declared having lacked food in their house during the month prior to the survey. ( l 998) indicated that the affordability of the Inuit diet is dependent on many factors including food prices, income, consumer choices and food availability. For l 993, the cost of food for a family of four represented as much as 83% and 90% of after-shelter family incomes in Kuujjuaq and Salluit, respectively (Lawn and Langner l 994a) . In the smaller, most northern Nunavik communities, food prices are higher and there are fewer people with full-time wage employment (Hodgins 1997). Hence, it follows that food security is a serious problem for some families, especially those on social assistance and those with a low family income (Lawn and Langner 1994b). Lawn and Langner ( 1994b) indicated that substitution of traditional/country foods by market foods such as prepared food items, is easier (less labour intensive), since market foods require less preparation, while Morrison et al. ( l 995) reported on the poor nutrient quality of many market food items consumed among some northern populations. Hence, the substitution of traditional/country foods, which are excellent sources of several key nutrients, by market foods is not always desirable, especially when the lower nutritional value of some market food substitutes are considered. We can argue that there is a need to educate Inuit populations about wise market food choices. However, despite the fact that higher nutrient intake has been observed among some sociodemographic Inuit groups, intake of vitamins A and C, folic acid, calcium and magnesium was insufficient for all sociodemographic E. Dewailly groups in this study when compared with the recommended nutrient intakes for Canada. These findings are consistent with other studies conducted among Inuit populations (Kuhnlein et al. 1 996, Lawn and Langner 1994a, Nobmann et al. 1992, Wein 1986). These nutritional deficiencies could be associated with insufficient consumption of dairy products, fruits, vegetables and whole-grain cereal products and also with a decrease in traditional/country food consumption. In the past, Inuit appear to have succeeded in avoiding nutritional deficiencies by eating all animal parts as well as several plant species and berries. ( 1995) indicates that in a transition towards the use of more market foods in northern contemporary diets, the nutritional value of diets has declined because less animal foods are being consumed and vitamin and mineral intakes are not being augmented by frequent consumption of vegetables, fruits and dairy products. We believe this argument to be applicable to our observations in Nunavik.

This study shows that sociodemographic factors such as age, sector of residence, level of education, work occupation, marital status and the household structure (especially in the case of nutrients) may be related to traditional/country food, contaminant and nutrient intake among the Inuit population of Nunavik. It is expected that the results of the present study will help public health authorities in Nunavik, such as the Nunavik Nutrition and Health Committee and the Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services, to target subgroups of the population more likely to be exposed to environmental contaminants or nutritional deficiencies, in order to design more effective food protection and promotion strategies dealing with Inuit traditional/country food consumption.

The promotion of safe food habits among the Inuit population presents several challenges. First, traditional/ country food consumption must be maintained or increased because it has given Inuit several advantages such as social well-being, cultural identity, economic value and food security. Moreover, the consumption of marine traditional/country foods, which are rich in n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, is believed to protect Inuit against cardiovascular diseases, a major cause of mortality in industrialized countries. The n-3 fatty acids are also increasingly recognized as having a beneficial effect upon visual acuity and contributing to increased birth weight. Similarly, the elevated selenium content in muktuk may reduce the potential risk of mercury poisoning among consumers. Second, according to our results, the distribution and access to local traditional/country food supplies could require attention, particularly among some specific groups of individuals such as separated/ divorced or widowed Inuit, which appeared to eat less traditional/country food, to lack food in their household at certain times of the year and to have very low intake of some important nutrients. Third, the consumption of healthy market foods, particularly good sources of vitamin A and C, folic acid, calcium and magnesium, should be promoted. Obtaining these foods would be easier if some market foods are made more available and accessible and promoted through effective nutritional education programs. Finally, the control of the quality of traditional/country foods with respect to contaminant levels should be maintained through regular monitoring, and public health dietary recommendations aimed at reducing exposure to these chemicals should ensure that major nutritional, social and cultural benefits related to traditional/country foods are maintained.

Spatial and Temporal Trends of PCB, PCDD and PCDF Concentrations in Human Milk from Arctic Canada Eric Dewailly, Public Health Research Unit, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Quebec (CHUQ), (CHUU, 2400 rue d'Estimauville, Beauport, QC Gl E 4G2; Phone: (418) 666-7000 (ext 222); Fax: (418) 666-2776; E-mail: Eric.Dewailly@crchul.ulaval.ca Daria Pereg and Gina Muckle, Public Health Research Unit-CHUQ (CHUU, Beauport, QC; Sylvie Dodin, Endocrinologie-reproduction-CHUQ, Centre de Recherche H6pital Saint-Frangois D'Assise, Quebec QC; Pierre Ayotte, Public Health Research Unit-CHUQ (CHUU, Beauport, QC; Brian Fowler and Coreen Hamilton, Axys Analytical Services Ltd., Sidney, BC Organochlorines are persistent food chain contaminants to which the Inuit of Nunavik (northern Quebec) are exposed through their traditional diet. The first objective of this study was to determine the current breast milk concentrations of dioxin-like polychlorinated biphenyls, polychlordibenzo-p-dioxins and polychlorodibenzofurans in this population, and compare these data with those obtained in a breast-milk survey carried out in 1990. Our results show a statistically significant 75% decrease in concentrations of dioxin-like compounds in breast milk during the last decade. This decline is consistent with results from other studies carried out worldwide, but seems to be of greater magnitude, and occurred despite the high deposition rates of dioxins and furans predicted in northern latitudes by long-range atmospheric transport models. The current levels of dioxin-like compounds found in breast milk from Nunavik women are now similar to those found in populations exposed to background levels in southern latitudes.
The breast milk concentrations of dioxin-like compounds in Inuit women of Nunavik have greatly decreased during the last decade.

The deposition of polychlorodibenzo-p-dioxins and polychlorodibenzofurans in Arctic Canada suggested by a recent modeling study is not reflected by the body burden of dioxin-like compounds in Inuit women of child-bearing age residing in Nunavik.
To evaluate the current concentrations of polychlorodibenzo-p-dioxins, polychlorodibenzofurans and dioxin-like polychlorinated biphenyls in breast milk samples from Nunavik women (2000 study group).
To compare these concentrations to those obtained in 1990 in the same region in order to derive a temporal trend .

Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polychlorodibenzo-pdioxins (PCDDs) and polychlorodibenzofurans (PCDFs) are ubiquitous environmental pollutants. These compounds are lipophilic, resist biodegradation and show a strong propensity to bioaccumulate and biomagnify in food chains. Long-range atmospheric transport modelling studies have suggested that they are carried away from their southern sources of emission and deposited in northern latitudes where they accumulate in Arctic ecosystems (Commoner et al. 2000, MacDonald et al. 2000). Data from laboratory animals and human populations accidentally exposed to dioxin-like compounds (DLCs, including PCDDs/PCDFs and non-ortho- and mono-ortho-substituted PCBs) indicate that these compounds can induce several toxic effects (Hansen 1998, Longnecker et al. 1997, Mukerjee 1998, Safe 1994). Hence, environmental exposure to these toxicants represents a potential health threat. The Inuit population of Nunavik (northern Quebec) is exposed to these compounds through the consumption of sea mammal fat as part of their traditional diet. A recent PCDD/PCDFs continental scale modelling study showed a linkage between U.S. sources of these compounds and their deposition to northern latitudes. The study also drew conclusions relative to human health implications and called for remedial action to protect the Inuit residing in the Canadian Arctic from the health hazard of airborne DLCs (Commoner et al. 2000). Earlier studies have compared the exposure of the populations of Nunavik and southern Quebec to DLCs. A breast-milk survey was carried out between 1989 and 1991 and showed that concentrations of organochlorines (OCs) were three- to seven-fold higher in Nunavik than in southern Quebec (Dewailly et al. 1994, Dewailly et al. 1993b, Dewailly et al. 1992, Dewailly et al. 1989). Another study carried out in 1992 on pooled blood samples from Inuit adults and Caucasians from southern Quebec showed a seven-fold difference between plasma concentrations of DLCs (Ayotte et al. 1997). However, recent data on the body burden of DLCs in the Inuit population of Nunavik are not available. Therefore, it was agreed by the Northern Contaminants Program management committee that the current concentrations of PCDD/PCDFs and coplanar PCBs in breast milk obtained from Nunavik women during 1996-2000 were to be determined in order to derive a temporal trend.

Forty-seven breast milk samples were provided by Nunavik women between 1996 and 2000 in the framework of an ongoing neurodevelopment study, and were analyzed for coplanar PCBs, PCDDs and PCDFs. All samples were sent to Axys Analytical Services Ltd (Sidney, B.C.) for OC analyses. Milk samples were spiked with 13C-labelled surrogate standards and were liquid-liquid extracted. Extracts were subjected to a series of chromatographic cleanup steps, resulting in two fractions. One fraction was analyzed for PCDDs, PCDFs and non-ortho substituted PCBs and the other fraction was analyzed for mono-ortho substituted PCBs. Organochlorine determinations were performed by high-resolution gas chromatography with high-resolution mass spectrometric analysis. Organochlorine concentrations in breast milk were expressed on a lipid basis (lipids measured gravimetrically) and concentrations were converted to dioxin toxic equivalent (TEO) concentrations using the latest set of international (World Health Organization) toxic equivalency factors (TEFs) (Van den Berg et al. 1 998).

Data obtained in 1996-2000 were compared with those obtained in a breast-milk survey carried out in the same region between 1989 and 1991. In the latter study, OC determinations were carried out according to a similar protocol, albeit in a different laboratory (Midwest Research Institute, Kansas City, KS, USA). DLCs concentrations obtained in 1 989 to 1 991 were re-converted to TEOs according to the latest TEFs.

Breast milk samples were obtained from 4 7 Inuit women living in three villages on the East Coast of Hudson Bay between 1996 and 2000 (2000 study group). The average maternal age in this group was 25 years (95% Cl: 23 .4 to 26. 7 .) and 21 % of these women were primiparous. Means and confidence intervals for DLCs concentrations in breast milk are presented in Table I . One sample was excluded from the analyses because of its abnormally low lipid content. Mean total TEO concentration found in breast milk in 1996 to 2000 (17 ng·kg-1 lipids) is mostly attributable to PCBs (62%), in particular to the mono-ortho congeners (40%). PCDDs account for 27% of total TEOs and PCDFs for the remaining I 1 %.

This study aimed to assess the current breast milk concentrations of PCDDs, PCDFs and dioxin-like PCBs in Inuit women of child-bearing age residing in Nunavik and compare them to concentrations in samples collected in 1990, in order to identify temporal trends. Our results show that PCBs (non-ortho and mono-ortno congeners) are the major contributors to total TEOs, followed by PCDDs and PCDFs, an observation previously reported in the Nunavik population (Ayotte et al. 1997). However, a striking 4.5-fold decrease in concentrations of DLCs in breast milk (not including mono-ortno PCBs) occurred during the last decade.

Both study-groups were comparable with regard to maternal age, but the area of residence of the participants differed slightly. All participants in the 2000 study group were residents of villages on the East Coast of Hudson Bay, whereas 20% of the 1990 study group resided in the Hudson-Straight area or the Ungava Bay area. However, this is unlikely to affect the results and conclusions drawn in this study. People residing in the Ungava Bay area are less exposed to OCs than on the east coast of Hudson Bay, but this difference is not statistically significant for DLCs (Dewailly et al. 1993a, Dewailly et al. 1993b).

According to a recent review of time trends of OCs found in breast milk, international data indicate a global decline in concentrations of DLCs for several industrialized countries over the last 30 years (LaKind et al. 2001) . This decline is clearly observed in several European countries as well as in Japan and Vietnam, but results remain more or less ambiguous for United States and Canada. In most cases, this trend is more pronounced from the 1 970s to the mid- l 980s and seems to reach a plateau in the early to mid-1 990s. According to LaKind et al. (2001), the most compelling evidence of this decline is brought by data collected in Germany showing a 60% decrease in PCDDs and PCDFs breast milk concentrations from 1 989 to 1996, a similar trend to that observed in the present study. The results reported here are therefore consistent with the decline observed in PCDDs and PCDFs concentrations in breast milk collected worldwide and, more specifically, they are consistent with data collected in Germany for the same time period.

Our data show that the high deposition rates of PCDDs and PCDFs in Arctic Canada predicted by a recent modelling study (Commoner et al. 2000) are not reflected in the body burden of DLCs compounds in the Inuit women of child-bearing age residing in Nunavik. The current breast 39 milk concentrations of DLCs in this population are now comparable to concentrations reported in the general population of Quebec in 1992 (Dewailly et al. 1992) and in several other populations exposed to background levels of dioxin-like OCs (La Kind et al. 2001 ). This decline in breast milk concentrations of DLCs may be attributable to decreasing concentrations of these compounds in Arctic biota, to a decrease in the consumption of sea mammal fat in the Nunavik population or to a combination of these factors, and further studies are needed to address these issues.

In summary, breast milk concentrations of all DLCs have greatly decreased in the last decade in samples collected in Nunavik. Therefore, the high deposition rates of PCDD/PCDFs in northern latitudes suggested by a recent modelling study is not reflected by the actual body burden of Inuit women of child-bearing age residing in Nunavik, and levels of DLCs in breast milk collected from these women are now close to concentrations observed in other populations exposed to background levels of DLCs. Other compounds such as polybrominated diphenyl ethers should be given more attention in future breast milk surveys to be conducted in the Canadian Arctic, in view of the rising concentrations of these compounds reported in other populations and their similar toxic properties to other OCs (Darnerud et al. 2001, de Boer and Denneman 1998, Hooper and McDonald 2000, Meironyte et al. 1999, Noren and Meironyte 2000).

Decision Making and Diet in the North: Balancing the Physical, Economic and Social Components Chris Furgal, Public Health Research Unit, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Quebec (CHUQ) (CHUU, 2400 rue d'Estimauville, Beauport, QC GlE 7G9; Phone: (418) 666-7000 (ext 555)·' Fax: (418) 666-2776; E-mail: Christopher.Furgal@crchul.ulaval.ca ' Susie Bernier, Public Health Research Unit-CHUQ (CHUU, Beauport, QC; Gaston Godin, Health-Related_ Behav!ours, Laval University, Quebec, QC; Suzanne Gingras, Dany Laverdiere, Jacques Grondin and Eric Dewailly, Public Health Research Unit-CHUQ (CHUU, Beauport, QC This project addressed two gaps in our understanding of how to effectively manage traditional/country food and contaminant issues in the North: the lack of understanding of how best to include social and cultural benefits and risks associated with traditional/country foods in decisionmaking processes; and the lack of understanding of the determinants of food choice. This project identified and reviewed potential social and cultural benefits and risks associated with traditional/country foods and foodrelated activities in the North. A process and the need for their consideration and inclusion in risk management concerning human health and contaminants were then outlined. Over the 2 years of this project, a culturally specific questionnaire was developed, tested and applied to 251 Inuit residents of Kuujjuaq to provide a quantitative assessment of determinants of food choice. Results indicate that perceived behavioural control (i.e. how easy or difficult a person perceives adopting a behaviour) is the strongest predictor of intention to eat traditional/ country food three times a week or more, while personal normative belief (i.e. personal feeling of obligation to adopt the behaviour), followed by emotion (i.e. personal feelings associated with the behaviour) and perceived behavioural control are the best predictors of intention to eat store-bought food every day. This is the first quantitative data on this topic in the North to date. Both the development of processes to include cultural and social benefits and risks in decision-making activities, and the identification of the determinants of food choice in Kuujjuaq, increase our understanding of how to effectively make decisions and implement intervention and education programs related to traditional/country foods and contaminants in the Canadian North.

Knowledge of contaminants was not found to be a major determinant of the intention to eat traditional/ country food. How easy or difficult a person thought eating traditional/country food three times a week or more would be, was the strongest determinant in intention to eat traditional/country food. Feelings, either like or dislike, for the daily consumption of store-bought food, personal belief in this behaviour and the perceived ease or difficulty of adopting it daily were the major influences on an individual's intent to consume store-bought food.

The determinants identified in the course of this study explain approximately half of the variance in intent to eat traditional/country food and more than half of the variance in intent to eat store-bought food.

2. To develop and apply a survey tool to increase our understanding of the determinants of food choice behaviour in northern communities.

While Western science has recently recognized the biological and economic benefits and risks related to traditional/country food, traditional knowledge has long since recognized the many benefits related to these foods in terms of their contribution to physical, social, and spiritual well-being (Borre 1991 , Borre 1994, Egede 1995). In some cases, there have been reports of the loss or disruption of these social and cultural components due to confusion and concern over food safety resulting from reports of environmental contamination (Sante Quebec 1992, Wheatley and Wheatley 1981, Wenzel 1986). In the face of the threats imposed by environmental contamination in the Arctic, northern health professionals, government representatives and advisory bodies have had the responsibility of "managing," protecting and promoting public health and its relationship to the environment through the balancing of available information, the provision of advice to the public and, in some cases, intervention activities. This has proven to be a difficult, and at times, contentious exercise, in particular because such things as the needs, expectations and preferences of the population have not always been well understood and considered . Little work to date has focused on investigating methods through which to include the consideration for, and balancing of, social and cultural components related to traditional/country food in decision-making processes. Similarly, little attention has been given to gaining a better understanding of the determinants of food choice behaviour in the North and their potential impacts on advisory reception and adherence. Those responsible for the protection and promotion of public health in the North must consider and have access to all available information, in an understandable and accessible manner, in order to make informed decisions. This is of paramount importance as the issues surrounding traditional/country food in the North are becoming increasingly complex.

This project conducted work to address two gaps in our understanding of managing and implementing decisions surrounding contaminants and food in the North, namely how better to involve information on the cultural and social aspects of traditional/country foods in the North, and to gain a better understanding of the determinants of food choice in order to better orient advisory and intervention activities as well as diet-related health promotion programs. Work conducted to address each of these two items is presented separately in this report, each followed by a presentation of general conclusions and implications for making decisions on diet and health in the North.

Part A: Considering the Social and Cultural Aspects of Traditional/Country Food in Decision-Making Processes In the first year of this project, a literature review was conducted to identify and organize the social, cultural and spiritual benefits associated with traditional/country foods in the North. This literature review then formed the basis for the development of a conceptual framework in year 2 for the explicit consideration of the benefits and risks associated with traditional/country foods and traditional/country food-related activities in decisionmaking processes. A review of processes and methods to assess the social and cultural impacts of changes in traditional/country food-related activities was conducted.

A review of contemporary risk management frameworks for environmental health was also conducted in cooperation with another project in which C. Furgal participated (see Jardine et al. 2000). Based on this review and expert consultation with northern health and environment officials, recommendations are made for methods and placement in the decision-making process to explicitly consider social and cultural benefits and risks of traditional/country foods and traditional/country food-related activities.

The work conducted under year 2 of this project followed a basic line of inquiry common to impact assessment in order to understand the social and cultural aspects of traditional/country foods in the North and how this information is currently treated in decision-making processes. These questions included: What is the relationship between traditional/country foods and the social, cultural and spiritual well-being among Aboriginal peoples in the North? What are the broad categories of potential impacts of environmental contaminants in the Arctic and where do the social and cultural importance of traditional/ country foods and their related activities fit in this hierarchy? Are the social and cultural impacts of advice based on contaminants issues currently considered when making decisions on health and the environment in the North, and if so, how? ls there a need to include these aspects in decision-making processes on traditional/ country foods and health? How should it be done and what are the challenges to their inclusion? and, How do we overcome these challenges?

Table I outlines the effects that certain traditional/country food-related activities have on specific aspects of social, cultural or spiritual well-being in northern communities, as reported in the literature. The collection, consumption, distribution and preparation of traditional/country foods are reported to define, maintain, express and increase aspects of social, cultural and spiritual well-being in the North. Distinct benefits are reported as being associated with individual activities (collection, distribution, preparation or consumption of traditional/country foods), and thus an appreciation for these activities and the unique benefits each contributes to social, cultural and spiritual health must be recognized when making decisions. Little work has been done on the specific aspects of cultural and social importance of these foods; many studies simply report the general significance - but with little empirical support or detail in their argument. However, a specific treatment of this issue is complex as the nature of the social, cultural or spiritual relationships to traditional/country foods are not easily identified, described or measured. Such a description would be Table 1. Specific categories describing significance of traditional/country foods in northern communities as identified through a literature review valuable to help understand the specific benefits and impacts of change in relation to traditional/country food related activities. Following the identification of these relationships and their importance, it is necessary to identify how they relate with other aspects of the relationship between individuals and traditional/country foods and the environment in northern communities.

Figure I provides a simplified overview of the broad categories of direct and indirect impacts of the presence and public awareness of contaminants in the Arctic ecosystem. Human exposure to environmental contaminants in the Arctic ecosystem has potential impacts on physical and mental attributes of human health. The knowledge of this contamination and its potential impacts causes Northerners, northern health and environment practitioners, and managers to attempt to minimize this exposure and protect public health (e.g. health advisory or consumption advice). Both the potential effects of contaminants and the effects of the actions to minimize human exposures to them have potential impacts on human health, community and individual economic status, and community and individual social and cultural wellbeing. In all cases, impacts refers to either positive or negative change. Because of their interconnected nature, impacts to one of economic, physical health, or socialcultural well-being has indirect impacts on the others.

Similarly, the presence of contamination in biotic components of the Arctic ecosystem (specifically, in wildlife species consumed by Northerners) has potential impacts on aspects of environmental change in the North (e.g. potential impacts to fertility, reproductive success and general wildlife health resulting in changes in population size, human availability and access to traditional/country food species) . The knowledge of this contamination, and attempts to minimize the impacts to wildlife and human health (e.g. through management Figure 1. Finally, simply the knowledge and awareness of contaminants in the Arctic environment have potential social, cultural and mental health impacts because of Northerners' close relationship with the land. Currently, direct and indirect human health impacts via numerous exposure pathways to contaminants are assessed and quantified through risk analyses conducted as part of the human health risk assessment process (e.g. Dewailly et al. 1998, Jardine et al. 2000) and these results are then available for consideration in the risk management process. Similarly, economic impacts and benefits are quantified, where data is available, through cost benefit analyses (e.g. Dewailly et al. 1998, Jardine et al. 2000) and can be made available for decision making regarding traditional/country foods in the North. Consideration for social and cultural benefits and risks, however, is conducted informally as part of the risk management process during consideration of what actions to take. No formal process is recognized for the assessment and analysis of potential social and cultural impacts of actions to minimize risks from exposure to environmental contaminants (Furgal 1999). Consideration of these factors is dependent upon the composition and experience of risk managers and others involved in the decision-making process. Further, the qualitative nature of these aspects presents certain challenges to their explicit inclusion. Additionally, the lack of understanding of specific social and cultural impacts limits the availability of this data - qualitative or quantitative - for consideration in decision-making processes that are often challenged by time, resources available to gather information, and inter-agency and organizational coordination and jurisdiction issues. Despite this, cases reviewed in Labrador, where these data were explicitly involved in the decisionmaking process surrounding contaminants in traditional/ country foods, showed that this information had a significant positive impact on the resulting action taken. This is in contradiction to cases in which the indirect social and cultural impacts of actions to minimize human exposure were not anticipated and the results had significant negative social and health implications for the population involved (e.g. Broughton Island, as in Kinloch et al. 1992; and Sugluk, as in Wheatley and Wheatley 1981 ). The documentation of these negative impacts supports a strong argument for work into how and when to include this information in risk management processes.

The evolution of processes and methods for impact assessment of large development projects in the North can teach us a great deal about how to include qualitative social and cultural impact data in making decisions on traditional/country foods and health. Methods and processes of social impact assessment have evolved out of the recognized need to assess the social consequences of projects, programs, and government policies on communities and individuals (U.S. Department of Commerce I 994). Methods and processes have been developed and documented for these purposes (e.g. Finsterbusch et al. 1983, Brudge 1994). The monitoring and projection of changes in quantifiable indicators (e.g. reports of social pathologies, cases of depression, etc.) or the specific identification of qualitative relationships between factors within the community and aspects of social health and well-being are the most common forms of data included in social impact assessments. In these cases, "impacts" can be either positive or negative, direct or indirect changes. They can include such things as exposure to new risks or benefits, and/or decrease in exposure to current risks or loss of current benefits. It 45 is the last form of social and cultural impacts that is perhaps most important for the case of changes imposed by actions to minimize human exposure to contaminants in traditional/country foods. Similar to processes of risk assessment and management, the social impact assessment process stresses the need to involve a diverse public (as it is about addressing concerns of the public), analyze impact inequities (to be specific regarding which segments of the population are impacted the most), focus the assessment (to take into account "concerns that really count, not those that are just easy to count"), identify methods and assumptions (to be clear on uncertainties and biases), define the significance of variables impacted, establish monitoring and mitigation programs (plan for the unexpected and follow up on activities), identify data sources, and plan for gaps in data (National Environmental Protection Agency l 998). However, to include consideration for these impacts in decision-making processes on human health exposure to contaminants requires certain forms of information. Baseline data (qualitative or quantitative) on specific relationships between social and cultural well-being and traditiona l/country foods and an understanding of these relationships and the factors influencing them is required. Development of qualitative or quantitative indicators of the relationship between social and cultural well being and traditional/country foods is also needed (e.g. what is the relationship between social health status indicators and level of hunting, or traditional/country food sharing activity in communities?) . Retrospective analyses of changes in social and cultural well-being induced by similar or the same factors (advisories or intervention programs) in other locations must be conducted and made available in order to project potential changes of future activities. Without the development and availability of this detailed information, it is impossible to expect consistent and appropriate consideration to be given to these important aspects of the issue in all decision-making processes. Currently, risk management processes are frequently challenged by time, resources (financial and human), uncertainty and availability of data, and organizational and jurisdictional complexities.

When to include consideration for potential social and cultural impacts of a decision is an important aspect to mention. As outlined in Figure I, for our purposes, social and cultural impacts of contaminants are a direct result of either contaminant-related changes in wildlife availability and accessibility (health and numbers), or actions taken to minimize human exposure to contaminants in the environment. Indirect social and cultural impacts result from increased awareness and perceptions and/or misconceptions of contaminant related risks, or indirect impacts of actions taken to minimize human exposure (i .e. impacts of changes in economy because of action). This understanding designates where in the risk mana0gement process information on social and cultural impacts is most appropriately presented and considered. Shortreed et al. (2000, as reviewed in Jardine et al. 2000) developed a composite "benchmark" risk management framework through comparing and contrasting all international frameworks currently available (Figure 2). In this process, the consideration for social and cultural benefits and risks of traditional/country foods is best included in the discussion when determining and assessing potential actions to take to minimize human exposure.

Part B: Application of the Survey Tool to Measure Determinants of Food Choice in the North The application of the survey tool developed in year I was successfully completed on February 27, 200 l. One member of our research team, a research assistant and 14 local interviewers, completed 251 interviews with Inuit residents of Kuujjuaq, Nunavik, 12 years of age and older. The questionnaire was tested and retested in both English and lnuktituut with 39 residents of Kuujjuaq and was then further adapted following statistical analysis for each question's validity and the survey's reliability. Composed of 50 questions, it measured frequency of use of foods, constructs of Triandis' theory for use of traditional/country food three times a week or more, use of store-bought food every day, degree of liking of foods, as well as basic socio-demographic information (see Table 2) . The project and consent forms were reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of Laval University Hospital Centre and the Nunavik Nutrition and Health Committee. Informed consent was obtained from all participants after having explained the objectives of the survey.

All questionnaire forms were reviewed and validated to eliminate logic or coding errors and all data for statistical analysis was captured twice. Statistical analysis was conducted using Statistical Analysis System (SAS) software (Statistical Analysis System Institute Inc. 1999). Results to questions related to health and safety value of traditional/country food When asked if eating traditional/country food three times per week or more over the next month would be very good for their health (measure of belief), 92.05% of participants responded probably/yes. When asked if they believed it would make them sick, 87.03% responded probably not/no. When asked if eating traditional/country food three times/week or more over the next month would be healthy/unhealthy (measure of attitude), 94.14% of participants thought it would be healthy/very healthy. When asked if this behaviour was safe or unsafe, 90.38% responded that they thought it would be very safe/safe.

The methods used in the first year of this study (Dewailly et al. 2000), to elicit the emic views of the etic constructs, contributed to the quality of our questions in the year 2 survey. The questionnaire was built from local knowledge and language, tested and retested, and further adjusted so it was easy to understand and answer. No questions in the applied survey were considered inappropriate or irrelevant by participants and thus the number of nonresponses was very low. Also, including an open-ended question at the end of the questionnaire allowed us to further ensure that we covered all possible answers in the previous questions as no new or different attributes were reported here. In viewing Table 4, we notice that all scores but one are higher (more positive) for traditional/ country food than store-bought food. Habit was the only construct scoring higher (more positively) for store-bought food. Does this mean that intention is overrated? This result may be due to the fact that the actual behaviour is also influenced by environmental factors such as reinforcements and facilitating conditions (Godin 1991). The answer to our question is probably in the amount of unexplained variance in our data. Differences between age groups in this data were expected since differences in consumption are also found in results from diet survey literature. However, we noted two types of differences in this data. Sometimes the dividing line falls between the teenagers and the adults or between teens/young adults and the rest of the population. This provides more detail on the differences between age groups beyond the teenager/adult comparisons regularly reported.

To predict behaviour, instead of intention, it would have been necessary to measure behaviour in this study, however, this was not possible. Instead, we rely on our proxy measurement for behaviour, which is intention. Metanalyses have shown intention to be the best proxy for behaviour (Godin and Kok 1996, Sutton 1998) but they have also shown that the amount of variance explained increased significantly when including a measure of perceived behavioural control. In this study, we improved upon this further through the inclusion of both perceived behavioural control and habit. Habit explained part of the variance in our data but perceived behavioural control came out as the strongest predictor. A test was also conducted to verify the relationship between the determinants and habit (also used as a proxy of behaviour even though it is also a predictor of intention). However, to have the best power of prediction we should have measured behaviour at the same level of specificity and not as a measure of past habit (Sutton 1998). This result is further limited by the fact that both variables were measured on different scales (continuous/dichotomous) and this has been shown to attenuate correlations (Courneya 1994). We can show the following factors have a significant association with habit: emotion, perceived behavioural control and personal normative belief (in order of decreasing strength of the relationship). We can not compare our results from the multiple regressions on intention with our logistic regressions on habit but we are able to identify which factors are the most important for each construct. For intention, they are perceived behavioural control, emotion, personal normative belief, habit, attitude (in decreasing order of strength) .

When looking at the results of the influence of barriers/ facilitating conditions on intention (having someone share traditional/country food with you, having to hunt/fish for traditional/country food and having access to traditional/ country food through the Hunter Support Program/ community freezer), it is interesting to view these results in combination with the results from the question on use of the community freezer; 82% of the participants reported sometimes/often/most of the time getting traditional/country food from the community freezer. This is an important issue to consider in relation to compliance to health advisories on the consumption of traditional/country foods, should any be conducted in the future.

In our survey, only three questions addressed the issue of the effect of contaminants on food choices and our results indicate that there is no effect. Two of the three questions on this issue were included in the composite measure of attitude (which did not come out as a major determinant of choice) and one was included in the measure of behavioural beliefs (and did not come out 51 as a major determinant either). Although these are not specific questions on contaminants, we believe the fear, or lack of fear for contaminants in traditional/country foods are filtered through the measure of attitude which was included in this study. It must also be emphasized that the methods used to build the survey aimed to elicit, through focus group interviews, salient &e/iefs about the consumption of traditional/country food and storebought food. This was done using very general elicitation questions. Therefore, if contaminants was not brought up by participants, it was not considered a salient concern and therefore not included as a specific question in the questionnaire (this protects the researcher from the situation of "suggesting" responses to the participant). With this study, we aimed to go beyond simply asking people to agree with predetermined statements. The only comments made regarding disadvantages of traditional/ country food in this study concerned food poisoning from preparation of igunaq or from zoonoses in raw meat. Participants had multiple opportunities to express their concerns during the test-retest since, for each question, precise reasons for answering in one way or another were requested. Although we recognize that all methods have limits in what information they elicit, we believe that if concern for contaminants was an issue when faced with the decision to eat tro.ditiona//country food or not (as the question was posed in this survey), it would have come out more often in participants responses.

This study addressed two identified gaps or challenges in the effective management and communications related to contaminants and traditional/country food in the North. In fact, in many respects this study has gone beyond its original goals as it has provided direction for future work in the areas of social impact assessment and indicators related to social and cultural well-being in relationship to traditional/country food and traditional/ country food related activities. Additionally, it has provided a basis of understanding of diet related behaviour in a northern community. This is the first quantitative data of its kind in a region where significant influences to, and changes in, diet have been observed in the last few decades and appear to be continuing into the future. Some of the shifts in diet have significant health implications. These results are intended to help health and environment officials in managing contaminants and health issues and in planning promotion or prevention activities to effectively target specific groups based on specific diet-related behaviours. If the objective of health advice and advisories is to inform people of the potential human health effects of exposure to certain contaminants through the consumption of traditional/ country foods, general communication methods are most appropriate. However, if the desired effect is to change behaviour, planning an intervention based on changing the perception people have of how easy or difficult it is to increase or decrease their consumption of a certain traditional/country food will have a greater chance at achieving the program goal. For example, to promote the consumption of Arctic char among pregnant women in Nunavik, the Nunavik Nutrition and Health Comm ittee made access to char easier for this group of the population. Another example might be the hypothetical case of a recommendation to decrease consumption of a specific traditional/country food that is met with non-compliance. The results of this study suggest that an argument based on the provision of health information alone would have little chance in changing behaviour if this traditional/country food was available for free through the community freezer or at other sources in the community (i.e. people do not choose their food solely on the basis of their value to health). The issue of ease of access would need to be considered in the development of the intervention strategy or release of health advice and expected outcomes.

To understand the larger picture of factors influencing food choice decisions by Arctic women and children, so that risks and benefits messages can be placed in relevant and appropriate context for effective education messages.
2. To understand children's use of traditional and market food.

Extensive dietary and sociocultural information are available for adults in Dene/Metis and Yukon First Nations communities. However, in order for this information to be useful to Aboriginal organizations and public health agencies responsible for food and nutrition education efforts that address benefits and risks of food use, the context of food choice decisions in the community setting are needed. As well, since food behaviour is learned, it would be helpful to understand how children use traditional and market food in these communities. It is clear in the global literature, that factors influencing personal food choice decisions must be known before effective food education interventions can be planned carried to effective completion (Ross 1995, Parraga 1990, Rappaport et al. 1992).
This is a report on the first year of a 2-year project.

Following a review of our existing data on food use and sociocultural factors influencing food use, discussions were held with staff of the Council of Yukon First Nations and the Dene Nation to generate a tentative list of food choice factors, and to enlist support for the project. Of several communities in Denendeh and Yukon that requested participation, five communities were selected: Fort McPherson, Tulita, Fort Resolution, Carcross and Old Crow. Ethics approval was given by McGill University, science licenses were obtained and research agreements with each community were signed.

Field work was conducted in each of these communities from late November 2000 to the end of January 200 l . Five focus groups were held (one in each community) with a total of 24 participants, and dietary interviews of l 0- to 12-year-old children were conducted (n = 115), with about 85% of children giving repeat 24-hour recall interviews during the winter season. Interviews with women who are mothers and/or caregivers of these children and who participated in the focus groups were conducted. In all, 20 interviews were conducted with women who participated in the focus groups, and 13 additional interviews (Fort Resolution, Old Crow, Carcross) were conducted for the purposes of ranking food choice factors. At this time, focus group data are in the process of transcription, and dietary data are being entered into a database.

Twenty-eight factors responsible for food choices were identified and were placed into five major categories: costs (in the broadest sense); availability (of both traditional and market food); cultural and pleasurable reasons for selecting food; physical and medical reasons (age, gender, appetite); and knowledge (traditional knowledge, contaminants, labels) . Preliminary information from the focus groups identified costs and availability of food as the most important factors for food choices in these communities. Contaminants were rarely mentioned as a reason why people selected, or would not select, one food or another. Interview information to be gathered during 200 l -2002 will further investigate these preliminary findings.

Reported here are selected analyses prioritized by foods and nutrients, and the need for additional data. Most of the values reported here are first reports of these nutrients in these foods. Nutrient data from this study are now incorporated into a database used for nutrient analysis of dietary records of Arctic Aboriginal peoples. New data are presented for fatty acids, proximate composition, minerals and vitamin D. These data contribute substantially to the existing traditional/country food composition database. Knowledge of nutrient contents in Arctic traditional/country food is important for nutrition education initiatives of Aboriginal peoples, and for understanding global food diversity. Several unique traditional/country food items of Arctic Aboriginal peoples were analyzed for their nutrient contents. Foods such as fat made from caribou bone and grizzly bear bone, caribou bone marrow, caribou brain, seal and walrus liver, fish roe, whale skin, berries and spruce sap were collected from Arctic communi~ ties in partnership with local residents familiar with these foods.
2. Arctic traditional/country foods are rich sources of nutrients.
3. Burbot liver is an excellent source of vitamin D, as is Arctic char and beluga fat.
5. General mineral levels in animal flesh foods are high; consuming these foods can contribute to good health.
To provide new knowledge of nutrients in traditional/ country foods frequently consumed by Arctic Aboriginal peoples.
2. To provide new knowledge of nutrients in favorite or unique traditional/country food items consumed by Dene, Metis, Yukon First Nations and Inuit.
3. To fill in gaps in the existing nutrient composition database resulting from inadequately sampled food items.

The Human Health Blueprint of the Northern Contaminants Program recognizes that benefiHisk assessment must include nutrient information on food consumed. Arctic diets are composed of both traditional/country and market food items. While most market foods have known values for the spectrum of nutrients in human nutrition, the complete nutrient profiles of traditional/country food items are not available. There are many nutrients in Arctic foods for which nutrient levels are not known or are not completely known . This information is needed to make informed decisions weighing contaminant risks with multiple nutrient and sociocultural benefits of traditional/ country food consumption in Arctic communities.

Further, nutrient compositions of traditional/country foods are in demand by nutritionists working with Arctic peoples in the areas of dietary evaluation, preparation of education materials and in individual counseling.

Projects carried out by the Centre for Indigenous Peoples' Nutrition and Environment (CINE) have assessed dietary benefits and risks in Dene/Metis, Yukon First Nations and Inuit communities (Kuhnlein et al. 2001 ). The traditional/ country food items most frequently consumed were sampled, but often sufficient sample size or sample number were not. Therefore, this project attempted to obtain additional samples of frequently consumed foods, as well as important food items that had not yet been sampled but were suggested to be good sources of nutrients. Analyses of several nutrients were developed during the previous year, and continued during this project. Nutrient analyses of food samples were conducted for proximate composition (protein, fat, moisture, ash, carbohydrate-by-difference, computed energy), fatty acids (polyunsaturates, monounsaturates, saturates, sum of n-6 and n-3 fatty acids), minerals (calcium [Ca], iron [Fe], copper [Cu], zinc [Zn], phosphorus [P], magnesium [Na], selenium [Se]) and vitamins (A [retinol], E [alpha tocopherol], c
The method for vitamin D was fully developed during this year and extensive work was conducted on fatty acids analyses of samples.

The first activity was to prioritize samples for analyses of each nutrient, since it was prohibitive to analyze all samples for all nutrients. Prioritizing was done by reviewing the rank-order of traditional/country foods consumed in each of the three large surveys as reported in 24-hour recalls. Items reported consumed by ?: 5 of the randomly selected adults were included in the prioritized list. Second, food items from this list without any nutrient data and for which samples were in hand were given priority. A final prioritization was made for each nutrient in each of the rank-ordered foods according to expectation of whether or not it would be a likely source of the nutrient (e.g. blubber or other pure fat samples were not analyzed for protein, minerals or the B vitamins).

Food samples were portioned for each nutrient and stored appropriately (e.g. as homogenates for vitamins, as freeze dried powders for minerals, as whole tissue for labile vitamins, etc.). Samples for vitamin analyses in the Health Canada (Health Protection Branch) laboratory were shipped on dry ice. Throughout this work, sea mammal mattak, a food with both blubber and skin, was dissected and analyzed separately as blubber or as skin (noted as mattak/skin). This was done because of the difficulties in assuming a consistent component of blubber and the very different nutrient contents of the two portions.

Nutrients were analyzed using standard methods (Behrens and Madere 1994, Esteve et al. 1998, Fellman et al. 1982 (modified), Helrich (ed.) 1990, Hidiroglou et al. 1993, Hoppner and Lampi, 1993, Hoppner and Lampi 1989, Horne and Patterson 1988, Kuhnlein and Soueida 1992, Kuhnlein et al. 1991 , Mattila et al. 1992, 1993, 1995, Tamura 1998, Thompson and Hatina 1979). Data were compiled as unit· I 00 g- 1 food as consumed for ease of insertion in the dietary analysis database.

Fifty-five samples of traditional/country foods were received from Inuit, Dene/Metis and Yukon First Nations areas. These included several samples of caribou bone marrow, lake trout, seal flesh, walrus blubber (fresh and aged), Arctic char, caribou flesh, seal liver, walrus liver, smoked and dried whitefish, cranberries, fat made from caribou bones, fat made from grizzly bear bones, caribou brain and clear spruce sap.

Traditional/country food resources of Arctic peoples have a significant place in this knowledge because of the excellent sources of nutrients contained in food systems primarily comprised of animal food species.

• To examine the neurophysiological and neurological long-term consequences of prenatal exposure to PCBs and methylmercury (MeHg) .

The effects of prenatal exposure to PCBs and MeHg resulting from fish consumption have been studied in fish eating populations from various countries. Prenatal exposure to PCBs have been linked to deficits in neurobehavioral development during infancy in three studies (Darvill et al. Only one study looked at neurobehavioural effects of prenatal MeHg exposure during infancy and no effects were found (Davidson et al. 1995, Davidson et al. 1998, Myers et al. 1995). Two PCB and two MeHg studies provided data for school age children (Crump et al. 1998, Jacobson et al. 1990, Jacobson and Jacobson 1996, Grandjean et al. 1997, Patandin et al. 1999), however, neuromotor as well as neurophysiological effects were poorly documented. Although neurophysiological testing was performed in one of these studies with school aged children exposed to MeHg, the study remained incomplete. Furthermore, no study has been aimed at investigating cognitive deficits under MeHg exposure using event-related potentials.

The purpose of this research is to examine the long-term consequences of prenatal exposure to PCBs and MeHg. This project is designed to extend previous findings by studying domains of effects that have been overlooked in most of the previous studies (neurophysiological and neurological endpoints) that could be related to learning difficulties and disabilities. The large number of highly exposed Aboriginal children in Northern Quebec provides a unique opportunity to:
1. study the impact of PCBs and MeHg on child development;

2. provide the information required for the development of blood guidelines, no effect thresholds, acceptable daily intakes, and health advisories for Canadian children and women of reproductive age; and 3. broaden our knowledge on the nature of specific deficits associated with the exposure to these environmental contaminants.

The sample will comprise 100 Nunavik Inuit children between 5 and 6 years of age. According to in utero PCBs and MeHg exposure levels (low and high), two subsets of 50 children will be formed. Prenatal exposure to PCBs and MeHg was documented from cord blood analysis at birth. Groups will be comparable regarding the socio-economic status. A neurological exam will be performed, the fine and gross neuromotor function as well as the visual system and the cognitive and attentional functions will be assessed. Demographic, socio-familial and biological potential confounders will be assessed via maternal interviews and blood sample analysis.
Two data collection trips were planned for the year 2000-2001. These two trips were conducted and enabled the testing of 59 children .

There are no results to present at this stage in relation to the study objectives. Nevertheless, data are available to describe the participation rate, socio-demographic characteristics of the sample, country food consumption, and prenatal and current exposure to PCBs and Hg.

Inuit women from Northern Quebec (Nunavik) were invited to participate in this study. This study is the continuation of the Cord Blood Monitoring Program in which they had participated at the birth of their child. The Nunavik region is located north of the 55th parallel; 7660 Inuit are scattered along a 2000-km seashore line along Hudson Bay, Hudson Strait and Ungava Bay - about 1500 km from Montreal and 2000 km from the Great Lakes. The Nunavik Inuit live in 14 villages, ranging from 125 to 1300 inhabitants per village. Among the eligible women, 7. 5% were excluded because they were outside of the targeted villages and 37.5% were unreachable. Among the women invited to participate in this study, 76.0% agreed to participate. Only two women did not complete the interview, and it was not possible to test two children. The study participants from Puvirnituk ( 12), Akulivik ( 1) and Ivujivik (1) were met by research assistants in the lnuulitsivik Health Center in Puvurnituk. Participants from the village of Inukjjuak ( 1 3) were met in the nursing station of that village, while participants from Kuujjuak ( 16), Kangiqsualujuak (7), Kangirsuk (3), Quaqtak (2), Tasujiak ( 1), Kangiqsujuak ( 1) and Aupaluk ( l) were met in Kuujjuak. Socio-demographic and personal characteristics were documented from interviews conducted by a highly G. Muckle experienced research assistant and are summarized in Table I .

A large proportion of women were married or living with someone. Among the women interviewed, 75.9% lived or have lived with the father of the child involved in the study. Only 5 .2% of the participating women were primiparous, and 82.8% had already delivered four or more children. High-school diplomas had been obtained by 29.3% of participants. The interview was done with an interpreter in 13.8% of the cases.

A blood sample was obtained from each participating child. One 5rmm diameter hair sample was also collected from the child. PCB congener and chlorinated pesticide concentrations were measured at birth in cord plasma and in the child's plasma collected at the testing session. Hg concentrations were determined in cord and the child's whole blood as well as in the hair sample collected at testing time. Organochlorine, heavy metals and selenium analyses were performed at the laboratory of the Centre de Toxicologie du Quebec, which is accredited by the Canadian Association for Environmental Analytical Laboratories. Blood samples containing EDTA as the anticoagulant were centrifuged and the plasma was collected in glass vials prerwashed with hexane. Plasma samples were stored at -20°C until time of analysis. A 1: 1 :3 mixture of ammonium sulfate/ethanol/hexane was first added to the plasma to extract PCB congeners. The extracts were then concentrated and purified on two Florisil columns. The 14 most prevalent PCB congeners (IUPAC nos. 28, 52, 99, 101, 105, 118, 128, 138, 153, 156, 170, 180, 183, 187) and 11 chlorinated pesticides or their metabolites (aldrin, archlordane, yrchlordane, p,p'rDDT, p,p'rDDE, HCB, prHCH, mirex, cisrnonachlor, transrnonachlor, oxychlordane) were measured in the purified extracts by highrresolution gas chromatography using two capillary columns (HewlettrPackard Ultra I and Ultra II) and dual Ni~63 electron capture detectors. Quality control procedures were described previously (Rhainds et al. 1999).

Percent recovery varied from 89% to 100% and the detection limit was approximately 0.02 μg·L-1 for all compounds. Coefficients of variation (n = 20, different days) ranged from 2.1 % to 9.1 % and biases from -10.9% to 3 .8%. Since organochlorines distribute mainly in body fat, concentrations in plasma samples are reported in μg·kg-1 of lipids. Total cholesterol, free cholesterol and triglycerides were measured in plasma samples by standard enzymatic procedures, while phospholipids were deterr mined according to the enzymatic method of Takayama et al. (1977), using a commercial kit (Wako Pure Chemical Industries, Richmond VA) . The concentration of total plasma lipids was estimated according to the formula developed by Phillips et al. Total Hg concentrations were determined in samples of whole cord and child blood and child hair by cold vapour atomic absorption spectrometry. Samples were digested with nitric acid, reduction of Hg was accomplished using anhydrous stannous chloride (SnCl 2) and the reaction was catalyzed with cadmium chloride (CdCl2). Metallic Hg was volatilized and detected by atomic absorption spectrometry (Pharmacia Model 120). The detection limit for blood Hg analysis was 1.0 nmol·L-1• Quality control procedures were described previously (Rhainds et al. 1 999). Coefficients of variation (n = 50, different days) at levels of 40 and 90 nmol·L-1 (inrhouse reference materials) were 5% and 5.5%, respectively. Relative biases were 2.4% and - 0.4%, respectively. The detection limit for hair Hg analysis was 1 nmol·g-1• Accuracy and precision data were obtained using certified reference material through Health Canada's hair Hg interlaboratory comparison program. The COr efficients of variation (n = 50, different days) at levels of 12.3 μg·g·1 (Bureau of Community Reference) and 4.42 μg·g-1 (National Institute for Environmental Studies) were 4.8% and 4.3%, respectively. The relative biases were - 2.2% and+ 1.9%, respectively.

Analyses completed in the past year corroborated previous findings relating marine mammal and fish consumption to increased mercury (Hg) and selenium (Se) body burden. Despite widespread knowledge regarding the presence of these contaminants in traditional foods, a large proportion of Inuit women increased their consumption of these foods during pregnancy, due primarily to pregnancy-related changes in food preferences and the belief that these foods are beneficial during pregnancy.

Prenatal exposure to PCBs in the Nunavik cohort is similar to that reported in the Dutch cohort but much lower than those in other Arctic cohorts (Faroe Islands and Greenland). Prenatal exposure to Hg was similar to that found in the Faroe Islands cohort but lower than that documented in the Seychelles Islands and New Zealand cohorts.
Levels of N3 polyunsaturated fatty acids in plasma phospholipids and Se in blood are relatively high in the Nunavik cohort.

The moderate correlations observed between organochlorine (OC) and methylmercury (MeHg) concentrations in the Nunavik cohort will allow us to tease out the specific developmental deficits attributable to each toxin.
