1. To examine the consequences of in utero and lactational exposure to PCBs on Inuit infants from birth to 12 months of age. Of particular interest is the impact of PCBs and Hg exposure on newborn's thyroid hormones, physical growth, physical and central nervous system maturity, on infant's overall health, mental, psychomotor and neurobehavioral development, and on functional and neural impairment in the domains of visual and spatial information processing.

To document the exposure to heavy metals, OCs and polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUF As) of newborns from selected communities in Nunavik. This ongoing effect study provides the opportunity to continue the cord blood monitoring program financed by the Northern Contaminants Program since 1993 and as a result, to be able to perform long-term time trend analysis of human exposure.

Organochlorines are carried from industrialized countries to the Arctic by long-range atmospheric transport, waterways, and oceanic currents. Due to their high lipophilicity and resistance to biodegradation, OCs bioaccumulate in fatty tissues or organisms and are biomagnified through the food chain, resulting in relatively heavy concentrations in the fat of predator species. Because fish and marine mammals represent an important part of the diet of the Inuit, exposure to OCs are of particular interest for public health authorities in the Arctic regions. Elevated levels of PCBs and Hg in Inuit adults and newborns have been reported by Dewailly et al. ( 1994, 1998) for the Northern Quebec (Nunavik) Inuit while high PCB and Hg concentrations have recently been reported by Bjerregaard and Hansen (2000) for Greenlandic Inuit mothers and newborns.

The developmental toxicity of heat-degraded PCBs was first recognized in Japan in the late 1960s and in Taiwan in the late 1970s. Infants born to women who had consumed rice oil contaminated with mixtures of PCBs and polychlorinated dibenzofurans had skin rashes and exhibit poorer intellectual functioning during infancy and childhood (Chen et al. 1992, Yu et al. 1991 ). Effects of prenatal exposure to background levels of PCBs and other OCs from environmental sources have been studied since the I980s in four major prospective longitudinal studies conducted in Michigan, North Carolina, the Netherlands and Oswego, New York. The source of PCB 73 exposure was fish consumption from the Great Lakes in both the Michigan and the Oswego studies, and consumption of dairy products in the Netherlands. Newborns from the North Carolina cohort were exposed to background levels of OCs, and there was no specific source of exposure. PCBs exposure was associated with less optimal newborn behavioural function (e.g. reflexes, tonicity and activity levels) in all four studies (Jacobson et al. 1984, Stewart et al. 2000, Rogan et al. 1986, Huisman et al. Adverse neurological effects of exposure to PCBs have been found up to 18 months of age in the Netherlands study (Huisman et al. 1995b). In Michigan and the Netherlands, higher cord serum PCBs concentrations were associated with lower birth weight and slower growth rate (Fein et al. 1984, Jacobson et al. One principal finding in Michigan was an association with poorer visual information processing ability during infancy, which indicated a deficit in visual memory or attention (Jacobson et al. 1985, 1990a, 1992). This effect was recently confirmed in the Oswego study at ages 6- and 12-months (Darvill et al. In press.). Although this association was not seen during infancy in the Netherlands study, PCB exposure has been linked to decreased attention and reaction time at preschool age in this study (Patandin et al. 1999). In North Carolina, deficits in psychomotor development up to 24 months were seen in the highest PCBs exposed children (Gladen et al. 1988, Rogan and Gladen 1991). Michigan and the Netherlands studies have linked PCB exposure to poorer intellectual function (Jacobson and Jacobson I 996, Patandin et al. I 999), specifically reduced intellectual quotient and deficits in reading and comprehension. All effects were related to prenatal exposure.

The data collection for this effects study began in November 1995. The main focus of this year's activity has been data collection. One major accomplishment during the current year was the training of a maternal interviewer/infant tester for the Greenland portion of the study and the initiation of data collection in Greenland. Subject recruitment and infant and maternal assessments in Nunavik continued throughout this year. So far, the participation rate in the present study has been high and very few women have withdrawn their collaboration during the course of the study. The participation and retention rates are very positive: the initial participation rate was 7 4% and comparable to the 80% we had projected; only 0.9% refused to continue in the study after completing the prenatal interview. 168 infants were assessed at 6.5 months of age and 156 were assessed at 11 months of age.

Objectives: To identify maternal characteristics associated with traditional food consumption and to examine food items associated with PCBs and Hg body burden in pregnant Inuit women from Northern Quebec. Methods: Women from three communities were interviewed in mid-pregnancy and at I-month and I I-months postpartum. PCBs, Hg and Se were measured in maternal blood, and Hg in maternal hair. Results: The women reported eating significant amounts of fish, beluga muktuk/fat, seal meat and seal fat. Although fish and seal consumption was associated with lower socioeconomic status, beluga whale consumption was uniform across strata. Fish and seal meat consumption was associated with increased hair Hg concentrations. Pregnancy traditional food intake was unrelated to PCB body burden, which is more a function of lifetime consumption. This study corroborated previous findings relating marine mammal and fish consumption to increased Hg and Se body burden. Despite widespread knowledge regarding the presence of these contaminants in traditional foods, a large proportion of Inuit women increased their consumption of these foods during pregnancy, due primarily to pregnancy-related changes in food preferences and the belief that these foods are beneficial during pregnancy.
Prenatal Exposure of the Northern Quebec Inuit Infants to Environmental Contaminants This manuscript was submitted to Environmental Health Perspectives.

The Inuit population residing in Nunavik (Northern Quebec, Canada) relies heavily on species from the marine foodweb for subsistence and is therefore exposed to high doses of environmental contaminants such as PCBs and MeHg, and to a lesser extent lead (Pb). In view of the neurotoxic properties of these substances, especially following developmental exposure, we initiated a study on infant development in this remote coastal population. Here we report the magnitude of prenatal exposure to these contaminants and to selective nutrients in Inuit mothers and their newborns who were recruited in three villages on the Hudson Bay coast. Interviews were conducted during pregnancy and at I and 11 months postpartum and biological samples were collected for Hg, Pb and OC analyses as well as Se and N-3 PUFA. Prenatal exposure to Hg was similar to that found in the Faroe Islands cohort but lower than that documented in the Seychelles Islands and New Zealand cohorts. Prenatal exposure to PCBs in the Nunavik cohort is similar to that reported in the Dutch cohort but much lower than those in other Arctic cohorts (Faroe Islands and Greenland). Levels of N3-PUFA in plasma phospholipids and Se in blood are relatively high. The moderate correlations observed between OC and MeHg concentrations in the Nunavik cohort may allow us to tease out the specific developmental deficits attributable to each toxin. Similarly, the weak correlations noted between environmental contaminants and nutrients will facilitate the documentation of possible protective effects afforded by either N3-PUFA or Se against neurotoxic contaminants.

Correlates of Infant Polychlorinated Biphenyls Body Burden at Birth and 6-Month Postpartum among the Northern Quebec Inuit PCBs are food-chain contaminants that have been shown to induce adverse developmental effects in humans. In the course of an epidemiological study set up to investigate adverse neurodevelopmental effects induced by environmental PCB exposure in the Inuit population of Northern Quebec (Nunavik), we studied the intercorrelations among various measures of PCB body burden in Inuit infants at birth and at 6 months postpartum. Concentrations of 14 PCB congeners were measured by high-resolution gas chromatography with electron capture detection in lipids extracted from maternal plasma, cord plasma, breast milk (collected at approximately 1 month postpartum) and 6-month-old infant plasma samples. PCB congeners (PCB 99, 118, 138, 153, 180 and 187) were detected in more than 70% of biological samples. Similar congener profiles were observed in all biological samples and PCB 153, the most abundant and persistent PCB congener, was strongly correlated with the other frequently detected PCB congeners in all biological media. Maternal plasma, cord plasma and milk concentrations were strongly intercorrelated. PCB 153 plasma concentrations in 6-month-old infants were poorly predicted by maternal plasma concentrations alone. Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that a model that included maternal PCB 153 plasma concentration, the duration of breast feeding and an estimate of the infant body fat mass provided a good prediction of PCB I 53 plasma concentration at 6 months postpartum (r2 = 0. 71 ; p < 0.001 ). Models developed in the present study may be used to reliably predict prenatal and postnatal exposure to PCBs in populations environmentally exposed to these compounds.

Contaminants and Human Health in the Canadian Arctic: an Update Northern Contaminants Program Human Health Review Team Jay Van Oostdam, Health Canada, Ottawa, ON; Sarah Kalhok, Indian and Northern Affairs Canada, Hull, QC; Pierre Ayotte, Public Health Research Unit-CHUQ (CHUL) and Laval University, Beauport, QC; Janet Beauvais and Mark Feeley, Health Canada, Ottawa, ON; Chris Furgal, Nunavik Nutrition and Health Committee and Public Health Research Unit-CHUQ (CHUU, Beauport, QC; Eric Loring, Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, Ottawa, ON; Erica Myles, Department of Health and Social Services, Government of the Northwest Territories, Yellowknife, NT; Ron Pearson, Department of Health and Social Services, Government of the Yukon Territory; Olivier Receveur, University of Montreal, Montreal, QC; Ann Roberts, Department of Health and Social Services, Government of Nunavut, Iqaluit, NU The Northern Contaminants Program (NCP) is midway through its second phase, and is at a stage in which several multi-year human health-related studies have been recently completed or are nearing completion. Meanwhile, the NCP and the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme are gearing up for their next major assessment reports. Consequently, a need was identified to take stock of the new state of knowledge with respect to contaminant exposure, effects, toxicology, and benefits and risks of traditional/country food consumption, and to synthesize results in a broader context. A workshop, Contaminants and Human Health in the Canadian Arctic: an Update, organized by the NCP Human Health Review Team, was held in Ottawa, Ontario on February 7 and 8, 200 I. It brought together approximately 60 key researchers and others with an interest in contaminants and health in the North to focus on contaminants-related research and results since the 1997 Canadian Arctic Contaminants Assessment Report. These recent findings will be used to revise the NCP Blueprints, as appropriate, and plan for Phase III. This report summarizes presentations given at the workshop; full proceedings of the workshop will be available by the fall of 2001.

Northern Contaminants Program Human Health Review Team 1. There is a need to take stock of new information on contaminant exposure, effects, toxicology, and benefits and risks of traditional/country food consumption, and to synthesize these results in a broader context of overall health in the North.

A workshop was held in February 200 I so that scientists and others identified as having an interest in contaminants and health in the North could 77 discuss recent study results, identify knowledge gaps and draw conclusions.

The information presented and discussed at this workshop will be incorporated in the upcoming major assessments by the Northern Contaminants Program (NCP) - the Canadian Arctic Contaminants Assessment Report II - and by the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme (AMAP), and will be used when revising NCP blueprints and setting priorities for NCP Phase III.

1. To examine the new state of knowledge with respect to contaminant exposure in the North, effects and toxicology, as well as benefits and risks of traditional/ country food consumption, and to synthesize results in a broader context.
2. To hold a workshop on human health and contaminants in the North, which focuses on contaminants-related research and results since the 1 997 Canadian Arctic Contaminants Assessment Report (CACAR).

To facilitate the incorporation of new findings on human health and contaminants in the upcoming major assessments by the NCP and AMAP, in revisions to the NCP blueprints and in priorities for NCP Phase III.

In 2000-2001, the NCP was midway through its second phase, and was at a stage in which several multi-year human health-related studies had been recently completed or were nearing completion. At the same time, the NCP and AMAP were gearing up for their next major assessment reports. Consequently, a need arose to take stock of the new state of knowledge with respect to contaminant exposure, effects, toxicology, and benefits and risks of traditional/country food consumption, and to synthesize results in a broader context.

To address this need, members of the NCP Human Health Review Team undertook the planning of a workshop on human health in the North, which would focus on contaminants-related research and results since the 1997 publication of CACAR (Jensen et al. 1997). This workshop was organized so that it would serve as an opportunity for researchers to present and discuss recent data and come to scientific consensus on the current state of knowledge, and, together with representatives of health boards, contaminants committees and Aboriginal organizations, to address any implications of these findings for a benefit/risk communication strategy. It would also provide an opportunity to identify gaps in scientific knowledge, which will be useful in making revisions to NCP blueprints and setting priorities for NCP Phase III.

An NCP workshop with similar objectives held in June 1997, The Northern Health Initiative Workshop, served "to gather information on all health related activities underway or required in the Arctic regions," with a focus on exposure to contaminants through traditional foods, water and air (Van Oostdam 1 997). The objectives for a workshop in 2000 built upon recommendations that emerged from the 1997 workshop.
A 2-day workshop, Contaminants and Human Health in the Canadian Arctic: an Update, was held in Ottawa on February 7 and 8, 2001. An abridged agenda is in Table 1.

Leaders of research in several contaminants and healthrelated fields who had conducted research under the NCP during NCP Phase II (since 1997), were invited to present an overview and synthesis of the state of knowledge in their particular field of expertise. Presenters were requested to draw upon research done within and outside of the NCP, and to provide a summation of current work being conducted by their research group, as well as by others. Presenters were also asked to provide a five- to six-page paper, including an executive summary, addressing the following: the current understanding about their topic; the potential implications of new information in terms of benefit/risk communication messages and recommendations in the North; whether or not the recommendations from CACAR still hold in light of new information in the 5 years since its publication; and an indication of knowledge gaps and priorities.

Attendance at the workshop was by invitation only. Invitations were extended to: researchers in fields related to contaminants and benefit/risk assessment of traditional/ country foods from research institutes, universities and federal departments; territorial health and social services departments and regional health committees; territorial contaminants committees; Aboriginal partners organizations; and regional contaminants coordinators . All workshop attendees participated in break-out sessions discussing either: research gaps and modification of the NCP blueprints; or conclusions and development of key messages.

Dietary surveys: what have we learned? Harriet Kuhnlein, Centre for Indigenous Peoples' Nutrition and Environment (CINE), Olivier Receveur, University of Montreal, and Laurie Chan, CINE In I 997, data from harvest studies, and from dietary surveys conducted in Sanikiluaq, Broughton Island, Wood Buffalo Park area, Fort Good Hope and Colville Lake, and four Yukon communities, together with preliminary results from the CINE study in 16 Dene/Metis communities were used to contribute to the main objectives of CACAR, (i.e. to assess the impact on human health of exposure to current levels of environmental contaminants; and to identify the data gaps for future human health research and monitoring). Conclusions reached at that time included:
I. Traditional food is central to the culture of Arctic Indigenous peoples.
3. Traditional food is an important source of nutrition.
Traditional food consumption varies widely both in type and quantity across communities;
The trend toward increased market food consumption, most noticeable among the youth, is likely to have adverse health effects in terms of nutritional status as well as risk of chronic disease.

Traditional food can also be a significant source of contaminants and the potential risks associated with exposure to multiple contaminants must be assessed and balanced against the better known benefits this food provides.

Since then, data collection was completed in 10 Yukon and 18 Inuit communities, following very closely the methods previously used in 16 Dene/Metis communities. The conclusions reached in I 997 based on limited data can now be generalized with confidence to the Canadian Arctic and much of the data needed for evaluating dietary benefits and risks are now available 1• For example, diets are described in terms of diversity of traditional and market food use, relative nutritional contributions of traditional and market food, and socio-economic and cultural attributes. Contaminants exposure levels are presented across regions, across age-groups, by food sources, and the distribution of these exposure levels are being compared to guidelines. Estimates of contaminant exposure were shown to be similar or lower than estimates available in 1997. At present, available estimates of dietary intakes and contaminants exposure can be used in benefit/risk analyses. These estimates, which could be improved with a limited number of additional food composition data and probabilistic description of exposure levels, need to be linked with estimates of health risks and benefits. To obtain estimate of health risks and benefits will require a critical review of the extensive literature available in nutritional sciences, as well as the more limited but growing understanding of the health risks associated with the levels of contaminants of concern. While a great deal of research interest centres on the development of benefit/risk analyses2, data already at hand can be used to provide useable information for personal decision making to maximize diet quality and minimize contaminant exposure. The need to improve the quality of market food is obvious in most communities as is the need to address the constraints to food choices, particularly among the youth in order to prevent the dramatic rise in chronic diseases that can be expected based on completed dietary assessments.

Maternal and cord blood contaminants in Arctic Canada Jay Van Oostdam, Arctic Section, Bioregional Programs, Health Canada Health Canada The 1994-2000 sampling of maternal tissues in Arctic Canada has allowed a baseline assessment of environmental contaminants in most regions of the North. Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are found at significantly higher levels in Inuit mothers and their infants, and Baffin Inuit have the highest levels in the regional studies conducted to date. A similar pattern has emerged for contaminants such as oxychlordane and trans-nonachlor, two derivatives of chlordane. Mercury (Hg) is also found at the highest concentrations in Inuit, and mothers from Nunavik have the highest maternal levels in the Canadian Arctic. Inuit mothers from Greenland have higher levels of many of these contaminants. For P-HCH (beta hexachlorocyclohexane) and DOE, the highest levels were seen in the 'other' mothers who had recently come from southeast Asia or Africa . P-HCH and ODE are still widely used in these regions. In comparing maternal and cord blood levels it was noted that Hg levels were I . 5 to 1 For final reports from each of these three large dietary surveys, check www.cine.mcgill.ca for a complete list of references.

80 Northern Contaminants Program Human Health Review Team 1.8 times higher in cord blood as has been found in other studies. Organochlorines such as PCBs were generally found at 0.7 to 0.9 times the maternal concentrations. A few organochlorines were noted to be 1 .4 to 3. 2 times the concentrations found in maternal blood. Some data is emerging for contaminant such as PCBs and Hg which indicate that more recent levels may be lower than those levels seen in the 1 980s but any conclusions based on only two data points need to be extremely cautious.

New and emerging persistent organic pollutants Derek Muir, National Water Research Institute, Environment Canada This presentation summarizes the current information on new chemical contaminant issues that are emerging in the Arctic. Unique characteristics of the Arctic - such as proximity to industrial areas of Europe and North America, long food chains with top predators that are also traditionally consumed by humans, and cold, ice covered seas - make the region vulnerable to persistent organic pollutants (POPs) like PCBs, chlorinated dioxins, and chlorinated pesticides, as well as Hg. Until recently, the focus of NCP as well as similar AMAP-related programs in other circumpolar countries was on the PCBs and chlorinated pesticides, and to a lesser extent, chlorinated dioxins/furans - because of the widespread capacity to make accurate measurements of these chemicals, as well as their known toxicity and biomagnification potential. International agreements are in place (although not ratified completely) that will ban or limit the emissions of "old" POPs and toxic metals like Hg. Temporal trend studies show that there are declines of PCBs and DDT in some species (e.g. seabirds) but not in others (e.g. seals, beluga). Mercury levels, on the other hand, appear to be increasing in Arctic marine animals. However, there are many other chemicals in current use that are also potentially persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic (PB& T) based on similar physical properties, structural similarity to the "old POPs" and, in some cases, known toxicology. Environment Canada's Commercial Chemicals Evaluation Branch (CCEB) has recently identified 100 chemicals with possible PB&T properties as part of its evaluation of chemicals in commerce in Canada. However, < l 0% of the chemicals on the CCEB list have been determined in the Arctic or anywhere else in North America. Progress has been made on measurement of a few chemicals that resemble the "old POPs." These chemical groups are chlorinated paraffins, chlorinated naphthalenes and brominated diphenyl ethers. Recent results on measurement of these "new" POPs in Arctic biota and air will be reviewed. Another group, the perfluoroalkane-sulfonates (part of the product "ScotchGard"), have also unexpectedly been detected in Arctic biota. The presence of these fluorinated chemicals, which have quite~different Northern Contaminants Program Human Health Review Team physical properties and mode of toxicity compared to the traditional POPs, but appear to be equally persistent, illustrates the need to be continually vigilant about the global movement and bioaccumulation of organic chemicals.

Toxicological consequences of toxaphene ingestion by cynomolgus (Macaca fascicularis) monkeys Douglas. L. Arnold, F. Bryce, H. Tryphonas, C. Baccanale, S. Hayward, J.R. Tanner, E. Maclellan, T. Dearden, S. Fernie and M. Hodgen, Toxicology Research Division, Bureau of Chemical Safety, Food Directorate, Health Products and Food Branch, Health Canada Toxaphene, a mixture of polychlorinated monoterpenes, was initially sold in 1945 by Hercules Co. as Hercules 3956. It was the most heavily-used pesticide in the U.S. and in many parts of the world prior to its being banned in the U.S. Most registered usages of toxaphene in Canada were cancelled in I 980 and similar actions were undertaken in other countries prior to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) cancelling most toxaphene registrations in 1982. The EPA had concluded that the use of toxaphene posed risks of: 1) chronic effects to wildlife;

2) acute toxicity to aquatic organisms; 3) population reduction in non-target organisms; and 4) increased potential for oncogenicity in humans. At the time, it was well known that the prevailing winds had transported toxaphene over long distances. Subsequently, toxaphene residues were found consistently where toxaphene was either never used or not used to any significant extent. The implications of these observations were evident when reports started to appear that the mean concentration of organochlorines in the milk fat samples obtained from lnuits were two to I O times greater than in similar samples collected in southern Quebec, and that traditional diets exceeded the "tolerable daily intake levels" for toxaphene.

Because of these findings, and the general lack of toxicological data regarding toxaphene that conforms to the present standards, the following study was undertaken. Forty female and two groups of five male cynomolgus monkeys were used in this study. The females self-ingested capsules containing dosages of 0, O. l , 0.4 or 0.8 mg of technical grade grade toxaphene·kg bw-1.d-1• The older males were proven breeders and were used exclusively for mating. Their capsules contained no toxaphene. The younger males' capsules contained 0.8 mg of toxaphene·kg bw-1.d- 1 • Statistical analysis did not reveal any effect of treatment upon body weight gain, feed consumption, water consumption or hematological parameters during the 75 weeks pre-mating phase. The only serum biochemistry parameter which was consistently affected by treatment was cholesterol which decreased 81 in a linear fashion as a consequence of dose; this difference increased with time on test (p = 0.037) . The no observed effect level regarding immunological effects in the females was 0.1 mg·kg-1• During mating, toxaphene did not affect: the number of matings needed to achieve impregnation (p > 0.05); the ability to maintain pregnancy (p = 0.41); gestation length (p = 0.010); sex ratios (p = 0.85); or birth weights (p > 0.25) . However, toxaphene did: increase femur length at gestation day 150 (p = 0.037); increase the dam's % reticulocytes (p = 0.0016) while decreasing cholesterol levels (p ::;; 0.0024) and thyroxine uptake (p = 0.003) . Toxaphene also increased neonatal female growth rate (p = 0.0047) and decreased the male's birth weight (p = 0.047) and growth rate (p = 0.040).

Toxicity of chlordane-related food contaminants Genevieve S. Bondy, Michael Barker, Gerard Cooke, Ivan Curran, Mark Feeley, Santokh Gill, Eric Lok, Rekha Mehta, Harvey Newsome, Olga Pulido, Paul Rowsell, Helen Tryphonas, Bureau of Chemical Safety, Food Directorate, Health Canada, Ottawa The pesticide chlordane, which is a mixture of structurally related organochlorine compounds, was widely used in North America until the 1980s. As a result of its stability and persistence it has accumulated in the environment and can be detected in foods and in human tissues and breast milk. Some Canadians are exposed to chlordane at levels higher than the Health Canada provisional TD! of 0.05 μg·kg bw- 1-d-1, particularly those consuming traditional diets high in marine mammal fats. In rodents, chlordane causes changes in the liver by inducing microsomal enzymes. In long term rodent studies, chlordane causes benign and malignant liver tumours. Other effects of chlordane on rodents include altered immune function and thyroid changes. In humans the acute effects of chlordane exposure include gastrointestinal upset, tremors and convulsions. The data for chlordane carcinogenicity in humans is weak, but the blood cell system and not the liver may be the target for potential chlordane-related carcinogenicity in humans. Most of the toxicological data for chlordane focus on the chlordane mixture, although trans-nonachlor and its metabolite oxychlordane are the most plentiful chlordane contaminants in traditional/ country foods and human tissues. Health Canada/NCP studies indicate that these major constituents may also be among the most toxic of the chlordane contaminants. Suggested future studies should include: long-term oxychlordane and trans-nonachlor exposure studies in rodents; multi-generational rodent reproductive studies focussing on oxychlordane/trans-nonachlor; investigations of the potential link between chlordane exposure and hematopoietic effects in humans.

Toxicological effects induced by exposure to complex food-chain contaminant mixtures Pierre Ayotte, Public Health Research Centre-CHUQ (CHUL) Most toxicological studies performed on POPs have focussed on individual compounds or technical mixtures, rather than on complex mixtures as they are found in the environment. Interactions between substances in a complex mixture may result in antagonism, additivity or synergism. In the few studies that were conducted on mixtures relevant to the Arctic environment, animals received either a reconstituted mixture or lipids extracted from wildlife species that contain relatively high concentrations of organochlorines. We conducted a developmental study using the pig as the animal model to investigate the effects on reproductive and immunological endpoints of in utero and lactational exposure to a reconstituted mixture similar to that found in blubber samples from northern Quebec seals. Administration of the mixture caused a reduction of body length at birth, and of testis weight and sperm motility in sexually mature boar. With regard to immunological effects, administration of the mixture (high dose) caused a decrease in the proportion of animals showing sustained antibody titres following vaccination against Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae. No effects attributable to contaminants were noted in other studies that investigated the toxicity of mixtures relevant to the Arctic environment.

Radioactive contaminants in the Canadian Arctic: health implications Bliss Tracy, Radiation Protection Bureau, Health Canada Since the publication of the first CACAR report, research at Health Canada on radionuclides has focussed on the uptake of radioactive 210Po through the lichen -+ caribou -+ human food chain. A two-year study, funded by the NCP, has just been completed with the University of Saskatchewan. Measurements of 210Po in excreta from 14 volunteers from Saskatoon who consumed known amounts of caribou meat confirmed that more than 50% of ingested polonium was absorbed by the human gastrointestinal tract. The retention time was found to be more than twice as long as the expected 50 days. Both of these factors mean that radiation doses to northern populations consuming caribou meat is significantly higher than expected. A further study has been undertaken, funded by the Toxic Substances Research Initiative, to measure the effects of 210Po alpha radiation at the cellular and subcellular level. The first phase involved the irradiation of cultured bovine endothelial cells at the University of Saskatchewan. Results from this phase have allowed an estimation of the relative biological effectiveness of alpha radiation compared to 250 kvp x-rays for cell lethality and reproductive capability in this animal system. Work is proceeding on the scoring of Northern Contaminants Program Human Health Review Team chromosome aberrations in the bovine cells. Human blood lymphocytes are also being cultured and subjected to the same treatment. This technique will be applied to northern populations consuming large amounts of caribou meat. It will be possible to detect subtle changes at the chromosome level long before clinical health effects become visible.

Emerging radiological health issues at the local level include the past exposures of uranium ore carriers from the community of Deline, NWT, and also the current impact of the Port Radium mine site on members of the community. Concerns have also been raised about diamond mines and a proposed beryllium mine in the NWT which can bring radioactive materials to the surface in the form of waste rock. Contaminants from nuclear facilities and other industrial operations in the temperate zone can be transported to northern regions by global atmospheric circulation patterns. Radionuclide measurements, aided by sophisticated computer models, are being used to unravel these circulation patterns.

Effects of nutrient interactions on methylmercury toxicity: current understanding and research initiatives Laurie Chan, Centre for Indigenous Peoples' Nutrition and Environment Several epidemiolog\cal studies have been conducted to study the health effects of exposure to methylmercury (MeHg) through fish and marine mammal consumption in different geographical areas: the Seychelles, the Canadian North, the Amazon, the Faroe Islands, Papa New Guinea and Sweden. There are inconsistencies in the lowest observable effect dose; for example the populations in the Amazon appear to be more sensitive. It has been suggested that dietary practice may be a significant factor affecting the susceptibility to MeHg. Of all nutrients, selenium (Se) has received the most attention as a potential protector against MeHg toxicity, particularly among seafood consuming populations, because the main sources of Hg in their diet are also rich sources of Se. Some studies have reported a correlation between Se and Hg in the serum or plasma, while others did not observe such a correlation. No epidemiological studies however, have ever shown a correlation between Se intake and the occurrence or absence of symptoms for MeHg intoxication. There are also inconsistencies in the protective effects seen in animal studies. The role of selenium remains to be confirmed. Macronutrients such as fat intake have also been correlated with MeHg toxicity. A positive correlation between dietary Hg and low density lipoprotein~cholesterol has been observed. Unsaturated fatty acids were also correlated with Hg exposure in populations frequently consuming seafood and fish, and there are suggestions that omega~3 fatty Northern Contaminants Program Human Health Review Team acids, particularly docosahexaenoic acid, may have beneficial effects. Since most studies did not collect sufficient detailed dietary information, exactly how dietary modifications, besides decreased consumption of Hg containing foods, can affect the risk of MeHg toxicity is still unclear. Even though there is little evidence of nutrient effects at the population level, there is plenty of evidence that nutrients interact with the metabolism of Hg at the physiological level. Nutrients can affect the bioavailability, the toxico~dynamics, the transport to target organs, and influence the immunological, biochemical or cytological functional responses to Hg. However, similar to the limited understanding of the mechanisms of MeHg toxicity, the overall mechanisms of modification of MeHg toxicity by nutrients are not well understood. This review paper provides an overview of our current understanding of how dietary factors affect MeHg toxicity and discuss some of the current research projects.

Neurodevelopmental studies of prenatal mercury exposure Gina Muckle, Public Health Research Centre-CHUQ (CHUU Since the publication of CACAR, there are new data indicating that prenatal exposure to MeHg resulting from fish and marine mammal consumption may be associated with negative neurodevelopmental effects, particularly in the domains of fine motor function, attention, language, visual~spatial abilities and verbal memory. However, there are dietary, economic, and cultural particularities of the Inuit lifestyle that required to be considered in the risk~management process. The ongoing prospective cohort study on the neurobehavioural effect of perinatal exposure to environmental contaminants have progressed well in Nunavik and this study will test the important hypotheses for Aboriginal Northerners that PCBs may modify the effects of MeHg, and that adverse neuro~ behavioural effects from exposure to environmental contaminants may be attenuated by high intake of Se and N3 ~polyunsaturated fatty acids. These nutrients are found in diets rich on fish and marine mammals. Community actions should be postponed until the results of this study go through the peer review process.

Neurodevelopmental studies of prenatal polychlorinated biphenyl exposure Gina Muckle, Public Health Research Centre-CHUQ (CHUU Since the publication of CACAR, there is no new data indicating that postnatal exposure to PCBs or other OCs via breast~feeding might be associated with negative neurodevelopmental effects at birth, and during infancy and childhood. Consequently, the recommendations formulated in CACAR regarding the encouragement of breast feeding due to its well~known benefits for the 83 infants health and mother-child attachment should be maintained. Even if there is a growing body of evidence linking prenatal PCB exposure to neurobehavioural subtle deficits during infancy and childhood, there are dietary, economic, and cultural particularities of the Inuit lifestyle that required to be considered in the risk-management process. The ongoing prospective cohort study on the neurobehavioural effect of perinatal exposure to environmental contaminants have progressed well in Nunavik and this study will test the important hypothesis for Aboriginal Northerners that adverse neurobehavioural effects from exposure to environmental contaminants may be attenuated by high intake of selenium and N3-polyunsatirated fatty acids resulting from a diet rich on fish and marine mammals. This information is needed to the benefit/risk characterization process and community actions should be postponed until the results of this study go through the peer review process. However, this should not delay the implementation of international actions aimed at reducing the increase of PCBs and other OCs in the environment .

Effect biomarkers for people exposed to metals and POPs in Canada's Arctic region Eric Dewailly, Frederic Dallaire and Daria Pereg, Public Health Research Unit-CHUO (CHUL) and Laval University The inclusion of validated biomarkers in epidemiological studies may help in identifying relevant associations between exposure to contaminants and detrimental health effects in the Inuit population. Over the past decade most of our efforts were focused on the characterization of exposure of Northerners. Epidemiological studies are now in place or in preparation. For most of these studies, health outcomes of interest are clinical : psychometric, neuro-physiologic, infection incidence, bone density and sexual maturation among others. However, knowing the mechanism of action of most toxicants and attempting to detect early biological changes preceding overt diseases, effect biological markers need to be validated and used. Effect biomarkers are early biological responses of the organism to an external toxic stress. The inclusion of validated biomarkers in epidemiological studies may help in identifying relevant associations between exposure to contaminants and detrimental health effects in Northerners.

Adverse effects on the immune system induced by exposure to food-chain contaminants in the Arctic Pierre Ayotte, Public Health Research Centre-CHUO (CHUL) Studies in laboratory animals and wildlife species have shown that exposure to organochlorine compounds can compromise immune system function and increase susceptibility to infectious diseases. In view of the relatively high exposure to OCs in the Inuit population and the very high incidence of certain infectious diseases in the Arctic, in particular respiratory tract infections and otitis media, we conducted a cohort study in the early 1990s to test the hypothesis that prenatal organochlorine exposure is associated with the incidence of infectious diseases in Inuit infants from Nunavik (Arctic Quebec) . Prenatal exposure to organochlorine was assessed by measuring the concentration of organochlorines in breast milk fat. We found an increased risk of otitis media during the first year of life with increasing prenatal exposure to some organochlorines compounds such as p,p' -ODE and hexachlorobenzene. The only comparable study involved a cohort of infants from Rotterdam (the Netherlands) and no association was reported between PCB or dioxin exposure and the incidence of infectious diseases. We are presently trying to replicate our initial findings in the course of the infant development study, which is approaching completion in Nunavik. The study design will allow a better characterization of exposure to OCs and to fully control for possible confounding factors.

Territorial health perspectives on benefit/risk communication Erica Myles, GNWT Health and Social Services The health status of northern Canadians depends on many factors outside of the traditional health care system. Social, economic, environmental and personal factors all play important roles in determining health. Under this broad population health approach, health cannot be achieved in isolation. Progress in other areas including environmental protection and social well-being are needed to make improvements in the health of a population. It is under this broad approach to health, that the issue of human health and environmental contaminants is addressed. It is also under this broad approach that health risks associated with environmental contaminants are communicated. Over the past decade the GNWT Department of Health and Social Services has worked actively to communicate information on contaminants and human health to NWT residents. The collaborative approach of Cooperative Risk Management has been used to develop balanced messages when communicating results of health hazard assessments, and to communicate general information on contaminants and human health . Essential to this process is the involvement of local communities, to ensure a two way exchange of information and to increase community participation in decision making. The renewal of people's confidence in the consumption of traditional foods, is the key objective of many communication materials produced . The consumption of traditional food is vital to the health, nutrition and culture of northern Canadians. The health risks associated with not consuming these foods are Northern Contaminants Program Human Health Review Team significant, as nutritious and economic alternatives to country/traditional food are very often not available. Subsequently, benefit/risk communication has focussed on promoting the nutritional, social and cultural benefits of traditional food consumption. Continued international action to reduce the levels of contaminants in the northern food chain remains important. As new information becomes available on the risks and benefits associated with the consumption of northern traditional foods, communication materials and key messages need to reviewed and updated. Now may be a key time to review past messages and communication materials, to ensure that residents are still receiving the necessary information to make informed decisions that will effect their health. Whether key messages change or remain the same, the importance of communicating balanced messages under a broad population health approach will remain constant.

Communicating on health and contaminants in Nunavik Chris Furgal, Nunavik Nutrition and Health Committee, Nunavik, and Public Health Research Unit-CHUO; Minnie Grey, Nunavik Nutrition and Health Committee, Nunavik, and Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services; Suzanne Bruneau, Nunavik Nutrition and Health Committee, Nunavik, and Public Health Research Unit-CHUO Traditional/country food is central to the cultural and personal well-being of Northerners. It is essential to the nutritional and social health of indigenous individuals. For some, few nutritious and affordable alternatives are accessible. Despite their vital importance, significant changes in the collection, use, consumption and attitudes towards these food sources have occurred over the past two decades, in part, due to the realization of and reported presence of industrial pollutants in the Arctic ecosystem. In Nunavik, a group of concerned individuals representing different organizations concerned with health, the environment, and nutritional issues has formed to address these issues, and communicate to and educate the public so that they may make more informed decisions on these issues. The Nunavik Nutrition and Health Committee, evolved from the PCB Resource Committee that originated in 1988. Between 1988 and 1994, this committee prepared and distributed written documents, participated in radio interviews, prepared videos, and discussed in various forums the issues related to food chain contamination associated with country food consumption and breast feeding. As it appeared unrealistic to consider environmental risks without integrating them into a wider health framework, the PCB Resource Committee was renamed the Food, Contaminants and Health Committee in 1 994 to formally recognize this shift in perspectives and simultaneously consider both benefits and risks. In 1 996 this committee was merged Northern Contaminants Program Human Health Review Team with the Avativut/Iiusivut (Eco-Research) Steering Committee to form the Nunavik Nutrition and Health Committee to consider not only research and communication on risks, but also different levels of benefits and health issues associated with the various foodstuffs or food preparation and transformation practices in Nunavik. The scope of the committee has broadened through time to contextualize and communicate scientific information on contaminants, health and nutrition within a framework that is more responsive to the population's needs and the multiple factors influencing health. This evolution is reflected in the approaches to communication, health promotion and education taken by the Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services. Valuable lessons have been learned through practice and research in this region regarding the delivery of balanced messages on these issues based on the best known science to date, all the while promoting healthy diet and lifestyle behaviours.

Aboriginal Perspectives on Contaminants and Health Eric Loring, Inuit Tapirisat of Canada Northern Aboriginal people rely on traditional/country food, which they hunt and harvest from the land, for much of their nutritional i"ntake, their cultural identity and for economic reasons. A traditional diet is healthy and well balanced; however, reports of heavy metals, radionuclides and persistent organic pollutants in traditional/country food sources have compromised the confidence northern Aboriginal peoples have in their food . Community members are confused and scared when they hear that their traditional/country food is contaminated - they need an answer to their question, "Is my food safe to eat?" Southern food is available in the North but the choices are limited, costs are high and the nutritional value is questionable. Further, there is more to traditional/country foods than nutrition. With it comes socio-cultural, economic and environmental benefits, as well as a knowledge of the land and the animals; it is often said, "When I eat traditional food I know who I am." Communicating knowledge on contaminants to Aboriginal people without creating fear and confusion is not an easy task. Levels of contaminants in ppm and substances with technical names mean very little to community members. Aboriginal people need to know in plain language what chemicals and how much is in the water, soil, sediment, air, wildlife and people, how much is getting into "me" and from where, and - perhaps the most important piece of information, and the hardest to obtain and communicate - what are the benefits versus the risks of continuing to consume traditional/country food .

Work has, and is, being undertaken to determine the relative risks of exposure to contaminants through consuming a traditional diet versus the nutritional, cultural, spiritual and economic implications of changing to a western diet, but more research on the effects of the levels of contaminants found in the Arctic and in traditional/ country foods is needed. We can provide information on where and how the contaminants are coming from but we cannot tell the community members what it means to them. Since 1 991, the Aboriginal partners and community members have become far more knowledgeable about the issues related to contaminants in the Arctic and have engaged community members in many studies, allowing traditional knowledge to become incorporated. Each year, more community-driven projects are being proposed. They have influenced Canadian domestic and international positions and gone to the United Nations where they enlightened the world to the unique environment of the Arctic and the value of the culture of Arctic indigenous peoples. Yet, we must still work harder to improve our ability to answer the question "What does this all mean to me?".

The workshop, Contaminants and Human Health in the Canadian Arctic: an Update, brought together approximately 60 key researchers and others with interests in contaminants and health in the North to focus on contaminants-related research and results since the 1 997 CACAR. Through a series of presentations and question-and-answer periods, workshop participants examined the new state of knowledge with respect to contaminant exposure in the North, effects and toxicology, as well as benefits and risks of traditional/country food consumption. In smaller working groups, participants also discussed research gaps and modifications to the NCP blueprints and, as an initiative to synthesize results in a broader context, looked at the conclusions that could be drawn and how these could be developed into key messages for delivery in the North.

Information presented and discussed at this workshop is being incorporated in the major assessments by the NCP - the Canadian Arctic Contaminants Assessment Report II - and by AMAP, both of which are scheduled for release in Fall 2002. This information will also be used in revising NCP blueprints and setting priorities for NCP Phase III.
The workshop was held in February 2001; full proceedings of the workshop will be available by the fall of 2001.

Northern Contaminants Program Human Health Review Team lnuvik Regional Human Contaminants Monitoring Program: Communication Activities Valoree Walker, Aurora Research Institute, c/o lnuvik Regional Health and Social Services Board, Bag Service #2, lnuvik, NT XOE OTO; Phone (867) 777-3298; Fax (867) 777-4264; E-mail: walker@gov.nt.ca Karen Tofflemire, Program Coordinator, lnuvik Regional Health and Social Services Board, lnuvik, NT; Bill Wrathall, lnuvik Regional Health and Social Services Board, lnuvik, NT; Eleanor Wein, Canadian Circumpolar Institute, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB; Jay Van Oostdam, Health Canada, Ottawa, ON The Inuvik Regional Health and Social Services Board initiated the Inuvik Regional Human Contaminants Monitoring Program in 1997. The overall objective of this study was to establish baseline levels of specific heavy metal and organochlorine contaminants in the blood of women and their newborns from communities in the Inuvik Region, Northwest Territories. Collection of data from this region completed the Northwest Territories database, since this type of data has already been gathered from all other Health Board regions of the Northwest Territories and Nunavut. Results of this program can be found in the Synopsis of Research Conducted Under the Northern Contaminants Program 1999-2000 (Walker et al. 2000), as well as in the regional report (Tofflemire 2000) .

Relationships were explored between contaminant levels in maternal blood and contaminant levels in neonatal blood. The program also described the relationships of contaminant exposure through the consumption of traditional food, and through certain other lifestyle factors. The focus of the 2000-200 I fiscal year was to distribute individual results, communicate regional results to communities, produce and disseminate a regional report and continue with educating professionals and the general public regarding contaminants in the North. The project came to a close in July 2000.
Most contaminants measured were found in low levels in the Inuvik region . The results tended to be lower than in the Eastern Arctic and other regions, such as Greenland.
Traditional food consumption is important for women of reproductive age.

To communicate the results of the lnuvik Regional Human Contaminants Monitoring Program to participants, communities and all interested parties, and to contribute to the territorial database on levels of environmental contaminants in Northerners.
2. To inform and educate professionals in the environmental and public health field.
To serve as a resource and disseminate timely information, to allow for Inuvik region residents to make informed decisions regarding their health, lifestyle and environmental contaminants.

Increasing concern surrounding long-range transport of contaminants prompted studies to establish a baseline of contaminant levels existing in Northerners, particularly among vulnerable populations, such as mothers and newborns.

Contaminants of concern are released into the environment from around the world, and carried northward by atmospheric and marine pathways. This study explores contaminant exposure from both traditional food consumption and lifestyle factors, while examining organochlorines and metals in maternal and umbilical cord blood, as well as mercury levels in maternal hair.

The program had a total of I 04 participants from the Inuvik region. During the sample collection period of June 1998 to June 1999, a total of 185 blood samples were taken (95 maternal and 90 cord), 73 hair samples were given and I 02 questionnaires were completed . Low levels of contaminants were found in the samples. The results of this program (Walker et al. 2000, Tofflemire 2000) were similar to existing data from other regions in the Canadian North, in particular, the western Arctic, Mackenzie region (Walker and Corriveau I 998). Levels of exposure to contaminants were generally within guideline levels, with only a few exceptions. This study also confirms the importance of traditional food among women of reproductive age.

The importance of timely communication of results cannot be underestimated. It has been shown that a need exits for development of communications in the local communities. This includes use of multiple media and pathways to deliver messages to a wider audience, and the need to deliver both risk and benefit information on these topics (Lampe et ~I. 2000). Similar discussion groups have also visited this conclusion, stating, "it is the utmost importance (and respect) to report findings back to the community - in plain language." The Inuvik Regional Human Contaminants Monitoring Program aimed to meet the needs of the region with respect to communications and made communication the focus of the conclusion of the project.
The communications and report generation phase of the project was completed between April and July 2000.

The presentations aimed to educate the community as a whole about contaminants, inform them of the regional results - including comparisons to other regions, discussed why pregnant women participated and suggested ways to reduce exposure. The activities described above were well received by local communities and medical personnel. The following numbers reflect the education and communication efforts that were received in the Inuvik Region, from April to July 2000:
• Every community in the region ( I 00%) received the regional report and additional educational handouts.
• All CHRs and nurses from every community ( l 00%) received detailed information and guidance regarding the program and plans for results dissemination.
• Presentations occurred in six communities (50%) in the Inuvik Region . The six communities were home to 79% of the women who participated in the study.

• Participant packages were created for all women in the study; however, some participants had migrated to different communities and/or provinces by the end of the study. Efforts were made to find any participant who had relocated. By the end of the study, 89% of participants received personal packages. In the case of a returned package, the personal results were destroyed.

While making community visits, it was noted that the CHRs were especially helpful in disseminating information and generating discussions. The various representatives appreciated being a key part of the project and thus helped with the success of results dissemination. The medical personnel in the Inuvik region were also responsive to being educated about contaminants and the project. Teamwork among various departments at the Inuvik Regional Hospital, the community health centres, and Government of Northwest Territories, Department of Health and Social Services, and local community organizations proved to be invaluable. More discussion can always be carried out in the various communities regarding contaminants issues; this need was noted at the conclusion of this project.

Communication of results from research is an important and integral part of the Northern Contaminants Program, and is of great importance for the communities in the Inuvik region. The explanation of data can be difficult and abstract; data must be presented in a contextual manner that answers the questions about which local communities are interested in learning. Most community members found it helpful to discuss the issues, as opposed to only reading the information. Reading and comprehension levels vary among community members. The communities were happy to have an opportunity to learn and voice an opinion on the subject. The women who participated felt pleased that they had made a contribution to the community and appreciated the personal results packages. Most women were content with the information they had received, while others required more discussion concerning their results.

Harvesting, sharing, processing and consuming traditional food are important to cultural identity. Any concerns about contaminants in these foods can affect both the physical and social well-being of people of the North. Traditional foods are nutritious and contain only low amounts of contaminants in the Inuvik region. However, it is important for communities to remain informed about what contaminants are and at what levels they may be of concern. Continuing with monitoring programs in the future will allow us to see if levels of contaminants are changing over time. Education regarding these issues will help local communities make healthy lifestyle choices.

New chemicals include substances not currently monitored by the Northern Contaminants Program but of potential concern based on known persistence, extent of usage and toxicology. Chemicals in this study include brominated flame retardants, polychlorinated naphthalenes (PCNs), coplanar polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), short-chain chloroparaffins (SCCPs), polychlorinated diphenyl ethers (PCDEs), modern agrochemicals, pesticide enantiomers, synthetic musks (artificial fragrances), chlorinated phenols and haloacetic acids.

Air samples collected at Arctic monitoring stations from January 1994 to January 1995 were analyzed for PCNs, coplanar PCBs (mono- and non-ortho congeners) and polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs). Ranges of LPCNs and Lcoplanar PCBs (pg·m-3) were Alert: 0.11 to 1.03 and 0.03 to 0.19; Dunai: 0.21 to 2.6 and 0.18 to 0.86. Opposite seasonal trends were found for the two compound classes. PCNs were highest in winter, early spring and late fall, and lowest in summer. Coplanar PCBs were elevated in summer and lower in the colder months. PCNs and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons show similar seasonality, su_ggesting that combustion may contribute PCNs to Arctic air. LPBDE concentrations (pg·m-3) ranged between 7 to 72, 1 1 to 860 and 42 to 2200 for samples collected at Dunai, Alert and Tagish, respectively.

Relatively high concentrations of PBDEs were observed during the summer months at Tagish . This could be attributed to volatilization of PBDEs from recent local incineration of discarded household/commercial items, 93 and/or from re-volatilization of PBDEs from the soil in the vicinity of the incineration sites. The source of PBDEs in Tagish area will be further investigated in 2001-2002. Concentrations of SCCPs in the Alert air samples were highest in the late summer months. SCCPs levels (pg·m-3) ranged from 1.07 to 7.25 and were dominated by contributions by the chlorododecanes. The above air samples, and 1998 sets collected in Arctic Finland and at the Swedish west coast, were analyzed for chlordane enantiomers. and cis-chlordane were non-racemic in the air samples, but racemic in surface water samples collected from the northern Canada Basin in 1994. Nonracemic chlordanes are commonly found in soils. This suggests that the source of chlordane in Arctic air has changed over time, with a greater proportion of "recycled" chlordane in recent years, whereas seawater under the ice cap retains the signature of older chlordane emissions.

LPCNs and Lcoplanar PCBs were determined in blubber of beluga from Pangnirtung and ringed seal from Kimmirut, collected in 1994 and 1993, respectively. PCNs ranged from 40 to 384 pg·g-1 in beluga and 29 to 63 pg-g-1 in ringed seal; ranges for coplanar PCBs in the two animals were 14 to 394 ng·g-1 and 15 to 33 ng·g-1 • An assessment of dioxin-like toxic equivalents (TEOs) from these two compound classes showed that, although PCNs were about 500 times less abundant than coplanar PCBs, they contributed 11 % of the TEO. Synthetic musks were determined in ringed seal blubber, Arctic char muscle and blue mussels from the Canadian Arctic, and lake trout from Lake Ontario. All Arctic samples were below the limit of detection ( < 1 ng-g- 1), except for one seal blubber sample which contained 5 to 12 ng·g-1 of the polycyclic musks HHCB and HHCB-lactone, and 5 ng-g-1 of musk ketone, a nitro musk. Lake trout samples contained a wider variety of musks and at generally higher levels.

Polychlorinated naphthalenes (PCNs) at Alert and Dunai were elevated in winter, early spring and late fall, and were lowest in summer. Coplanar polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) showed the opposite trend, being higher in late spring through early fall, and lower in winter; they were three times higher at Dunai than Alert. The seasonal differences may reflect a greater contribution of combustion sources for PCNs and evaporative sources for coplanar PCBs.

The rationale for undertaking a study of new chemicals in the Arctic environment was presented in previous reports to the NCP (Bidleman et al. 1999, Muir et al. 1999). "New" chemicals are those which are currently used and/or not presently included in monitoring programs. Substances undergoing investigation in this project include: brominated flame retardants (polybrominated diphenyl ethers IPBDEs], hexabromocyclododecane IHBCDD], decabromobiphenyl and tetrabromobisphenol-A ITBBPA]); industrial chemicals (PCNs, coplanar PCBs (mono- and non-ortho-congeners), SCCPs, PCDEs, chlorophenolic compounds]; modern agrochemicals; pesticide enantiomers; synthetic musks; and haloacetic acids (HAAs). The research proposed here directly relates to the NCP Blueprint for International Activities, Section 1.3, Other Chemicals of Potential Concern. Certain aspects also contribute to other sections of the Blueprint. Investigation of enantiomers aids in detecting and interpreting trends in relation to emission control strategies by providing a means of distinguishing "recycled" pesticide from new releases.

Chlordanes in air at Great Lakes monitoring stations showed downward trends from 1992-1995 with t, 12 of 3.2 to 6.9 years for TC, 5.9 to 23 years for CC and 5.0 to 33 years for TN (Cortes et al. 1998).

Concentration data were divided into winter-spring (November to April) and summer-fall (May to October) periods and analyzed by simple linear regression of In (TC + CC) vs . year (first order plot). The fraction of TC = Frc = TC/(TC + CC) was also plotted vs. year to examine long-term changes in isomer proportions.

Chlordane enantiomers in air samples from the Arctic stations at Alert and Dunai (mostly 1 994-1995, with a few from 1993 and 1996; Pallas 1998), and the temperate station at Rorvik on the Swedish west coast were determined as an indicator of historical residue emissions, since non-racemic chlordanes have been found in soils (Aigner et al. 200 I, Wiberg et al. 2001) and in ambient air from the Great Lakes region (Bidleman et al. 1998, Ulrich and Hites 1998). The samples from Alert and Dunai were mostly monthly composites of archived weekly extracts (see PCN section above) with a few additional individual weekly samples. Those from Pallas and Rorvik were 7-day samples collected once per month. Enantiomers were determined using published methods (Bidleman et al. 1998).

Regressions showed significant declines of In (TC + CC) over the l 4-year period in both seasons (p < 0.00 l) (Table 6). Apparent values of t 112 were 7.7 years in winterspring and 6. l years in summer to fa ll, similar to the time trends found by Hung et al. (200 I) for the 1993-1997 period. Many years of observation indicates that the ratio of TC/CC undergoes seasonal cycles in Arctic air, higher in winter to spring and lower in summer to fall (Bidleman 1999, Halsall et al. 1998, Hung et al. 2001).

Between l 984-1997, Frc declined significantly in both winter to spring (p < 0.002) and summer-fall (p < 0.03) seasons (Table 6). This suggests that sources of chlordane in Arctic air have changed over the last l 4 years and are now depleted in TC. The Frc in technical chlordane is 0.54, and when weighed for the slightly higher vapour pressure of TC, the expected atmospheric Frc in equilibrium with technical chlordane is 0.62 (Jantunen et al. 2000).

The Frc in soils is about the same or lower than in technical chlordane (Aigner et al. Confounding the interpretation of Frc values is the fact that technical heptachlor was also used in agriculture and as a termiticide. Technical heptachlor is contaminated with chlordane isomers, especially TC, so higher Frc in soils or air could be associated with this source. (200 I) identified occasional spikes of high Frc in Arctic air samples during l 995 and associated them with transport events from Russia. A number of these events also showed elevated heptachlor levels.

Nearly all were non-racemic, with depletion of the first-eluting enantiomer, except for two Pallas samples in February and March. The average EFs were significantly non-racemic at Pallas (0.487, p < 0.05) and Rorvik (0.472, p < 0.001). Enantiomers of heptachlor exo-epoxide (HEPX) were determined in four to eight samples from each station and results showed strong enrichment of the ( +) enantiomer in all cases (average EFs: Alert = 0.684, Dunai = 0.663, Pallas = 0.665, Rorvik = 0.696).

The non-racemic chlordanes and HEPX in Arctic air provides evidence that soil-derived pesticides are revolatilizing in warmer regions of the Northern Hemisphere and undergoing long-range atmospheric transport. Have chlordanes in Arctic air always been non-racemic, even in the mid- I 980s and earlier? This is difficult to answer because no air samples from the 1980s are available for examination. However, chlordanes in surface water collected from the northern Canada Basin collected in 1994 were racemic (EFs = 0.499 for TC and 0.50 I for CC). HEPX in seawater was non-racemic with an average EF = 0.639. Most of these samples were collected between 72° to 90° latitude and under ice cover. Chlordane and HEPX EFs in Arctic cod (Boreogadus saida), which feed on zooplankton, are similar to those in water (Wiberg et al., 2000). It is likely that these enantiomer signatures represent chlordane and HEPX loadings to the Arctic Ocean sometime in the past.

In this study, temporal trends of atmospheric polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and organochlorine pesticides from 1 993 to 1 997 have been examined. Declining trends were observed for several of the lower PCB congeners reflecting falling levels in source regions and subsequently less material being subject to long-range transport to Alert. No apparent trends were observed for the higher congeners in contrast to southern measurements, except for PCB 180, indicating a lag time for rates of decline between the Arctic and source regions. Most organochlorine pesticides manifested declining trends except the current-use pesticides, such as endosulfan I. From the time series of trans-/cis-chlordane ratios, heptachlor and back trajectory analysis, it can be inferred that sporadic uses of technical chlordane and/or heptachlor in eastern and western Russia and Europe/ North Atlantic might have resulted in fresh input into the Arctic atmosphere between 1995 and 1997.

Operate a major long-term trends measurement station at Alert, Nunavut (in operation since 1992) in parallel with an eastern Arctic site (Kinngait) and a western Russian Arctic station to contribute to the next assessments by the Northern Contaminants Program and the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme, and to advise Canadian negotiators in preparing contaminant control strategies.

Atmospheric measurements of persistent organic pollutants, including herbicides, pesticides, synthetic industrial compounds and PAHs, have been made on a weekly basis in the Canadian (Alert, Tagish, Kinngait [Cape Dorset]) and Russian Arctic (Dunai, Amderma) since January 1992. These measurements are essential since there has been growing concern about contamination of the Arctic environment by OCs and PAHs, whose environmental persistence and fate are influenced by a diversity of physicakhemical properties. Long-term time series will help to determine whether the atmospheric concentrations and deposition of priority pollutants in the Arctic is increasing or decreasing in response to various national and international control initiatives.

Regular weekly atmospheric measurements of OCs and PAHs continued at Alert. This involved the collection, extraction and analysis of air samples. The site of Kinngait was re-activated in October 2000 to quantify the change in the eastern Canadian Arctic by comparison with observations made four years earlier. Similar measurements were conducted at Amderma, Russia, with co-support from the Canadian International Development Agency, Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Northern Contaminants Program and MSC.

Data analysis has been progressing well with the recent publication of a paper describing PCB trends at Alert (Hung et al. 200 I a) and the submission of a companion paper on OC pesticides trends (Hung et al. Results from these two publications are outlined below.

Figure 1 shows the seasonal cycles and trends of PCB congeners 31, 101, 138 and 180 at Alert, determined by the digital filter (OF) trend analysis technique (Nakazawa et al. 1997). By comparing the trends, it was noted that the lower chlorinated congeners, such as PCB 28 (not shown), 3 1 and 5 2 (not shown), declined from 1 993 to 1 997. In each case, both the seasonal minimum and maximum declined over the 5 years. However, no clear trend was apparent for most of the penta- and hexa-chlorinated congeners, such as PCB 105, 118, 138 and 153 (PCB 138 is shown as an example in Figure 1 ). First order half-lives (tv,) were estimated using the linear regression slopes (m) of the OF trend lines:

For the PCBs, no pattern was apparent between half-lives and the degree of chlorination, with half-lives ranging from 3 to 17 years. The half-lives at Alert were typically longer than those derived from temperate background/ rural sites from the early 1 990s (Simcik et al. 1999).

Figure 2 shows the seasonal cycles and trends of selected OCs at Alert and the weekly average temperature recorded at the sampling site. Most of the selected OCs showed declining trends over the 5 years, except dieldrin and endosulfan I. The trans-/cis-chlordane ratio (TC/CC) increased above unity on various occasions (Figure 3) . These increases were coincident to periods when the levels of heptachlor were unusually high.

From Figure 1, it can be seen that levels of some of the lower chlorinated congeners do appear to be dropping in the Arctic atmosphere, albeit at a slower rate (i.e. longer half-lives) than temperate studies. This trend for the lighter congeners is probably due to the dominating effect of long-range transport whereby levels in the Arctic will simply reflect the falling levels encountered in the source regions. This, in combination with their relatively fast hydroxyl radical (OH) depletion rates during the Arctic summer, may explain the temporal decline of the lighter congeners. The lack of a declining PCB temporal trend for the more chlorinated congeners may be due to several factors. The lower temperatures encountered in the Arctic, coupled with winter darkness, will slow both biotic and 105 abiotic degradation relative to temperate regions. Importantly, global fractionation (Wania and Mackay 1996) - a process by which chemicals may be latitudinally 'fractionated' according to the ambient temperature and their physicakhemical properties - may have the effect of maintaining Arctic air concentrations, while levels in temperate regions are showing apparent reductions. However, the picture is complicated by notable exceptions; for example, PCB 180 (heptachlorinated) shows a clear downward trend and has a calculated half-life of only 4 years at Alert (compared to 17 years for PCB 153, which showed an almost constant level over the 5 years of study). It is possible that heavier congeners might be subject to different removal processes than the lighter ones. Precipitation or scavenging processes (e.g. particulate deposition and snow scavenging) might be more important for the heavier congeners, while degradation via reaction with OH radicals was the dominant process for the removal of lighter congeners.

Elevated concentrations of OC pesticides were generally observed before and after the warmest time of the year (Figure 2). This pattern is especially apparent for "currentuse" pesticides, such as the HCHs and endosulfan I, and indicates that the atmosphere at Alert was mainly influenced by long-range transport and results of application patterns at temperate locations. Most of the banned OCs showed declining trends over the five years and the half-lives measured in the Arctic were generally longer than at temperate locations. This is probably due to slower transformation processes at lower temperatures in the Arctic, as well as the general lack of air mass movement out of the Arctic environment, especially during winter when air originating from the strong Siberian anticyclone curves eastwards around the Arctic region (Barrie et al. 1992) making dissipation difficult.

The half-life of cis-chlordane was very short compared to trans-chlordane. This seems improbable because the trans-isomer is less stable than the cis-isomer. A hint of why this should occur might be found by examination of the TC/CC ratio. The technical mixture used in the U.S. contains TC/CC in the range of 1.26 to 1.35 (Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme 1998). The ratios in the Arctic atmosphere were generally < 1 in recent years (Oehme et al. I 996, Arctic Monitoring and Figure 1. Although this is a huge region, and, therefore, it is not possible to distinguish actual source areas, it does suggest that for many of the weeks (where TC/CC > 1) the air originated from the Eurasian side of the Arctic as opposed to the North American continent. The high TC/CC ratios observed during these weeks may reflect the influence of a source area(s) where relatively recent chlordane usage has occurred.

Also plotted on Figure 3 are the concentrations of heptachlor measured. The concentrations of heptachlor, a past-used pesticide, were usually very low and mostly below detection limit. However, around those periods when the TC/CC ratios were high, the concentrations of heptachlor were also unusually high. There seems to be new supply of heptachlor into the Arctic air during the winters of 1995- 1996 and 1996- 1997, coincident with TC/CC > I. Based on global import figures (United Nations Environment Programme 1996), it is possible that there was indeed fresh input into the Arctic atmosphere. Technical chlordane mixtures usually contain some heptachlor (- 7 %) When the TC/CC peaked together with heptachlor, it could suggest fresh usage of chlordane mixtures as well.

In summary, some PCBs (lower chlorinated congeners) and most of the OCs (except current-use pesticides) monitored at Alert have shown declining trends over the five years of study, albeit at slower rates than in temperate regions. The Arctic atmosphere is still strongly influenced by long-range transport and acts as a sink for both OC pesticides and PCBs. It is thus important to continue the atmospheric measurements of these compounds at Alert.
