Spatial Trends in Loadings and Historical Inputs of Mercury Inferred from Arctic Lake Sediment Cores Venghuot Cheam, National Water Research Institute, Box 5050, Burlington ON L7R 4A6; Phone: (905) 336-4755; Fax: (905) 336-6430; E-mail: ven.cheam@cciw.ca; Derek Muir, National Water Research Institute, Box 5050, Burlington ON L7R 4A6; Phone: (905) 319-6921; Fax: (905) 336-6430; E-mail: derek.muir@cciw.ca; Doug Halliwell, Atmospheric Environment Branch, Environment Canada, Yellowknife NT XlA 1E2; Phone: (867) 669-47 41; Fax: (867) 873-8185; E-mail: doug.halliwell@ec.gc.ca Gino Sardella, National Water Research Institute, Burlington ON; John Smol, Queens University, Kingston, ON; Marianne Douglas, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON; Reinhard Pienitz and Warwick Vincent, Laval University, Quebec, QC Historical deposition and fluxes of mercury (Hg) were studied on five sediment cores. The cores were collected from northern Nunavut (Lake Baird Inlet and Lake AXAJ), central Northwest Territories (Lake Rummy and Lake TK-54) and northern Quebec (Lake Oksana). The Hg, iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn) data were assessed as a whole in regards to the co-movement of Hg with Fe and Mn during diagenesis. To date, our data indicate no redistribution or co-movement of Hg with Fe and Mn after deposition at the sediment surface, i.e. the Hg depth profiles truly represent the historical deposition of Hg onto the sediment. Recent Hg fluxes are higher than pre-industrial fluxes, resulting in a range of enrichment factors of 1.2 to 2.7, which are in general agreement with those reported by Lockhart et al. ( 1998, 2000a) in other parts of the Canadian Arctic. Surprisingly, the lead (Pb) profiles for the lakes in Nunavut and the Northwest Territories show no maxima corresponding to the use of leaded gasoline, as opposed to Lake Oksana, which showed a maximum matching the maximum use of alkyl Pb used in fuel.
Recent mercury (Hg) fluxes are higher than the pre-industrial fluxes.
The Hg enrichment factors range from 1. 2 to 2. 7.
A definite Hg deposition pattern is not yet obvious in Canada's North.
To determine the depth profiles of Hg, lead (Pb), manganese (Mn) and iron (Fe) in fifteen dated Arctic sediment cores over a 3-year period, with the main focus on Hg.
To quantify geographical trends in fluxes of Hg and its enrichment factors in Nunavut, the Northwest Territories (NWT) and Nunavik.

To link Hg findings with those of paleolimnological indicators, persistent organic pollutants (POPs), as well as indicators of biogeochemical processes of Mn and Fe, all of which are obtained from the same cores or cores from the same sites, whenever possible.

To complement existing data on Hg in Arctic sediment cores with data generated over a much wider latitudinal and longitudinal range than previous work, in order to provide a better understanding of Hg in Canada's North.
To provide loading data for Pb, which may help elucidate the understanding of Hg pathways and sources.

Mercury has emerged as a priority contaminant in the Arctic and in inland lakes of central and eastern Canada, given evidence for increasing levels of Hg in biota (Braune I 999, Muir et al. 1997, Pierce et al. 1998) and in lake sediments (Barrie et al. 1997, Landers et al. 1998). Several recent Northern Contaminants Program (NCP) studies have dealt with Hg pollution, for example: Mercury and their contaminants in a laminated sediment core (Lockhart et al. 2000a); Atmospheric transport, oxidation and fallout in Nunavik (Poissant 2000); Mercury measurements in Alert (Schroeder 2000); Mercury in Salluit (Dewailly 2000); and Mercury in fish (Lockhart et al. 2000b). This project attempts to address the major gap identified by Landers et al. ( 1998) - the need for a wide spatial scale of Hg deposition as inferred from sediment cores - and proposes to study 1 5 sediment cores over a 3-year period; five sediment cores are reported here. The project, which began in April 2000, complements the NCP study at Devon Island (Lockhart et al. 2000a) by investigating the fluxes time series for Hg in sediment cores collected from various parts of the High Arctic, central NWT and northern Quebec. In addition to Hg, Pb, Mn and Fe are included. Results that assess the diagenesis (redox cycling) of Hg, if any, by using similar approaches used by Gobeil et al. (1999) are also reported.

The five sediment cores studied were taken from Lake AXAJ, Lake Baird Inlet, Lake Oksana, Rummy Lake and Lake TK-54. Figure I shows their approximate locations and indicates those that have been and will be cored. These cores were collected for a Toxic Substances Research Initiative study on POPs and paleolimnologicals (Muir 2000), and the sediment slices were shared for this study. Sediment cores were obtained with a I O cm diameter KB corer or a Glew corer (Glew 1 988) through holes drilled into the ice, from a small boat or from a float-equipped Cessna 206 or other aircraft. Cores were extruded on site and slices placed in polyethylene (Whir!Pak®) bags. Slice thickness depended on apparent sedimentation rates. In low sedimentation systems, typical of High Arctic lakes, slice thickness was 0.5 cm for the top 5 cm (i.e. to achieve maximum temporal resolution while obtaining sufficient mass for 2 10 Pb dating and contaminant analysis) . At more southerly locations, with typically higher sedimentation rates, slice thickness was I cm. Table I lists the lake sediment cores studied this year with their positions, dated radioisotopes and sedimentation rates. Lakes Baird Inlet and AXAJ were 210Pb-dated at the National Water Research Institute (NWRI), Burlington, whereas the other three lakes were dated with 210pb and 137Cs at the Freshwater Institute, Winnipeg.

The vessel was assembled, sealed and fitted onto a microwave rotor, which was placed in a high-pressure microwave oven (MLS 1200 Mega, Milestone). The sample was digested in the microwave field and the temperature maintained at 200°C for 15 minutes. The vessel was removed from the microwave oven and the cooled digest was brought to 100 mL volume with deionized water. The high temperature and the strong oxidizing conditions of the digestion ensured destruction of the substrate and good recovery of analytes. The resultant solution was analyzed for Pb by inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) (PO-2, VG Elemental); Hg by cold vapour atomic absorption spectrometry (CV-AAS); and Fe and Mn by ICP atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES). Mercury (II) was reduced to elemental Hg in an automated continuous flow system by the action of stannous chloride. The Hg was sparged from the solution with a stream of purified air and passed through an absorption cell of a Hg analyzer (LDC/Milton-Roy). For reactive Fe and Mn, a 1 N HCl extraction was used (Leventhal and Taylor 1990, Gobeil et al. 1999). Both reactive and total extractable Fe and Mn were analyzed using ICP-AES. The National Laboratory for Environmental Testing (NLET), NWRI, Burlington, analyzed all samples. NLET is a certified analytical laboratory, which participates regularly and performs consistently very well in the NCP interlaboratory studies as well as in the regional, national and international intercomparison exercises.

Prior to the actual analysis, methods validation was carried out to ensure precise and accurate long-term data generation of Hg, Pb, Fe and Mn. Certified sediment reference materials were used to ensure precise and accurate recoveries of metals. Different weights of real sediments were tested to arrive at a small, optimum weight to be used so that thin slices of sediment (small weight) could be effectively analyzed to give reliable results. Furthermore, we tested the long-term ruggedness of methods by having two different analysts analyze 40 different sediment samples 6 months apart. All the validation results were satisfactory and have been presented elsewhere (Cheam et al. 2000, 2001 a, 2001 b).

The excess 210Pb data for the five sediment cores, shown in Figure 2, indicates a general rapid decline of the isotope from the 1990s to the 1900s; this indicates overall that the slices are date-distinguishable and thus can be used to study spatial loadings of pollutants. Some of the cores are also supported by the mes data (Figure 2). For Lake TK-54, the 137Cs data show a spike in 1987, which corresponds well to the Chernobyl reactor accident in 1986. Also, it shows a large spike in 1958; this corresponds closely to the testing of nuclear bombs which released mes into the atmosphere in the early 1960s. Lake Rummy has a spike of mes around 1988, approximately coinciding with the Chernobyl accident in 1 986, but does not have an apparent peak around 1960s. However, since the deposition dates are estimated based on mid-points of slices, the "possibly-abundant " mes activities around 1960 (in the middle of 1973-1948 time span, which corresponds to the point furthest away from the 1 973 and I 948 mid-points) could well have been missed in the measurement process. Lake Oksana has a broad peak of mes activities covering the 1987-1971 time span, but curiously has no peak around the 1960s.

Figure 3 shows the depth profiles for Hg, Fe, Mn and Pb in the five sediment cores. For Hg, the recent slices (- 1970-2000) contain higher fluxes than the preindustrial slices (- 1860 or older). Although it is not readily obvious for Lake Oksana and Lake TK-54, the calculation of fluxes indicates excess in the recent slices.

For Hg, Fe and Mn, there is no indication of movement of Hg with Fe and Mn as their profiles are not synchronous, i.e. they do not have the same general pattern as observed by Gobeil and Cossa ( 1993) for marine sediments from the Laurentian trough. Even in their situation, the authors showed that the redistribution of Hg represented only a minor fraction of the total Hg deposited at the surface.
Thus, it seems there is no redistribution of Hg in our sediment cores and the observed Hg profiles represent the true deposits at the surface.

While most studies using lake sediments have shown that Hg profiles reflect atmospheric trends and fluxes (e.g. Fitzgerald et al. 1998, Lockhart et al. 1998, Landers et al. 1998), there is a potential for post-depositional movement during diagenesis producing distortions in vertical profiles (Rasmussen 1994, Gobeil et al. 1999). To evaluate this possibility, this study included determination of Fe and Mn using a IN hydrochloric acid extraction (Gobeil et al. 1 999) to liberate the reactive phases such as Mn and Fe oxyhydroxides. While Gobeil et al. ( 1999) observed some correlation between the percent reactive Fe and total Hg concentration in marine sediment cores from the Arctic basins, indicating some degree of Hg movement with Fe, our data to date indicates no apparent correlation between the two concentrations. Figure 4 plots the percent reactive Fe versus total Hg concentrations for four cores (the fifth core from Lake Baird Inlet did not have enough mass for this experiment) and shows a lack of any correlation . Also, it must be noted that in Gobeil et al. ( 1999) sediments were quite different from this study's as they were marine in nature, collected from a Figure 2. 210Pb and 137Cs activities in core slices from Lakes Rummy, TK-54, Oksana, Baird Inlet and AXAJ 1.4 '---__ ... Fluxes of Hg, Fe, Mn and Pb (μg·m-2·yr-1) Baird Inlet Baird Inlet uJ 0 0.E+00 .. 2 .. very deep depth ( ~ 2500 m to 4500 m) and the sedimentation rates were extremely low ( < 1 cm·ka-1) . Our data is in agreement with those of Lockhart et al. (2000c), who showed negligible diffusion and remobilization of Hg after deposition for three different sediment cores from Clay, Giauque and Stuart Lakes, where profiles corroborate very well with the well-recorded historical Hg emissions nearby those lakes.

The Pb profile for Lake Oksana is a revealing one; it peaks in the period of 1970 to 1980, when the maximum of alkyl Pb in gasoline was used, up to the early 1970s, followed by the gradual phase-in of unleaded gasoline, until 1980. The other four cores did not have Pb peaks, as in the Lake Oksana core. It is somewhat surprising that no Pb peaks were observed in these four cores, especially when Cheam et al. ( 1998) observed Pb pollution peaks in a snow pit during the period from 1 986 to 1 993 at Agassiz Ice Cap, Nunavut, or when other researchers observed the rise and fall of Pb concentrations in ice cores from Greenland (Candelone et al. 1995). Analyses of several sediment samples were also made for Pb isotopes 206, 207, 208 and 204, although no definite pattern was apparent and no specific information could be derived from the data at this time. Additional attempts will be made and will hopefully provide some useful information as to the metal origins.

The metal flux in sediments (μ,g·cm-2·yr-1) was calculated as the product of sedimentation rate (g·cm-2·yr-1) and concentration (J-Lg·g-1) in the samples. The fluxes were obtained for the five lakes for Hg, Pb, Fe and Mn. By assessing the relationship between metal fluxes in the pre-industrial era and fluxes in the recent era, an enrichment factor or flux ratio could be calculated.

Figure 5 compares the enrichment factor for the studied lakes to those in other parts of Canada, the United States and Europe.

The results of the first year of this research add significant findings to the existing data available for North America and Europe. Recent fluxes in Hg are higher than preindustrial ones, and the resulting enrichment factors range from 1.2 to 2.7, which are in general accordance with the published data for other northern regions. So far, the data on Hg, Fe and Mn (total and reactive) altogether strongly suggest that there is no remobilization/ redistribution of Hg with the Fe and Mn during the diagenesis. We are looking forward to further research in 2001 -2002 with anticipation as five more cores will be studied. It is hoped that more significant findings will be reported, which further confirms the no co-movement of Hg with Fe and Mn. Additionally, new data on Hg and Pb isotopes could be useful in determining the metal origins. Finally, as more data accumulate, we hope to generate the general pattern of Hg deposition in Canada's North and to assess the concept of cold condensation raised byWania and Mackay (1993).

Eddy Carmack, David Paton, Mary O'Brien and Darren Tuele, DFO, IOS, Sidney BC; Bruno Rosenberg, Dan Savoie and Harold Welch, DFO, Freshwater Institute, Winnipeg MB The Surface Heat Budget of the Arctic (SHEBA) project has provided a unique opportunity to collect organochlorine data during a complete year in the western Arctic Ocean. Analyses have been completed for air, water and ice, particles, algae, zooplankton (sorted size fractions), inverte~ brates and fish. Preliminary examination of the data reveals that ocean processes are important contributors to contaminant distributions. In particular, the interior ocean carries a polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB) signature that contains enriched lighter PCBs characteristic of distillation whereas the Chukchi Shelf water appears similar to Arochlor formulations with prominent contribution from the pentaCBs. Pesticides appear to be redistributed in the water column through biological productivity, which removes dieldrin, DDT and chlordane from surface water but releases them again in water below about 100 m during biological regeneration.

Water entering from the Bering Sea, measured in April 1998, contains an Arochlor 1254 or Sovol~like signature in contrast to the interior water of the Canada Basin which clearly carries a PCB signature containing a "distillation" component favoring the lighter chlorinated biphenyls (CBs).

In contrast to hexachlorocyclohexane (HCH), where concentrations are found to decrease from their highest values near the surface to very low values below 200 to 300 m, preliminary data for DDT, dieldrin and chlordane show trends suggestive of vertical transport and enrichment at depths where biological particles regenerate.

• Measure the intra-annual variability of contaminant transport and food-web accumulation in the Canada Basin from October 1997 to October 1998 from the drifting platform provided by the Canadian Coast Guard Ship (CCGS) des Grosel/iers and the Surface Heat Budget of the Arctic (SHEBA) project.

The SHEBA project was planned around the intentional besetting of a research vessel (CCGS des Groselliers) in the permanent pack of the Beaufort Gyre for a complete year beginning in early October 1997 (Welch 1998, Perovich et al. 1999). Given the platform and the physical studies to be conducted, SHEBA provided an invaluable opportunity to conduct research on the physical and biological processes that deliver, redistribute and biomagnify organochlorine (OC) contaminants in this region.

The Beaufort Gyre can be thought of as a large, relatively isolated ice-covered "mesocosm" in the interior Canada Basin. Previous work has shown this region to contain high concentrations of HCH (e.g. Hargrave et al. 1988, Macdonald et al. 2000a, Macdonald et al. 20006) and it was suspected that other pesticides with low Henry's Law constant might similarly be enriched. Several factors are thought to contribute to this region's sensitivity to persistent organic pollutants (POPs), including cold water, ice cover, low particle fluxes in the water and long residence time of the surface water (Macdonald et al. 2000a). Recent studies have shown the Canada Basin to contain a large reservoir of surface water which cannot easily shed its contaminants and which will therefore affect downstream locations (especially the Canadian Archipelago) for years to come (Macdonald et al. 1997, Macdonald et al. 1999b).

During the SHEBA drift (Figure l), samples were collected at intervals to measure POPs concentrations in air, water and ice, particles, algae, zooplankton (sorted size fractions), invertebrates and fish with the intention of observing how the ocean maintains contaminant burdens in the euphotic zone and how such contaminants transfer into the food web. The samples retrieved during SHEBA will provide information about the relationship between seasonal ice formation and melt, seasonal atmospheric transport and water column OC concentrations in the Canada Basin, and the coupling of water-borne contaminants into and up the food chain. Because personnel remained on the platform throughout the year's drift, there was an opportunity to collect large-volume samples using Infiltrex pumps and filters to yield valid data for OCs of concern like PCBs, chlordane and toxaphene. A full biological program allowed the collection of many different species which could be sorted on site into trophic levels. Analysis of stable isotope composition (8 13C, 8 15N) and OC concentration will allow a detailed look at the distribution of OCs as a function of trophic level and/or predator-prey relationships. Finally, physical and chemical data collected during the drift will allow the interpretation of OC data in the context of oceanographic processes which include seasonal stratification/ destratification and changes in water masses experienced during the drift. Data such as these are impossible to collect from ships carrying out transects simply due to time constraints and are, therefore, noticeably absent from recent assessments (e.g. Barrie et al. 1998, Macdonald et al. 2000a).
• Completing the analyses of samples collected during SHEBA.
• Collating the OC and isotope data into spread sheets.
• Interpreting ancillary physical and geochemical data to understand the oceanographic context of the SHEBA drift.
• Conducting a preliminary examination of the OC data.
At this time, all data are in hand, but the large task of interpreting and publishing the data in journals remains.

During the planning stages, we anticipated that the seasonal ice cover would provide a dominant influence on surface-water concentrations of OCs, and that we would witness the entry of contaminants from the ice surface in spring when the ice melted, discharging its inventory to the surface ocean . In view of the large size of the reservoir of the interior ocean and its slow decline in HCH burden as measured since the late 1980s, we did not expect there to be an obvious spatial signal, nor did we expect to see a significant downturn in contaminant inventories over the I -year period of the drift. Accordingly, SHEBA was viewed as a large mesocosm representative of the interior surface pool of the Beaufort Gyre, providing an opportunity to produce detailed, accurate vertical profiles for most of the OC contaminants in the top 250 m * The SHEBA drift is indicated by the open squares which identify where conductivitytemperature-depth (CTD) profiles were collected. OC profiles in the water column were collected during the six time intervals indicated along the drift as marked (November 1997, December 1997, February 1998, April 1998, July 1998 and September 1998) and to determine the pathways of these OCs into biota (both pelagic and ice algae).

SHEBA drifted westward, rapidly at times, exiting the Canada Basin before February to drift over the Chukchi Cap for 6 months before re-entering deep water in the Mendeleyev Abyssal Plain late in the program (Figure 1 ). As a consequence, the SHEBA time-series was primarily a transect which passed through watermass changes that clearly must be taken into account when interpreting trends in the OC data. The first complete set of transect data for OCs (bottle samples for a- and y-HCH ! Macdonald et al. l 999c]), showed relatively high concentrations of HCH under the pack ice in the interior Beaufort Sea. When SHEBA passed over the Chukchi Cap, the concentrations dropped dramatically reflecting the concentrations of HCH isomers in Pacific Ocean water that had recently entered the Arctic Ocean through the Bering Strait. This section, therefore, provided the first coherent transect connecting two regions where HCH time series have been maintained, one in the Canada Basin (Hargrave et al. 1988, Macdonald et al. 1999c) and one in the Bering and Chukchi Seas (Jantunen and Bidleman 1995, Jantunen and Bidleman 1998). The spatial distribution of HCH suggests that the marginal seas are clearing more rapidly than the interior ocean due partly to enhanced air-sea exchange over the shelves, which have less severe ice cover, and partly to more rapid replacement of shelf water by inflowing Pacific Ocean water.

During the I990s, the Arctic Ocean underwent dramatic change in watermass distribution and ice drift trajectories (Carmack et al. 1995, Macdonald 1996, McLaughlin et al. 1996, Carmack et al. 1997, Proshutinsky and Johnson 1997, Dickson 1999, Macdonald et al. 1999a). This change became all too evident during the launch of SHEBA when thick, multi-year ice could not be found and the ocean 's surface was observed to be exceptionally fresh (Welch 1998, Perovich et al. 1999).These two observations - thin ice, fresh surface water - have caused many to infer enhanced ice melt in Canada Basin during the 1 990s.

However, our SHEBA stable isotopic data (8 180) which allow us to discriminate between ice melt and runoff show that most of the freshening was caused by enhanced amounts of run off (Figures 2a, 2b) . The source of fresh water is important not only for understanding the recent changes in the oceanography but also for understanding the potential sources for contaminants. Recent work has uncovered a large shift in Arctic Ocean water properties and ice drift trajectories forced primarily by atmospheric pressure fields (McLaughlin et al. 1996, Proshutinsky and Johnson 1997, Macdonald et al. 1999a). Perhaps even more relevant to contaminant transport pathways, it has been discovered that runoff entering the Laptev and Kara Seas no longer feeds the transpolar drift but during the 1990s appears to have been diverted to the east to enter the Canada Basin (Ekwurzel et al. 2001 , Guay et al. 2001).

What these watermass changes will mean for contaminants is not yet clear, but some startling images are emerging from the SHEBA data. In Figures 3a to 3d, the PCB data collected from Infiltrex pumps deployed over the top 250 m of the water column show a remarkable transition from the Canada Basin to the Chukchi Cap (compare Figure 3a with 3b). The February profile, on the eastern flank of the Northwind Ridge (Figure 1) suggests a twocomponent PCB mixture: there are enhanced lighter PCBs (mono, di and tri congeners) but there is also an underlying envelope similar to PCB technical mixtures or the Russian technical mixture called Sovol (Schulz et al. 1989, Ivanov and Sandell 1992; Over the southern edge of the Chukchi Cap (April; Figure I), the profile looks far more strongly influenced by the technical mixture component (Figure 3b). As SHEBA drifted back toward the interior ocean, the profiles in July (Figure 3c) and September (Figure 3d) revealed a strengthened light PCB component. Although variations are evident within the vertical profiles, the predominant feature of these data is one of a two-component mixture distributed unevenly in space. It seems much more plausible that the PCB compositions along the track reflect the various water masses through which SHEBA passed. The oceanographic properties along the SHEBA drift track clearly show structure associated with the bathymetry of the Chukchi Plateau and that SHEBA passed through boundaries along its drift through this complex bathymetric region (Figure 2a). The dominant contribution of technical mixture, seen in April (Figure 3b), suggests strongly that this profile has been imported from the Pacific Ocean. The profiles collected in February, July and September, on the other hand, probably reflect a stronger influence of Canada Basin interior water which has accumulated an important component of its PCB inventory through the atmosphere. The inference to be drawn here is that PCBs have been delivered via the Pacific Ocean in water directly contaminated through, for example, runoff or spills, whereas the interior Arctic Ocean owes a significant portion of its PCB content to condensation and/or air~sea exchange which favours the lighter components as one progresses northward (Wania and Mackay 1993, Muir et al. 1996). Total PCB water concentrations, averaged over the entire vertical collection range, for April, July and September were 115.3, 31.3 and 45.4 pgxL-1, respectively.

Preliminary data for DDT, dieldrin and chlordane (Figures 4a to 4c) reveal vertical distributions very different from those observed for the HCHs where concentrations are found to decrease from their highest values near the surface to very low values below 200 to 300 m. From the oceanographic and PCB data shown in Figures 2 and 3, we can anticipate that changes in the pesticide profiles might in part be caused by watermass change. However, taking DDT as perhaps the best example, it seems likely that there is also a seasonal signal related to the biological cycle. In April and February of 1998, the DDT profiles were somewhat noisy, but reasonably uniform at about 2 pg·L-1 through the water column down to 250 m (Figure 4a) . By July, however, this uniformity has been destroyed with much lower DDT concentrations evident in the top I 00 m to 150 m and higher concentrations at about 200 m to 250 m. In September, the surface concen~ trations of DDT are again centred at about 2 pg·L-1 but higher concentrations are evident at or below about 150 m. Although watermass changes may contribute partly to the observed behaviour, there appears also to be a transfer of DDT from surface to deeper water in spring when biological production produces a vertical flux of organically rich particles.

SHEBA has produced a large, complex and unique data set for oceanographic properties and OC contaminants in water, air and biota. The small part of the data discussed here and elsewhere (Macdonald et al. 1999c) show a remarkable potential to apply these data to understand the transport processes for the various OC contaminants and their cycling in the upper ocean. Not shown here is an accompanying data set for OCs in biota. Together, the two data sets will shed light on how contaminants have entered the western Arctic Ocean, how they are distributed in the water column and how they enter the food web.

Atmospheric Mercury Transport, Oxidation and Fallout in Northern Quebec (Nunavik): an Important Potential Route of Contamination Laurier Poissant, Meteorological Service of Canada, Atmospheric Toxic Processes Section, Environment Canada, 105 McGill, Montreal, QC H2Y 2E7; Phone: (514) 283-1140; Fax: (514) 283-8869; E-mail: laurier.poissant@ec.gc.ca Marc Amyot, lnstitut national de la recherche scientifique - Eau (INRS-EAU), Sainte-Foy, QC; Michael Kwan, Nunavik Research Centre, Kuujjuaq, QC; Yves Begin, Centre d'etudes nordiques, University of Laval, Sainte-Foy, QC Recent observations of mercury and ozone concentrations along Hudson Bay in Kuujjuarapik, Quebec, (latitude 55° N) showed that mercury and ozone depletion events, originally observed in the high Arctic region, appeared at latitudes as low as 5 5° N. Depletion events were concomitant with large bromine monoxide concentration clouds, such as observed by the Global Ozone Monitoring Experiment satellite over Hudson Bay. Gaseous mercury speciation, air-snow mercury gas exchange flux measurements, as well as mercury concentrations surveyed in snow during a depletion event suggested that most of the mercury fallout occurring during depletion events is in the particle phase, is labile and very reactive (photoreducible). Indeed, following a depletion event, mercury concentration in the snow pack increased by up to 1600% of its pre-depletion event concentration, but about 50% of this newly deposited mercury in snow was lost within I 2 hours following deposition . It is suggested that fresh ly deposited mercury is quickly emitted back to the atmosphere through air-snow gas exchange fluxes .

Mercury is one of the most toxic chemicals in the environment. It is of particular concern in northern areas as it can reach these regions through long-range transport (Poissant 1999, Poissant 2000, Cheng and Schroeder, 2000) and be chemically transformed (Schroeder et al.
Moreover, Hg bioaccumulates in the Arctic food chain (Macdonald et al. 2000) .

Atmospheric ozone and Hg depletion events were recently discovered in the high Arctic region during polar sunrise experiments (Barrie et al. 1988, Schroeder et al. 1998). It is accepted that catalytic cycles involving bromine monoxide (BrO) are responsible for the majority of observed ozone losses; smaller contributions being proposed for cycles involving chlorine monoxide (CIO) and iodine monoxide (10) (Barrie et al. 1988, Richter et al. 1998). Reactive bromine species contribute significantly to the destruction of ozone in the polar stratosphere as well as the underlying troposphere (Barrie et al. 1988, Bottenheim et al. 1986) and can be an effective oxidant for Hg (Schroeder et al. 1990, Schroeder et al. 2000) . However, the complete Arctic Hg oxidation mechanisms are still enigmatic (Schroeder et al. 2000). Chemical conversion of Hg 0 would yield either particle-phase or reactive gaseous Hg species associated with dry deposition (Schroeder et al. 1998).

Bromine monoxide columns are observed over the Hudson Bay area and parts of the Canadian Arctic (Richter et al. 1998). Satellite observations, from the Global Ozone Monitoring Experiment (GOME), showed that tropospheric air masses enriched in BrO are always located close to sea-ice and typically extend over areas of about 300 to 2000 km. The BrO abundance remains enhanced for periods of 1 to 3 days, especially in late winter and springtime The sources of bromine in polar spring are not well understood but would involve a marine source (Richter et al.

This study presents measurement data that offer a unique opportunity to study the temporal evolution of ozone and Hg depletion events in the low Arctic, and contributes significantly to the discussion on atmospheric Hg transport and its fate in northern environments. This issue is critical for assessing the mechanistic route of Hg contamination into the North and its further transfer to the biosphere.

Various activities were done in the second year of this Northern Contaminants Program (NCP) research project. The study site is located in Kuujjuarapik, Nunavik, at the Centre d'etudes nordiques (CEN), University of Laval. Meteorological data are available from the CEN and Navigation Canada. Gaseous elemental mercury, previously referred to as total gaseous mercury (TGM), and ozone instruments were installed in mid-August 1999 and Hg and ozone data (GEM at I 5-minute intervals; 0 3 at 5-minute intervals) were collected daily through telemetry (Poissant et al. 1996). Gaseous elemental mercury measurements were audited (quality controlled) at the site during a national audit conducted by CAMNet in mid-November 2000. Internal audits are conducted every 4 months following the same protocol (Poissant and Casimir 1998). GEM data are quality controlled through the Research Data Management and Quality Assurance System TM Hg package (National Atmospheric Chemistry Database), Measurements and Analysis Research Division, Meteorological Service of Canada, Downsview).

A cost effective and high quality monthly sampling protocol for Hg and major ions was developed and applied. Precipitation samples have been collected since September, 1999, and analyzed for Hg, bromide and chloride at INRS-Eau by M. Amyot. In spring 2000 and 2001, two intensive field campaigns were completed. Mercury snow surveys were done in the Kuujjuarapik area; sample analysis is ongoing. Also, snow-air Hg gas exchange flux experiments were conducted. These were the first Hg flux measurements conducted in the Arctic . Measurements of reactive gaseous mercury, GEM, ozone, GEM flux and Hg in snow were done simultaneously.
Daily satellite data for BrO concentration in the Arctic domain were collected by GOME (GOME 2000).

In the spring of 2001, a European research team did parallel chemistry measurements using differential optical absorption spectroscopy. In situ measurement of BrO has revealed a mixing ratio of up to 30 ppt (G. Hoenninger, personal communication).

This atmospheric Hg project in Kuujjuarapik is in its second year of development and is part of one of the first studies to conduct atmospheric chemistry measurements in northern Quebec. Important findings were made within this period, 2000-2001 . Mercury depletion events are extended over the whole Arctic area in the springtime. Fresh Hg deposition is volatilized further in the days following the depletion event and Hg depletion seems to be connected with BrO episodes.

This study collects baseline gaseous elemental mercury (GEM) data to study spatial and temporal trends of mercury in the Canadian Arctic. Through this project, a significant discovery was made that sparked international interest. It was found that during the springtime, mercury is transformed from the stable species (GEM) to a much shorter-lived, more reactive species that can have a significant impact on the Arctic environment. To date we have annual data from 1995 to 1999 (quality assured and quality controlled) and have collected data from 2000. As in previous years, the annual GEM data showed distinct seasonal patterns. Snow samples were collected during the winterspring of 2000 and showed concentrations similar to those collected in the previous 2 years. In the winter of 200 1, an automated reactive gaseous mercury (RGM) and particulate mercury (PM) analyzer was installed at Alert to further study the behaviour of mercury in the Canadian Arctic. To collect baseline ambient air concentration measurements of gaseous elemental mercury (GEM) at Alert, Nunavut, for the purpose of establishing:

• ambient air concentrations in the Canadian Arctic and their linkage to elevated levels of Hg in the Arctic food chain • emission sources through long-range transport studies, and • a scientific information base to use in developing Canadian strategies for international controls.

Mercury is a toxic metal and has been identified as a priority pollutant by various national and international organizations. Levels of Hg in many Arctic wildlife are elevated (Lockhart 1999), creating a concern among northern communities. In I 995, continuous GEM* measurements began in the Canadian Arctic at Alert, Nunavut. Since this time, significant advances in our knowledge of atmospheric Hg in this environment have been made. It was discovered that during the springtime, Hg is transformed from the relatively long-lived stable species (GEM) to a much shorter-lived, more reactive form (Schroeder et al. 1998). It is thought that this conversion of Hg after the polar sunrise may provide a pathway for the introduction of these more reactive Hg species to the Arctic environment and may be impacting large areas of the Northern Hemisphere (Lu et al. 2001 ).

This Hg measurement program provides long-term data on the spatial and temporal trends of Hg in the Arctic environment. These results can be used in developing and implementing Canadian international strategies, and negotiating positions to achieve appropriate controls for priority pollutants of concern, such as Hg. Results from this program have generated international interest and have resulted in similar measurements being made in Alaska, Norway, Denmark (Greenland) and Russia. These data (Canadian and other) will provide important information on the transport, transformation and deposition processes of this priority pollutant throughout the polar regions.
Ground-based atmospheric GEM measurements continued at Alert. The mercury measurement program at Alert continues to be a participant in the Canadian Atmospheric Mercury Measurements Network (CAMNet).

The least variation in concentration levels is seen in the autumn (October to December). This period is thought to be the most representative of northern hemispheric background GEM concentrations (mean: 1.55 ± 0.08 ng·m-3). The largest concentration distribution is found in the spring (April to June). This is expected, as it is the time of episodic Hg depletion events and concentrations fluctuate considerably. The winter season shows outliers that are biased to the lower concentration values and the summertime outliers are biased towards the higher values. Every year in the summertime, an increase in the GEM levels is observed; it is thought that the summertime increase is due to an emission of the Hg that was deposited during the depletion periods in the spring.

The CRPU was employed i.n 1998 to assess the hypothesis that Hg(0) is converted to other Hg species in ambient air in the springtime at Alert. This assumption was confirmed in the 1 998 study but the data were limited since there was only one Hg depletion event during which this unit was employed (Schroeder et al. 1999). Therefore, the experiment was repeated again in 2000. Results from this experiment are shown in Figure 3. The CRPU is a front-end unit through which ambient air is drawn and separated into two different streams. One stream of air is pulled straight into a Tekran Hg vapour analyzer as ambient air. The other air stream is drawn through an unfiltered heated oven (filled with quartz chips retained at 900°C) that pyrolyzes all Hg species in the incoming air to their elemental form and is then detected by the Tekran instrument. The concentrations of Hg from these two streams are then compared. Results show that the two streams track each other well when there is no depletion event, indicating that ambient air consists mainly of Hg(0). When a depletion event occurs, the ambient . GEM concentrations drop well below the pyrolyzed air Hg concentrations. This confirms that there is conversion of Hg(0) during a depletion event and that other Hg species are present in the air. It is noted, however, that the entire GEM converted or "missing" from ambient air is not recovered by pyrolysis. Present estimates indicate that pyrolyzing unfiltered air can account for up to 62% of the GEM previously oxidized (using the 2000 data) . This result supports the idea that a significant amount of the oxidized Hg in the air during depletion times is unaccounted for. Such oxidized Hg(II) species have higher deposition fluxes than the Hg(0) precursor and, thus, are more readily deposited onto the snow and ice surfaces. Results from freshly fallen snow samples at Alert confirm this.

Interest in the study of atmospheric mercury in Arctic environments has grown considerably in the past several years since the discovery of springtime mercury depletion episodes in Alert, Nunavut, and the possible impact that this discovery has on the Arctic environment. Very few, if any, measurements have been made in the Russian Arctic. The measurement of gaseous phase mercury will begin in Arnderma, located in the Russian high Arctic, in June 200 I . This study, in conjunction with four other polar sites (in Canada, Norway, Denmark and the United States), is intended to assess the not yet fully understood behaviour of mercury in Arctic regions and whether mercury concentration levels are increasing or decreasing. The Arctic ecosystem is exhibiting increasingly disturbing evidence of contamination by a host of persistent, bioaccumulating toxic substances including heavy metals, such as Hg (Jensen et al. 1997). The atmosphere is the first medium in which to observe trends of pollutants and the effects of various national and international control efforts. By monitoring atmospheric Hg, the effect of these efforts can be observed.

Significant advances in the knowledge of atmospheric Hg in the Arctic environment have been made since the inception of Hg research at Alert, Nunavut. The discovery of the "Arctic springtime depletion of mercury" (Schroeder et al. 1 998) laid the foundation for subsequent significant discoveries regarding the transformation and deposition of Hg in the Arctic . It has been found that in the springtime, the annual accumulation rate of Hg in the snow is enhanced by a factor of four (Lu et al. 2001 ). These discoveries can have profound effects on the Arctic environment and have sparked international interest and scientific investigations into this phenomenon in the Arctic and the Antarctic by various international agencies.

Gaseous elemental mercury is currently being measured at six different international Arctic sites on a routine basis (Alert, Canada; Pt. Barrow, U.S.A.; Svalbard/Spitsbergen, Norway; Station Nord and Nuuk, Greenland; Thorshaven, Denmark) but there is a significant gap of information from the expansive Russian Arctic (see Figure 1 ). In support of international environmental commitments, such as the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme, Hg is being measured at a site in northern Russia (Amderma, 69°N, 61 °E). Amderma is also the site for which persistent organic pollutant (POPs) measurements have been made between 1999-200 1.

In June 2000, a Tekran Hg vapour analyzer, and associated equipment and instrumentation were brought to Obninsk, Russia. This is the location of the scientific team (SPA "Typhoon") that is responsible for the operation in Amderma . The Russian scientists were trained by Environment Canada personnel on the set-up and operation of the equipment. In March 2001 , final approval from the Russian authorities to initiate installation of the instrumentation in Amderma was granted. The instruments were installed at the site and, pending the arrival of the instruments' operational gases, collection of data will begin in June 2001 .
As of May 200 I , there has been no data collected. Results will be forthcoming when data collection is initiated.

This investigation will greatly enhance the current understanding of the behaviour of Hg in the Arctic environment by providing new information on the spatial extent and temporal transport trends of this toxic metal Figure 1. Circumpolar map of Arctic sites at which GEM measurements are ongoing from northern Russia. This study will fill in gaps of knowledge regarding the distribution of Hg to the Arctic environment as a whole and will provide important information for the development of long-term international strategies for the sustainable development and protection of polar regions. The addition of the Amderma site to the circumpolar network will help close the gaps in knowledge about key atmospheric transport, transformation and deposition processes of this priority pollutant - processes that can lead to contamination of the Arctic ecosystem and traditional food sources for Aboriginal people in Russia and all circumpolar countries. As well, the data generated from this network will help to ascertain whether atmospheric Hg concentrations are increasing or decreasing in the Arctic environment.
This project is expected to continue for 5 years, until March 2005 .

Quantifying and Reducing Uncertainty in Model Calculations of Global Pollutant Fate Frank Wania, WECC Wania Environmental Chemists Corp., 27 Wells St., Toronto, ON M5R lPl; Phone: (416) 516-6542; Fax: (416) 516-7355; E-mail: frank.wania@utoronto.ca Ying Duan Lei, WECC Wania Environmental Chemists Corp., Toronto, ON; Alexander Wong, University of Toronto at Scarborough, Toronto, ON Current assessment methods for long-range transport potential of organic chemicals rely on the calculation of a characteristic travel distance or spatial range. A complementary approach uses an existing zonally averaged global distribution model to estimate the potential of a chemical to reach, and accumulate in, the Arctic region. The criterion to quantify this Arctic accumulation potential (AAP) is the fraction of the total global amount in environmental surface media that is accumulated in Arctic surface media after a certain time period. The simulations use hypothetical emission estimates with a generic spatial and temporal distribution . We have used this approach to assess the AAP of a multi-dimensional "space" of hypothetical chemical property combinations. The AAP was found to be determined by highly complex interactions and to be dependent on the partition properties, the degradation rates in atmosphere and surface media, and the mode of emission of a chemical.
The global distribution model can be employed to identify chemical properties and emission situations that favour accumulation in Arctic ecosystems.

The main objective of the project is to describe quantitatively, with model calculations, the global distribution behaviour of persistent organic pollutants (POPs), and to establish credibility in the results of these simulations. Specifically, the following objectives are: the global model calculations for a-HCH and PCBs to increase credibility in the descriptive and predictive capabilities of the model.

2. Use the global model in an evaluative fashion to investigate the global distribution behaviour of organic chemicals as influenced by (a) their physicalchemical properties, (b) their persistence in various media and climates, (c) hypothetical environmental and (d) emission scenarios.
3. Compare results obtained with the zonally averaged global distribution model with those obtained by other global modelling studies for POPs.

For several years we have been developing, improving, and using a zonally averaged global distribution model for POPs (Wania and Mackay 1995). A version for public distribution, called Globo-POP, was released in 2000 (Wania and Mackay 2000) and is posted for downloading on the Web site: www.scar.utoronto.ca/-wania . There are two principal means to employ this global distribution model for POPs: (I) simulation of the observed environmental fate of a specific contaminant using realistic historical emission estimates and environmental parameters; and (2) use of the model in an evaluative fashion using hypothetical emission scenarios, simplified environmental parameters, and sometimes hypothetical .chemical property combinations.

The simulations of the historical fate of a-HCH and PCBs, conducted as part of this project in previous years, are examples of the first type of use (Wania 1999, Wania et al. 1999a, 1999b, Wania et al. 2000). The second type of model use can facilitate the identification of chemical property combinations that enhance the potential for long-range transport and accumulation in the Arctic. The type of questions that can be addressed are: What chemical property combinations make a chemical most likely to be transported to, and accumulate in, polar regions? ls high persistence or intermediate volatility more important in determining the potential of a chemical for long-range transport? Are there threshold values for these chemical properties beyond which transport to, and accumulation in, polar regions increases substantially? For which chemical property combinations, if any, can we expect a delay between the maximum global release and the occurrence of maximum concentrations in the Arctic? What effect on global transport behaviour does the mode of emission have (i.e. whether the chemical is emitted into air, water or soils)?
Uncertainty analysis of the global model calculations for a-HCH and PCBs.

A paper on the influence of forests on the overall fate of semivolatile organic substances was published (Wania and Mclachlan 200 I). This allows for the estimation of the effect of increased deposition to forests on the potential for POPs to reach the Arctic.

Use of the global model in an evaluative fashion to investigate the global distribution behaviour of organic chemicals The first step in this undertaking was the identification of a suitable model outcome. Of particular interest to the Northern Contaminants Program is predicting a chemical's potential to be transported to Arctic regions and accumulate in the Arctic marine, freshwater and terrestrial environments. Accordingly, we identi fied the Arctic accumulation potential (AAP) as the model outcome of principal interest and defined it as the fraction of the total global amount in environmental surface media (i.e. the environmental media other than the atmosphere) that is accumulated in the surface media of the North polar model zone. However, that fraction depends on a number of model parameters, most notably the duration and location of chemical discharge to the global environment. Unless steady state conditions are assumed (which would be inappropriate on a global scale), the AAP is also a function of time. Therefore, it is assumed that for calculations of the MP, the emission of a chemical occurs steadily for I year (January I to December 31) with a zonal distribution that reflects the global population distribution. The MP is calculated at the end of I year of emission, and again after an additional nine years without emissions have passed. The first fraction is termed AAP 1 and reflects the MP of a currently emitted substance. The second is termed MP 10 and describes the potential for long-term Arctic accumulation after emissions have ceased. Using these definitions of AAP, we calculated AAP 1 and MP 10 for numerous hypothetical physicakhemical property combinations (see Figure I for the range of physical-chemical property combinations being simulated) of a perfectly persistent chemical. These calculations were undertaken for emissions to air, water and soil. We also calculated AAP1 for chemicals that undergo environmental degradation assuming variable rates of transformation in atmosphere and surface media.

(2000) by comparing estimates of the potential for cold condensation (cc) at the poles, as defined by Scheringer et al. These authors express the extent of accumulation at the poles by calculating the ratios of the exposure values at the poles, e1 and en, to the minimal exposure values of both hemispheres, thus CCN = eifeN,min and CCs = enfes,min for the northern and southern hemisphere, respectively. Exposure in this context is defined as a time-integrated concentration in the various model compartments, weighted according to their volume fractions. The total amount of a chemical in the total global environment and the Arctic surface media is obviously smaller if a chemical is no longer assumed to be perfectly persistent. However, the MP may actually increase, decrease, or stay the same, if the chemical is assumed to degrade in the atmosphere or the surface media or both. It turns out that the effect of degradation on the MP is not a simple one, but depends on both the physicalchemical partitioning characteristics of the chemical and the mode of its emission into the environment. If assumed perfectly persistent, the AAP 1 was only I .4%. If emitted into water or soil, different degradation properties lead to an enhancement of the AAP 1 of that chemical. Similar maps have been drawn showing the dependence of the calculated MP on persistence for other physical-chemical property combinations, revealing that the dependence of AAP on persistence in air and surface media is very different for chemicals with F. The food habits of the Arctic fox differ between summer and winter, and between inland and coastal/island environments. Results from stable isotope analyses of Arctic fox samples from Ulukhaqtuuq (Holman), Northwest Territories, show that trophic position (as inferred from stable nitrogen values) of Arctic fox is positively correlated with increasing stable carbon isotope values, suggesting that Arctic fox feeding from the marine environment occupy a higher trophic level.

However, comparison of stable isotope data with organochlorine (OC) concentrations indicates that trophic position may not influence OC levels for all major OC groups. Preliminary results suggest that while OC levels are highly variable, Arctic fox from Ulukhaqtuuq may be exposed to OC levels above the lowest-observed-adverseeffect levels for adverse effects on mammalian reproduction. Further research is required to properly elucidate the potential wildlife health risk from OC exposure to this species.

The Arctic fox (Alopex lagopus) is a circumpolar species that is widely distributed across northern Canada (Banfield 1987). It is one of the most economically important species of the Canadian Arctic because of its valuable pelt (Banfield 1987, Hiruki and Stirling 1989). Large numbers are harvested in both coastal and inland communities with communities such as Oamanittuaq (Baker Lake), Salliq (Coral Harbour) and Arviat each trapping hundreds of animals annually (Gamble 1987). Residents of Holman report eating Arctic fox meat when the animals look healthy (Kassam 1 999).

The Arctic fox is one of the few species which constitutes an important component of both the terrestrial and marine ecosystems (Hiruki and Stirling 1989). Generally, the diet of the Arctic fox consists of small mammals such as lemmings, Arctic hares and ground squirrels - as well as the eggs and fledglings of ground-nesting birds such as geese, ducks, ptarmigan and seabirds (Banfield 1987). However, the food habits of the Arctic fox in winter are necessarily different from those in summer, based on the seasonal distribution and abundance of available prey species (Chesemore 1968, Fay and Stephenson 1989). As well, there are distinct differences in the summer and winter diets of inland and coastal/island foxes (Chesemore 1968). On land, Arctic foxes feed mainly on lemmings, birds and their eggs as well as scavenge on caribou remains (Chesemore 1968, Kennedy 1980, Garrott et al.

1983 , Stickney 1991 , Fay and Stephenson 1989, Smits et al. 1989, Bantle and Alisauskas 1998, Kapel 1999). Coastal foxes will also eat marine invertebrates (Fay and Stephenson 1989, Kapel 1999) and fish (Banfield 1987) in summer. In winter and spring on the sea ice, Arctic foxes scavenge the remains of ringed seals and bearded seals killed by polar bears (Stirling and Smith 1977, Andriashek et al. 1985, Fay and Stephenson 1989, Hiruki and Stirling 1989, Kapel 1999) and they will also actively prey on newborn seal pups (Smith 1976, Andriashek et al.

Arctic foxes are quite capable of swimming considerable distances (Banfield 1987, Quinlan and Lehnhausen 1982, Strub 1992) allowing them access to ice floes where marine mammal carcasses may be found.

Stable isotope analyses can be used to distinguish populations feeding at different trophic levels, and in a marine versus a terrestrial/freshwater environment. In single system studies, it is possible to use stable-nitrogen ratios ( 15N/ 14N) to delineate trophic relationships (Hobson and Welch 1992) since these ratios increase by regular increments from one trophic level to the next (Peterson and Fry 1987). Measurements of naturally occurring stable isotopes in foodwebs can also be used to delineate relative inputs from freshwater and marine biomes (reviewed by Hobson et al. 1997). This is based on the fact that stable isotopes of carbon (8 13C), nitrogen (8 15N), sulfur (834S) and hydrogen (80 ) are typically enriched in marine as compared to terrestrial/freshwater systems and these isotopic signatures are passed on to consumers.

Arctic foxes on Svalbard in the Norwegian Arctic feed mainly on reindeer, ptarmigan and seabirds with seals being regionally scavenged in late winter (Prestrud 1992, Frafjord 1993). Arctic foxes from Svalbard contained high levels of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) (8 mg·kg-1 in adipose tissue) (Skaare 1996) which are comparable to mean PCB levels of 8.3 mg·kg-1 in fat of foxes on the Norwegian mainland (Wang-Andersen et al. 1993) . PCB congener patterns are similar to those found in polar bears and there appear to be no significant differences in PCB levels between the sexes or with age (Wang-Andersen et al. 1993) . There does, however, seem to be a negative correlation between PCB levels and the amount of body fat suggesting a "dilution" of PCBs in heavier animals (Wang-Andersen et al. 1993). Comparison of PCB levels in Arctic foxes with earlier data (Norheim 1978) shows that levels remained unchanged from 1973- 1974 to I 983- Based on a review of the literature, Kamrin and Ringer ( 1996) suggest that fat concentrations above I O mg·kg-1 are linked to reproductive impairment in mammals. Given that the mean PCB levels in Norwegian foxes was about 8 mg·kg-1 with some individuals having up to 41 mg·kg-1 in the fat (Wang-Andersen et al.
, this would suggest that toxic effects, particularly related to reproduction, may be a concern for Arctic foxes.

As part of a project, Human and Chemical Ecology of Arctic Pathways by Marine Pollutants, being conducted in Ulukhaqtuuq as well as in communities in Alaska, one of the principal investigators (D. Muir) made arrangements for sampling of Arctic foxes trapped at Ulukhaqtuuq during the November to March 1999-2000 trapping season. The reason for this was that, at Ulukhaqtuuq (Holman), the only Canadian location of the project, consultations and interviews with community members indicated that a variety of other animals besides marine mammals and fish were important to their community, including Arctic foxes. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration/ Cooperative Institute for Arctic Research project was largely directed at analysis of marine biota and did not include land animals such as Arctic foxes.

The Arctic foxes from Ulukhaqtuuq have been analyzed for organic compounds. A total of 100 PCB congeners and 30 OC pesticides and related compounds were quantified by gas chromatography-electron capture detector (GC-ECD) using a series of authentic external standards. Toxaphene was analyzed by CC-electron capture negative ion mass spectrometry using selected ion monitoring (Swackhamer et al. 1987, Glassmeyer et al. 1 999) on a HP 5973 mass spectrometer detector. Toxaphene was quantified using a single response factor based on technical toxaphene and 24 chlorobornane congeners were quantified separately using authentic standards.

During the winter of 2000-2001, 50 carcasses of Arctic foxes were collected with the help of local hunters and trappers from each of two communities: one coastal community (Arviat) and one inland community (Oamanittuaq ! Baker Lakel) for comparative purposes. The samples collected from Arviat will complement information collected for the second coastal community (Ulukhaqtuuq) in 1999-2000.

Also, a large collection of wolverine carcasses collected from the coastal community of Ourluqtuuq (Coppermine) is available from Government of the NWT (B. Elkin). Information on age, sex, morphometrics, pathology, etc. for these animals has already been documented. Carcasses of 12 wolverines (six adult males, six adult females) collected from Ourluqtuuq (Coppermine) during 1999- 2000 have been shipped to the NWRC for analyses of mercury (Hg) and a suite of metals including selenium (Se) and silver (Ag) in liver, and cadmium (Cd) in kidney.

Subsamples will be sent to the National Water Research Institute (D. Muir) for OC and toxaphene analyses, as well as stable isotope analyses. Samples were received late in the fiscal year and therefore have not yet been analyzed.

As a pilot study, 20 Arctic foxes collected from Ulukhaqtuuq during the period November 1 999 to March 2000 were aged, sexed and analyzed for PCBs and persistent OC pesticides as well as stable isotopes ratios of carbon and nitrogen (Table 1 ).

Stable nitrogen isotope values were positively correlated with increasing stable carbon isotope signatures. Stable isotopes have been used to assign trophic status of biota and could provide insight into bioaccumulation of OCs into marine zooplankton. The I 5N/ I4N isotope ratio in biota increases in a predictable manner between trophic levels (Kelly 2000) allowing trophic positions and OC concentrations to be interpreted along a continuous variable.

Carbon isotopes (13C/ 12C) are not enriched significantly between trophic positions and can be used to evaluate energetic pathways between regions with differing carbon sources. As a result, stable carbon isotope signatures can differentiate an organism's dependence on inshore/ benthic and offshore/pelagic regions (Kidd 1998). Our findings demonstrate that the trophic position of Arctic foxes from Ulukhaqtuuq, NWT, is positively correlated with an increasing stable carbon signature (I 13C/ 12C] = 1.26 1I 5N/ I4N] + 40.29, r2 = 0.55, p = 0.002). This suggests that as the Arctic fox population shifts its feeding dependence (or carbon source) from the terrestrial/ freshwater systems to the marine environment, its relative trophic position significantly increases.

PCBs and chlordane-related compounds were the major OCs present in Arctic foxes (Table 1 ). While mean levels of all major OC groups were < 100 ng·g·1 wet weight there were a few animals with very high levels of oxychlordane, the persistent metabolite of chlordane. Age of the animals ranged from < 1 to 6 years with most being about 1 year old. Concentrations of several OC groups in both liver and muscle samples were found to be positively correlated with increasing trophic position based on 15N/ 14N values (p < 0.05 for all comparisons) . LHCH had the strongest positive relationship with trophic position (p < 0.001 , r2 = 0.618) (Figure 1 ). The low correlation coefficient (r2) between OC concentration and trophic position for all major OC groups suggests, however, that the relationship between OC levels and trophic position is weak.

The stable isotope data suggest that increasing trophic position of Arctic fox sampled in this study is directly correlated with an increasing influence of marine dietary influence. However, most OC levels for sum-groups (i.e.

It has been suggested that Arctic fox may be exposed to PCB levels indicative of adverse effects on mammalian reproduction (Brustrom and Halldin 2000). Brustrom and Halldin (2000) observed that PCB levels in Arctic fox liver samples from Svalbard ( I 9931994, n = 20) were above the lowest observed adverse effect level (LOAEL) value for reproductive impairment in mink (Mustela vison). In some cases, observed PCB levels were above the EC50 value for PCB-induced reproduction inhibition. PCB liver concentrations in Arctic fox from Ulukhaqtuuq are generally lower than the levels associated with LOAEL for negative reproductive effect in mink. During the first year of this project, trends of HCH data in Arctic biota (thick-billed murre (Uria lomvia) and ringed seals (Phoca hispida)) were examined; HCH concentrations, including P-HCH, were determined in water from the eastern Archipelago of the Canadian Arctic; and Henry's law constants (HLC) were determined for a-, y- and P-HCH. Spatial trends in the relative proportions and concentrations of HCH isomers were observed in the thick-billed murres and ringed seals, although the patterns did not follow any discernable geographic trends. Temporal trends varied among the HCH isomers and among stocks of ringed seals. and I:HCH concentrations declined in ringed seals from Hudson Bay but not Holman Island between the 1980s and early 1990s. P-HCH has not declined in ringed seals between the 1980s and 1990s, although recent data suggest the start of a decline. Concentrations of a-HCH and y-HCH are significantly declining while P-HCH is increasing in eggs of thick-billed murres. The variability in spatial and temporal trends between HCH isomers in biota suggests that using I:HCH is not appropriate for assessing these chemicals in the Arctic. Concentrations of a- and y- HCH in eastern Archipelago ocean water are similar to past work, P-HCH concentrations are an order of magnitude lower than a- and y-HCH. The HLC value determined for P-HCH is I 0 times lower than a- and y- HCH. This lower HLC would delay the transport of P-HCH to the Arctic and may in part explain the delay in P-HCH decline in the Arctic.
The Arctic water concentrations and HLC values are among the first reported for P-HCH.

There are spatial trends in the relative proportions and concentrations of hexachlorocyclohexane (HCH) isomers in ringed seals and thick-billed murres from the Canadian Arctic. However, these trends do not follow geographical patterns and may be confounded by differences in collection years and feeding habits at different sites.

Temporal trends in HCH isomer concentrations in ringed seals vary among stocks. and I:HCH concentrations declined in ringed seals from Hudson Bay but not Holman Island between the 1980s and early 1 990s. P-HCH has not declined in ringed seals between the 1980s and 1990s, although recent data suggest the start of a decline. Concentrations of a-HCH and y-HCH are significantly declining while P-HCH is increasing in eggs of thick-billed murres.
3. P-HCH concentrations in Arctic marine water are an order of magnitude lower than y-HCH and two orders of magnitude lower than a-HCH.
The Henry's law constant (HLC) for P-HCH (HLC = 0.036) is approximately 10 times lower than those of a- and y- HCH.
• To assess the spatial and temporal patterns of the a-, P- and y- isomers of HCH in the Arctic biotic and abiotic environment, specifically:
Compare concentrations and ratios of HCH isomers over time in air, water, seals and seabirds to determine any shifts in isomeric ratios and how those shifts interrelate among the various media.
2. Compare concentrations and ratios of HCH isomers spatially in the abiotic and biotic media and explore reasons for any patterns.

HCHs are pesticides that have been manufactured as two predominant products: technical HCH (60% to 70% a-HCH, 10% to 15% y-HCH, 5% to 12% P-HCH) and lindane (y-HCH). Only y-HCH displays significant insecticidal properties although P-HCH (Willett et al. 1998) and a-HCH have been shown to disrupt endocrine processes (Kendall et al. 1998). The key physical properties that control the ultimate fate of HCH in the environment are high volatility, low Henry's law constant (HLC) but with a strong dependency on temperature (a-HCH partitions into water about seven times more strongly at 0°C than at 2 5 °C (Kucklick et al. 1991 )), low affinity for particles and resistance to degradation in cold water (Nga be et al . 1993). These physical-chemical properties result in the evaporation of HCH from temperate and tropical regions (Takeoka et al. 1991), dispersion through the atmosphere and deposition into the Arctic. Partitioning of HCHs from air to water is favoured at lower temperatures (Kucklick et al. 1991) with the result that concentrations of HCHs in the Arctic Ocean are typically an order of magnitude or higher than those in tropical waters, although the distribution of HCHs in the Arctic Ocean is far from uniform . Although HCHs are the most abundant organochlorine in the Arctic Ocean, few measurements have been made for P-HCH.

Two significant drops in global technical HCH usage have been identified. In 1983, China banned the use of technical HCH and in 1990 India and the former Soviet Union reduced or banned the use of technical HCH (Li et al. 1998a, Li et al. 1998b). Significant drops in atmospheric a-HCH in the Arctic were observed between 1982 and 1983 and again between 1990 and 1992 (Li et al. 1998a). No temporal data for P-HCH are currently available. Concentrations of HCHs in Arctic waters have a different trend from those in air. The strong partitioning of HCH from air to water means that water phases ultimately become more important reservoirs than the atmosphere, containing over 90% of the inventory. The result of the dramatic decrease in atmospheric HCH concentration is that the surface water in some oceanic regions became undersaturated and therefore started to outgas (Jantunen and Bidleman 1995, Jantunen and Bidleman 1996). In other words, the concentration of a-HCH (and probably P-HCH) in Arctic waters increased until around 1 990- 1992 and y-HCH reached an equilibrium stage around 1 993 . Since contamination of the marine environment by HCH depends mainly on the concentration of HCH in water, concentrations of both a-HCH and P-HCH in Arctic marine biota should show a decrease after 1992. Preliminary analyses of data for ringed seals, polar bears and seabirds indicate that P-HCH increased during the 1 980s and may now be decreasing (in ringed seals and seabirds) as predicted (Addison, personal communication; Norstrom, personal communication).

Little is known about P-HCH in the Arctic or how its HLC varies with temperature. P-HCH is present at low levels in Arctic air (Halstall et al. 1998) and sea water (Jantunen and Bidleman unpublished data) but is found in increasing concentrations at higher trophic levels although the 153 percentage of P-HCH in I:HCH does not increase smoothly with trophic level (Muir et al. 1988).

A large data set on HCH isomer concentrations was compiled for Arctic marine biota for interpretation of HCH dynamics and fate in the Arctic. Data for ringed seals and seabird eggs were the most complete and were used for interpretation of trends in biota. Six high volume water samples were collected from the Canadian Arctic Archipelago for analysis of HCH isomers, including P-HCH, and initial data are reported. Initial results for P-HCH HLC are also presented.

The long-term trend in Arctic air concentrations of a-HCH has been presented by Li et al. Two sharp decreases in concentration occurred in 1982-1 983 and between 1990-1992. These seem to be responses to the change of global technical HCH usage or a-HCH emissions given that global emissions of a-HCH and mean air concentrations in the Arctic regions from 1 979 to earlyl 990s are strongly correlated. However, after 1990, global emissions and Arctic air concentrations are not correlated. This indicates that since the early- I 990s, the concentrations of a-HCH in Arctic air have not responded to the global a-HCH emission trends. In fact, the concentrations of a-HCH in the air and seawater in the Arctic have been in an equilibrium state since the early I 990s. The background air concentration should decrease accordingly after 1 996 when a-HCH concentrations in the Arctic seawater decrease gradually.

Since P- and a- HCH are both in technical HCH but not in lindane, P-HCH should behave in many respects like a-HCH. The estimated air concentration of P-HCH in the Arctic would therefore have been in the range of 57 to 72 pg·m-3 from 1970 to 1980, and in the range of 70 down to 20 pg·m-3 from 1981 to 1990.

Several research groups have measured air concentrations of both a-HCH and y-HCH in the Arctic, however data for P-HCH are sparse. If the P-HCH in the source regions can reach the Arctic air via atmospheric long-range transport along with a-HCH, then it should not have been very difficult to measure concentrations of P-HCH in the Arctic air at the beginning 1 980s when the air concentration of a-HCH in the Arctic reached the highest values. The fact that there were no reports of P-HCH in Arctic air during the early- to mid- l 980s may indicate that atmospheric long-range transport was not able to bring enough P-HCH into the Arctic air to be detected. Therefore, the estimated concentrations of P-HCH in the Arctic air as calculated above may not represent the real situation.

This study has confirmed that the concentrations and relative proportions of the three HCH isomers vary in Arctic marine biota (e.g. Muir et al. 2000a, Moisey et al. 2001 ). Variation in HCH isomer patterns has been shown to be related to differences in biotransformation capacity among species (Moisey et al. 2001 ). Because of this, the use of I:HCH to assess the temporal and spatial trends of individual HCH isomers may lead to false conclusions and needs to be considered in studies of HCH. The use of different analytical methods was also examined due to concerns about differences between electron capture (ECD) and mass spectrometer (MSD) detectors. Comparison of HCH isomer concentrations in seabird eggs using the same sample extract on ECD and MSD detectors found that these detectors gave similar results supporting the use of HCH data generated by either ECD or MSD.

Spatial and temporal trends of HCH isomers in Arctic marine biota Examination of the HCH isomers in ringed seal blubber and thick-billed murre eggs shows that concentrations and relative proportions of HCH isomers vary spatially in the Canadian Arctic (Figure 1). Efforts to properly evaluate these trends are limited by the small amount of data. No strong relationship between concentration or relative proportions with latitude or longitude were observed for either species, which suggests that exposure levels and differences in feeding habits are likely important variables. Concentrations in seals collected in the east are lower than those from the west (Figure I), although this is somewhat confounded by differences in collection year and latitude. The sites that had the lowest LHCH concentrations, Hudson Strait and Northern Baffin Bay, also had the lowest proportion of a-HCH (Figure 1). Concentrations and relative proportions of HCH isomers in thick-billed murre eggs showed no trend with latitude (Figure 1 ). However, the diet and migration pattern vary between these murre colonies (Braune et al. 200 I), which may influence and confound geographical trends. The Digges and Coats Islands birds were feeding on higher trophic-level prey. The murres of Prince Leopold and Coburg Islands winter off southwestern Greenland whereas the Digges and Coats Islands murres spend the winters off Newfoundland. Levels of organochlorines are likely higher in the waters off Newfoundland compared with southwestern Greenland. As with the ringed seals, LHCH concentrations in ringed seals and thick-billed murres appear to have started to decline as of the late I990s, after a period of no decline in the 1980s and early 1990s. In both ringed seal blubber and thick-billed murre eggs, there has been a decrease in the relative proportion of a-HCH with time (Figures 2 and 3) due to a decrease in concentration of a-HCH but also because of no change in P-HCH concentrations. The declines in HCH concentrations with time began at a later date than other persistent organic pollutants (POPs) groups, such as PCBs and DDTs, in part because HCH is still widely used around the globe and because the Arctic Ocean is considered a continuing source of these chemicals to the Arctic. This lag in declining concentrations of HCH in biota was predicted by Addison and Smith ( 1998). The lack of a decline in P-HCH likely reflects the recalcitrant nature of this isomer and its lower HLC as compared with the other HCH isomers, but is likely to decline in the Arctic with continuing decline in HCH use around the globe .

In the BS method, nitrogen is bubbled through a column of water to strip dissolved HCHs and the HLC is calculated from the concentration decrease with time. In the OH method, dissolved HCHs are stripped by bubbling with nitrogen and the volatilized HCHs are trapped on a sorbent cartridge. The partial pressure of the chemical is calculated from the quantity of HCHs trapped on the cartridge and the air volume, using the ideal gas law. The HLC is the partial pressure divided by the concentration in water. The OH technique is especially useful when the HLC is low and the chemical strips very slowly, as is the case for P-HCH at the colder temperatures.

The HLCs for a-, P- and y-HCHs were determined at 5, 20, 30 and 3 5 °C in deionized water. Agreement between the OH and BS methods averaged 1 5% for a- and y -HCH at 20 and 5 °C and for P-HCH at 20 °C. Only the OH method was used for P-HCH at 5 °C because of slow stripping.

This project has shown that the spatial and temporal trends of concentrations and relative proportions vary among HCH isomers, among species and among populations of seabirds and marine mammals. Future work on HCH should consider all isomers and not just IHCH. The results also support the continued monitoring of organochlorine contaminants in a number of species and at a number of locations. P-HCH concentrations are much lower than a- and y-HCH in Canadian Arctic waters. The low water concentrations support conclusions that higher levels of P-HCH in organisms are due to the recalcitrant nature of this isomer. The HLC of P-HCH is an order of magnitude less than a- and y-HCH. This lower HLC suggests that migration of P-HCH to the Arctic and outgasing from Arctic Ocean waters will be slower than the other HCH isomers. This will likely result in delays in the decline of P-HCH in the Arctic environment, and advocates more attention to this isomer in future studies in the Arctic. Future work will focus on examining trends in abiotic matrices based on data generated in the past year and comparing abiotic trends with biotic trends.
