We have previously measured the levels of organochlorines and mercury in archived Arctic seabird eggs and confirmed that the concentrations of most organochlorine compounds have been decreasing and that mercury concentrations have been increasing in Arctic seabirds. To evaluate whether temporal trends of organochlorines vary between species we compared the temporal trends of organochlorines among seabird and marine mammal species. Although somewhat limited by sample sizes and access to temporal trend data sets, our analysis has shown that the rate of change of organochlorine contaminant concentrations in Arctic seabirds and marine mammals varies among species. These results support the continued monitoring of organohalogens in a suite of Arctic species. A number of halogenated organic contaminants, which have never been measured in Canadian Arctic seabirds, were also quantified. Preliminary results from seabird livers sampled from 1975 and 1993 showed that concentrations of most dioxins and furans decreased in northern fulmars and black-legged kittiwakes but increased in thickbilled murres. Levels of polybrominated diphenyl ethers have increased in all three species and concentrations of non-ortho PCBs have increased in northern fulmars. Levels of some dioxins, furans, non-ortho PCBs and polybrominated diphenyl ethers in seabirds are higher than levels found in marine mammals. Toxaphene, halogenated dimethyl bipyrroles, chlorinated terphenyls, hexabromo biphenyls and TCP-methane were also detected in seabirds, but concentrations were low.

Temporal trends of organochlorine (OC) concentrations vary between Arctic seabird and marine mammal species suggesting that a suite of species is needed in order to assess these chemicals in the Arctic.

A number of halogenated organic contaminants, which had not previously been reported for Canadian Arctic seabirds, were measured. Among these, levels of dioxins, furans, non-ortho PCB congeners and polybrominated diphenyl ethers were considered significant and require additional analysis and evaluation in seabirds.

To address the question of the utility of Arctic seabird eggs as an indicator of contaminant temporal trends under the Northern Contaminants Program "Monitoring" Blueprint (NCP 2000), it was proposed that:

Archived Arctic seabird egg contents be re-analyzed for OCs according to a standardized pooling and analytical protocol in order to confirm whether those residues have been decreasing since the mid- l 970s.

The mercury (Hg) and selenium (Se) data for Arctic seabird eggs be analyzed to determine whether or not those levels have been increasing or decreasing since the mid- I 970s 3. Egg contents and adult livers be analyzed by full scan and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry to identify any "new" or previously unidentified OCs (MS full scan) or metals (ICP) which may have entered the Canadian Arctic food chain.

Eggs of seabirds have been used to monitor contamination of the Canadian Arctic marine environment since 1975 (Noble and Elliott 1986, Nettleship and Peakall 1987, Noble 1990, Muir et al. 1999). At the time of egg formation, OC compounds are transferred along with fat to the eggs (Mineau et al. 1984) thus reflecting the contaminant burden in the female at the time of laying (Braune and Norstrom 1989). Both Hg (Fimreite 1979, Lewis and Furness 1993) and Se (Heinz 1996) are also transferred to the eggs. Contaminant burden is comprised of residues assimilated over a long time period and, particularly in migratory species, may represent exposure from a number of different locations (Hebert 1998, Monteiro et al. 1999).

Biomagnification of many chemical residues has been shown to result in higher concentrations of many compounds with increasing trophic level (Riisgard and Hansen 1990, Jarman et al. 1996, Kidd et al. 1998). Therefore, interpretation of contaminant concentrations in seabirds may be confounded if seabird populations shift their dietary patterns over trophic levels through time. Fortunately, retrospective analysis of trophic level in seabirds is possible through the measurement of naturally occurring stable isotopes of nitrogen (8 15N), and to a lesser extent, carbon (8 13C) (Hobson and Welch 1992, Hobson et al. 1994, Hebert et al. 1999). This is also true of seabird eggs since stable isotope ratios in egg material are expected to reflect the diet of the female prior to or during laying (Hobson 1995, Hebert et al. 1999).

Few long-term data sets exist to give a clear picture of how concentrations of contaminants have changed over time at northern latitudes. In the Canadian Arctic, previous contaminant trend information is available for seabird eggs collected on Prince Leopold Island in Lancaster Sound, Nunavut. Contaminants data from samples collected in the mid- l 970s (Nettleship and Peakall 1987) have been compared with data from eggs collected in the late 1980s (Noble 1 990) and early 1 990s (Muir et al.

1999), all of which suggested that levels of many OCs were declining. Those samples were, however, analyzed at different times using different analytical techniques. As well, time trends for metal concentrations are nonexistent because concentrations of trace metals In this study, we provide new insight into contaminant trends in seabirds from the high Arctic by reanalyzing archived samples using standardized laboratory protocols and by extending the trend analyses of eggs from earlier studies. These data have already been presented (Braune 1999, Braune 2000) .

Newly identified organohalogen compounds and metals in seabirds Liver samples of all three seabird species from 1975 and 1993 as well as egg samples from 1993 were analyzed at the National Wildlife Research Centre (NWRC) laboratories for dioxins (PCDDs), furans (PCDFs) and non-ortho PCBs (NOPCBs) using GC/MS Selected Ion Monitoring (SIM).

GC/MS Total Ion Chromatography (TIC) was used to confirm the presence and to estimate the levels of toxaphene, polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs), polychlorinated diphenyl ethers (PCDEs), halogenated dimethyl bipyrroles (HDBPs), hexabromo biphenyls, TCP-methane, TCP-methanol and chlorinated naphthalenes using GC/MS TIC. Egg samples from 1993 as well as the 161 liver samples were also analyzed for multiple elements using Elan ICP-MS.

Results of the ANCOVA showed that concentrations of HCB, ~HCH and LPCB were significantly different among species, had significant temporal trends, and rates of these temporal trends varied between species (all p values < 0.05). Including data for all species, HCB is significantly declining with time and at a greater rate than LHCH, LPCBs and DOE. The greatest rate of decline was observed in the ringed seals, although not statistically different than black-legged kittiwakes, thick billed murre or polar bears; the rate of decline in northern fulmars was significantly slower. LHCH concentrations were actually found to be increasing, although marginally, in these seabirds and marine mammals. Again, only northern fu lmars had a statistically different temporal trend. LPCB concentrations in all species were significantly declining with time (Figure 1 ). Black-legged kittiwakes had the greatest rate of decline, which is statistically different than the other species (p < 0.05). DOE is significantly declining in all species (p < 0.05) but no differences were observed between species (p = 0.06) or in the rate of decline among species (p = 0.08) . LCHLOR is significantly declining in all species (p < 0.05) but no differences were observed between species (p = 0.31) or in the rate of decline among species (p = 0.32).

In fulmar liver samples, concentrations of total PCDDs and PCDFs decreased and non-ortho PCBs increased from 1975 to 1993, and in murre liver samples, concentrations of total PCDDs and PCDFs increased and non-ortho PCBs decreased from 1975 to 1993 (Table I). In fu lmars, the PCDFs constituted the dominant fraction in both 1975 and 1993 livers. Calculated TEO values were highest in northern fulmars both in 1975 and 1993 (Table I).

Although somewhat limited by small sample size, statistical analysis of the temporal trends of OCs in Arctic seabirds, ringed seals and polar bears suggest that trends are significantly different among species. Efforts to draw more statistically powerful comparisons of temporal trends between species found differences at the p value of 0.05 but the statistical method, using ANCOVA model with a Bonferroni multiple correction, required p < 0.005 to be significant. Despite this, the ANCOVA method provides concrete evidence that the rates of decline of most OCs vary among species. Therefore, future monitoring of OCs in Arctic biota should consider a suite of species that represent relevant groups of animals in the Arctic.

Newly identified organohalogens and metals in seabirds Concentrations of HxCDDs, PnCDFs and HxCDFs, in particular, found in Arctic seabird livers exceed levels reported for marine mammals in the Canadian Arctic (de March et al. 1998) by several orders of magnitude. Ringed seals, polar bears and walrus in the the Canadian Arctic tend to contain relatively high TCDD and low PnCDD and PnCDF levels (de March et al. 1998) whereas Arctic seabirds show the opposite pattern. Concentrations of PCDD/F homologs in the Arctic seabirds are in the range reported for seabirds from temperate North America and Europe (Hebert et al. 1994, Van den Berg et al. 1987).

PCBs with 2,3, 7,8-TCDD-like activity have been shown to adversely affect patterns of survival, reproduction, growth and metabolism with PCB- 126 being among the most toxic of all PCB congeners to birds (Eisler and Belisle 1996). (1 996) have suggested a no observed effect level (NOEL) of I 00 ng·kg-1 and a lowest observed effect level (LOEL) of 210 ng·kg-1 TEO on a whole egg (wet weight basis) for bald eagle chicks, and Bosveld et al. (2000) have estimated the LOEL for induction of CYP 1 A in the common tern as approximately 25 ng·g-1 TEO liver lipid. (2000) have calculated TEOs based on PCDD/ Fs in livers and eggs of piscivorous birds from a heavily polluted lake area in China to be 552 pg·g-1 and I 07 pg·g-1 , respectively. The TEOs for livers and eggs of Canadian Arctic fulmars (Table I ) are certainly within the range of the Chinese samples, and the liver TEOs (lipid conversion: 1975 : 27 ng·g-1 lipid wt.; 1993: 8.2 ng·g-1 lipid wt.) exceeded the LOEL TEO for induction of CYP l A in common terns in the 1975 samples.

Although laboratory studies have shown considerable variation in species sensitivity, developing embryos are consistently more sensitive than adult birds to TCDD-like chemicals (Peterson et al. 1993). Coplanar PCBs have the potential to contribute more to total dioxin-like toxic activity in biota than chlorinated dioxins and dibenzofurans, and therefore monitoring for PCDDs and PCDFs is ill advised without comparable data for coplanar PCBs (Metcalfe and Haffner 1994). Given that there is evidence to suggest that : (i) the TEOs for the Canadian Arctic fulmars may be nearing levels of concern, (ii) levels of some PCDD/Fs in Arctic seabirds exceed levels found in marine mammals by several orders of magnitude, and (iii) levels of PCDD /Fs in thick-billed murres may be increasing - it is proposed that a detailed retrospective analysis be undertaken to examine temporal trends of PCDDs, PCDFs and coplanar PCBs in Canadian Arctic sea birds.

Although the data suggest that exposure to toxaphene has increased from 1975 to 1993, the highest level reported (64 ng·g-1 wet wt) is still an order of magnitude lower than levels reported for black duck eggs where reproduction was normal, and one to two orders of magnitude lower than levels reported for marine mammals from the Canadian Arctic (Muir et al. 1999). Therefore, monitoring of toxaphene in Canadian Arctic seabirds is probably not warranted at this time. Halogenated dimethyl bipyrroles, which are naturally occurring, mixed bromine/chlorine, persistent organic compounds, have been shown to bioaccumulate in seabird eggs (Tittlemier et al. 1999). Given that these are naturally occurring marine compounds, no further monitoring of these compounds in Canadian Arctic seabird eggs is planned at this time.

Although the data suggest that exposure to PBDEs has increased from 1975 to 1993, the highest level reported is an order of magnitude lower than levels reported for Swedish black guillemots (Sellstrom et al. 1993), but is still higher than levels reported for Canadian marine mammals (Addison 2000, Stern and Ikonomou 2000) . Given that evidence from several sources suggests that PBDEs seem to be increasing in the Canadian Arctic and elsewhere, it is proposed that a detailed retrospective analysis be undertaken to examine temporal trends of This is part of an ongoing monitoring program. The next sampling period will be in 2003 .

2. Archived samples of oldsquaw wing bone will be analyzed for stable isotopes ( l 3C/12C; 15N/14N and 34S/32S) and strontium (Sr) to discriminate whether birds from certain geographical areas of the Arctic B. Braune are overwintering in freshwater (i.e. Great Lakes) or marine environments.

North American populations of oldsquaw (Clangula hyemalis) are declining in the west, but are apparently stable in the east (Canadian Wildlife Service et al. 1 997). Nevertheless, oldsquaw are considered to be a Species of Continental Conservation Concern. This species nests in greater numbers in the high Arctic than any other duck (Bellrose 1 980). Oldsquaw nesting in the eastern Canadian Arctic likely winter along the Atlantic coast whereas western Arctic birds winter in the Bering Sea and along the Pacific coast of Alaska and British Columbia (Bellrose 1980). Considerable numbers also winter on the Great Lakes. It is unknown where the dividing line occurs between the two breeding populations.

Oldsquaw are harvested by Aboriginal people and sport hunters alike, but numbers taken are unlikely to be the cause of the decline (Canadian Wildlife Service et al. 1997). Heavy metal contamination from benthic organisms they eat may be an important threat to oldsquaw. As well, high Pb levels, resulting from spent shot ingested on the breeding grounds, are suspected of impairing reproductive success of oldsquaw nesting in the Alaskan Y-K Delta (Flint et al. 1 997).

Measurements of naturally occurring stable isotopes in foodwebs can be used to delineate relative inputs from freshwater and marine biomes (reviewed by Hobson et al. 1997). This is based on the fact that stable isotopes of carbon (o 13C), nitrogen (o 15N), sulfur (o34S) and hydrogen (8D) are typically enriched in marine systems, as compared to terrestrial or freshwater systems, and these isotopic signatures are passed on to consumers. Upon arrival on the breeding grounds, metabolically active tissues of birds that wintered in freshwater environments can be distinguished isotopically from those that wintered in marine areas. Stable isotope values in bird tissues are in dynamic equilibrium with local foodwebs and so it is necessary to choose a tissue with a slow turnover rate to delineate between freshwater and marine wintering ducks. Bone collagen was chosen because it has a turnover rate slow enough for isotope measurements to represent lifetime average values (Hobson and Sealy 1991). This information will be used to determine if birds overwintering on the Great Lakes risk greater exposure to contaminants than those overwintering in marine environments.

Metal residue data for breast muscle from oldsquaw collected from across the Canadian Arctic during 1991 to 1994 suggest that western Arctic populations generally have higher levels of Cd and Se than eastern populations (Braune et al. 1999). It is not known whether or not the birds are more exposed to metal contamination on the Arctic breeding grounds or on their overwintering grounds. The stable isotope measurements should discriminate those birds which overwinter on the Great Lakes, a known contaminated area. As well, Sr measurements should help to corroborate stable isotope findings since Sr levels are known to be higher in marine than freshwater systems. It should then be possible to determine if those birds overwintering on the Great Lakes also contain higher tissue residue levels than the others. The connection between risk of exposure and overwintering area can then be investigated, if such a link exists. Alternatively, if no association between metal levels and overwintering area can be established, the source of contamination may, in fact, be in the Arctic.

This study made use of the tissues of 10 1 adult oldsquaw from the Canadian Arctic archived in the CWS Specimen Bank: 59 birds from the eastern Arctic (east of 95°W) and 42 birds from the western Arctic. Liver, kidney and bone samples were retrieved from the Specimen Bank for each of the IOI birds and analyzed for Hg, Se and Cu in liver, Cd in kidney, and Pb in bone.

2. To monitor contaminant exposure in caribou as a representative species of the terrestrial Arctic ecosystem.
To provide information on temporal trends in radionuclide and metal levels in several caribou herds to determine whether levels are increasing, decreasing or remaining the same over time.
To determine the efficacy of international controls in reducing or eliminating pollutants entering the Canadian Arctic terrestrial ecosystem.

Barren-ground caribou (Rangifer tarandus groenlandicus) are found across northern Canada, and are a major component of the traditional diet in communities across the NWT, the Yukon and Nunavut. Caribou are strict herbivores that have a winter diet consisting primarily of lichen, which accumulate contaminants more readily than vascular plants because of their large surface area, longevity and ability to bind heavy metals. Because of their diet, longlived ungulates such a caribou can accumulate significant levels of some metals such as Cd (Froslie et al. 1984, Scanlon et al. 1986), which has implications for both caribou health and human consumption. Caribou are a primary source of food for people and wolves, and their level of contamination is therefore of concern (Muir et al. 1999).

Until recently, information on heavy metal, radionuclide and organochlorine contaminants in caribou and other terrestrial herbivores in Canadian Arctic and sub-Arctic regions was extremely limited, and data on temporal trends were nonexistent (Muir et al. 1999, Thomas et al. 1992). During the 1990s, tissue levels and spatial trends of persistent organic pollutants, heavy metal and radionuclide contaminants were assessed in 10 major barrenground caribou herds across the NWT (Elkin and Bethke 1995). A wide range of contaminants were detected and provided a good baseline to assess current exposure and changes in residue levels over time. This work indicated levels of some metals and radionuclides were elevated, and led to follow-up work to confirm the levels and potential effects of Cd and 210Po in caribou from south Baffin Island.

This study is part of a larger program to monitor contaminant levels in selected sentinel caribou herds at 5-year intervals. The importance of caribou as a major country food species makes the monitoring of ongoing baseline residue data particularly important. In addition, the defined ranges of caribou herds across the Canadian North and the simple lichen-caribou food chain make caribou a good species to monitor spatial patterns and temporal trends of contaminant deposition in the terrestrial ecosystem.

Twenty-five female caribou from the Beverly herd were harvested at Nonacho Lake (61 ° 59' N, 109° 28' W) on April 1 to 3, 2000. The collection was done in collaboration with hunters from the South Slave Metis Tribal Council and the Salt River First Nation # 195. Liver and kidney from a subset of 20 animals were analyzed for metals and radionuclides.

Metals were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry by the Canadian Association for Environmental Analytical Laboratories-accredited Envirotest Laboratories in Edmonton, AB, using standard methods recommended by the United States Environmental Protection Agency and the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment. Quality assurance and quality control of the analyses included blanks, spiked samples, reference materials (dogfish liver) and duplicates. Radionuclide analyses will be conducted at Whiteshell Laboratory in Pinawa, MB, as per Macdonald et al. Gamma-emitting radionuclides (137Cs, 40K, 226Ra, 210pb, 232Th) were analyzed using a p-type well detector in tissue ashed at approximately 500°C. 210Po was analyzed by alpha spectrometry using a 209Po tracer, after plating onto silver discs. 210Po concentration at the time of sampling was calculated as the sum of the supported fraction at the time of plating (210Pb concentration) and the unsupported fraction, corrected for decay from counting date to plating date.

Mean values for all metal and radionuclide data were calculated with log transformed data, and are reported as geometric means with geometric standard deviations. Means are calculated for elements with detectable amounts in > 50% of the samples. Sets of samples with < 50% above detection limits are reported at the detection limit.

Kidney and back fat, which are indicators of the general health of the caribou at the time of sampling, show a normal range of variation and show that most of the females had good fat reserves at the end of the winter. For example, back fat, a key energy source, varies from trace levels to 45 mm in depth, and sizeable amounts of fat are present on the kidneys. This is an indication that the animals were in reasonable health and nutritional status at the time of harvest.

Baseline contaminant levels were first established in 10 major barren-ground caribou herds across the NWT between 1991 and 1995 (Elkin and Bethke 1995, Macdonald et al. 1996). A wide range of metal, radionuclide and organochlorine contaminants were found in herds across the North. Some caribou are known to accumulate high concentrations of Cd in their kidneys and liver, and kidney levels have been shown to increase with age. The levels of Cd reported here for the Beverly herd are at the top of the range of values reported for caribou in the NWT and Nunavut, but are lower than the extreme levels found in mineralized areas of the Yukon. These Cd levels may be considered "normal background" in caribou, as relatively high levels are seen on a circumpolar basis. But they exceed Canadian environmental quality guidelines (30 μ,g·g-1) for wildlife (Muir et al. 1999) and, in some individual animals, exceed threshold values believed to cause kidney dysfunction.

Baseline levels were also established for aluminum (Al), chromium (Cr), copper (Cu), iron (Fe), lead (Pb), manganese (Mn), Hg, nickel (Ni) and zinc (Zn). While levels of these metals were generally within normal ranges, there was some variation both between and within herds with elevated levels of some metals at different sites. Ongoing monitoring will include these metals to examine spatial patterns, temporal trends and potential for elevated tissue residues of individual metals within different herds.

In a survey of radionuclides in 15 caribou herds throughout the Arctic, Macdonald et al. ( 1996) reported high levels 171 of 210Pb and 210P0 in some herds, consistent with results of other studies (Thomas et al. 1994). The highest levels of these 238U decay products have been observed in south Baffin Island caribou, where mean concentrations of 210pb and the alpha~emitter 210P0 exceeded I 000 Bq·kg-1 wet wt in liver and bone, with one individual exceeding 3-500 Bq·kg-1 of Pb210 and Po210 in bone. The doses is some herds are approaching levels at which effects are expected in some individuals, although no evidence of effects due to radioactivity have been documented (Macdonald et al. 1996).

This study provides further support for the general observation that, although metal and radionuclides levels may occasionally reach concentrations which could be toxic to individual animals, they probably do not reach levels at which the populations are affected. An Investigation of Factors Affecting High Mercury Concentrations in Predatory Fish in the Mackenzie River Basin Marlene Evans, National Water Research Institute, Environment Canada, 11 Innovation Boulevard, Saskatoon, SK S7N 3H5; Phone: (306) 975-5310; Fax: (306) 975-5143; E-mail: marlene.evans@ec.gc.ca; Lyle Lockhart, Freshwater Institute, Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), 501 University Crescent, Winnipeg, MB R3T 2N6; Phone: (204) 983-7113; Fax: (204) 984-2404; E-mail: lockhartl@dfo-mpo-gc.ca George Low, DFO, Hay River, NT; Gary Stern, DFO, Freshwater Institute, DFO, Winnipeg, MB; Tog Jackson, National Water Research Institute, Environment Canada, Burlington, ON; Bill Strachan, National Water Research Institute, Environment Canada, Burlington, ON We had a productive research year on this study. Our research effort consisted of completing the analyses from samples collected in 1 999 and in conducting new sampling in Tsesto, Sibbeston and Willow Lakes, in addition to visiting Cli and Little Doctor Lakes again. Mercury concentrations are not high in the water of these lakes. As well, these lakes do not have many of the limnological conditions that favour relatively high mercury methylation rates. In particular, the lakes are not acidic. We have reexamined the fish collected during the original 1 996-1 999 stock assessment studies to determine if high mercury levels are associated with their feeding behaviours and/or age. We note that the fish in many of the lakes are relatively old. Mercury concentrations in predatory fish do not approach 0.5 μg·g-1 until these fish approach 10 years of age. Fish also grow more slowly than in more southern regions and so the potential for growth dilution is less. Increased harvesting of larger fish may improve fish growth rates and lower mercury levels.
We have expanded our mercury (Hg) study to investigate Tsetso, Sibbeston, and Willow Lakes, in addition to our continuing work on Cli and Little Doctor Lakes.
We conducted laboratory studies that suggest Hg is transformed more rapidly into forms concentrated by the fish in coloured streams than in the clear streams flowing into Cli Lake.

Overall, our five study lakes do not appear to have conditions that are especially favourable for Hg to accumulate at a fast rate in predatory fish . Mercury M. Evans and L. Lockhart concentrations are not very high in the water and high Hg lakes are not small and acidic.

We have conducted more studies of the fish that were analyzed during the 1996-1999 stock assessment studies. It is starting to look like the fish have high Hg concentrations in some lakes because they are old and slow growing. Predatory fish start to approach a Hg concentration of 0.5 μg·g-1, the limit established for the commercial sale of fish, at about 10 to 12 years of age when they are eating more and more small, forage fish .
Continue investigations of the factors affecting elevated Hg levels in predatory fish in Cli and Little Doctor Lakes.
Conduct preliminary studies of methylation and demethylation rates in Cli Lake stream sediments.
Conduct baseline limnological and Hg studies at Sibbeston and Tsetso Lakes, upstream of Little Doctor Lake, and Willow Lake, located on the Horne Plateau.
Investigate the role of trophic feeding in affecting Hg levels in predatory fish in the five study lakes.

For many years, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has been working with First Nations communities in the Mackenzie River Basin on stock assessment studies. Several lakes have been sampled and fish species composition, length, weight and age determined as part of these studies. In addition, Hg concentrations have been determined in these fish . Researchers were surprised to learn that predatory fish in many of these lakes have Hg concentrations that exceed the 0.5 μg·g-1 limit established for the commercial sale of fish and the 0.2 μg·g-1 limit established for the frequent consumption of fish. As a consequence of these high levels, Health Canada has issued consumption advisories for many of these lakes.

It is not known why Hg levels are high in predatory fish in some lakes and not others. These lakes are located in pristine, undeveloped regions in the Mackenzie River Basin. Therefore, elevated Hg levels cannot be due to localized anthropogenic factors such as industrial waste discharges, flooding caused when reservoirs are created, or by disturbances in the watershed as a result of logging (Jackson 1986, 1991, Tremblay and Lucotte 1997, Garcia and Carignan 2000). Thus, naturally-occurring limnological features such as low pH, high dissolved organic carbon concentrations, humic stained water, a large watershed size, and shallow lake depths (Winfrey and Rudd 1990, Cope et al. 1990, Miskimmin et al. 1992, Parkman and Meili 1993, Bodaly et al. 1993) may be more important in affecting Hg levels in predatory fish. Local geological features have been shown to be important in some settings and may be important in some of the lakes in the Mackenzie River Basin (Shilts and Coker 1995). Mercury concentrations also increase with fish size and age (Munn and Short 1997) and with trophic feeding (Vander Zanden and Rasmussen 1996). Therefore, elevated Hg levels may be a function of the population structure and feeding characteristics of the fish populations in high Hg lakes. Our study is designed to elucidate these issues.

Initially, our research effort focussed on the limnological investigation of Cli and Little Doctor Lakes located to the west of Fort Simpson in the Nahanni Mountains. Advisories have been issued for the consumption of lake trout in Cli Lake and walleye and pike in Little Doctor Lake. In 1998 and 1999, we obtained new limnological information on these lakes including lake bathymetry (depths), watershed size, stream inflows, pH, dissolved organic carbon concentrations, water colour, ionic composition and nutrients. Mercury was measured in Cli Lake stream inflows (the data from the first year were suspect) and in sediments. Of particular interest was the possibility that elevated Hg concentrations were associated with some aspect of geological fault lines that underlie both lakes. Limited stable isotope and Hg studies were conducted on the Cli Lake food web. In comparison to other studies where elevated Hg concentrations have been reported in fish and other components of the environment, Hg levels were not especially high in Cli Lake stream and lake water, sediments and invertebrates. A dated sediment core from Cli Lake revealed that Hg flux rates to Cli Lake sediments have increased in recent decades, as has been observed in many other regions of the Northwest Territories (Lockhart et al. 1995). In 2000, we broadened our study to include three additional lakes -Tsetso, Sibbeston and Willow Lakes. Tsetso and Sibbeston Lakes were selected because they drain into Little Doctor Lake and because Hg levels were lower in whitefish in these lakes than in Little Doctor Lake (Lockhart and Evans 1999). These lakes also contain pike and walleye populations but not lake trout. Willow Lake was selected because it contained lake trout that had lower Hg concentrations than Little Doctor and Cli Lake.

Research activity in 2000 focussed on the completion of analyses of samples from the 1 999 field season and the new analysis of archived fish samples from the original stock assessment studies. These activities continue. In August 2000, we conducted new and additional research sampling of the five study lakes (Cli, Little Doctor, Tsetso, Sibbeston and Willow) in order to elucidate the potential limnological factors affecting elevated Hg levels in predatory fish in some but not all of these lakes. Weather was poor, with rain and strong winds during much of the trip, so that not all of the sampling could be completed during this 2-week period.

The five study lakes have different fish communities, with lake trout found only in Cli, Little Doctor and Willow Lakes during the original stock assessment studies (Figure l ). Whitefish from the five study lakes varied markedly in mean length and Hg concentration (Table 1). Cli Lake had the largest mean whitefish size, and Little Doctor and Willow Lakes had the smallest. Mean Hg concentration, adjusted for fish length, was highest in Little Doctor Lake and lowest in its two upstream lakes. Ad justed mean Hg concentrations were higher in Willow Lake than Cli Lake whitefish. Cli Lake whitefish, while large, were relatively young; growth dilution may have been a factor in affecting the somewhat lower Hg body burdens (unadjusted) in Cli Lake whitefish. In contrast, Little Doctor Lake whitefish were small relative to their age. Elevated Hg levels may be related, in part, to low whitefish growth rates in this deep, highly coloured lake although other factors relating to Hg methylation also must be important.

Little Doctor Lake has the largest drainage basin while Tsetso Lake has the smallest (calculations have not been performed for Willow Lake) . Lake size has been implicated as a factor in affecting Hg concentrations in predatory fish (Bodaly et al. 1993) (i.e. Hg concentrations tend to be higher in fish in smaller than larger lakes). Our five study lakes varied markedly in size from Tsetso Lake, with a surface area of 12 km2, to Willow Lake, with a surface area of 152 km2 (Table 2). In contrast to the Bodaly et al. (1993) study, whitefish inhabiting the smallest lakes had the lowest mean (adjusted) Hg concentration while higher Hg concentrations in whitefish were observed in the larger lakes.

Wetland area is an important variable affecting Hg concentrations in fish in some regions (St. Louis et al. 1994). Little Doctor Lake, with the largest wetland area, had the highest adjusted Hg concentration in whitefish. However, Hg concentrations also were relatively high in Cli Lake whitefish, a lake with a small drainage area, and low in Sibbeston Lake, a lake with a relatively large wetland area. Overall, there is not a strong relationship between Hg levels in whitefish and factors such as lake size, drainage basin area, and wetland area. During our August 2000 sampling, we obtained new limnological information on Willow, Tsetso and Sibbeston Lakes and additional data for Little Doctor and Cli Lakes. This allowed us to explore the relationship between Hg levels in fish and factors such as pH, dissolved organic carbon (DOC}, and other variables that affect Hg transformations and lake productivity.

It was not possible to conduct bathymetric (depth) mapping of Willow Lake because of the poor weather that limited boat travel on this very large lake. Willow Lake is assumed to be at least 20 m deep (Table 3) because of its size and the fact that lake trout are abundant in the lake. The lake is irregular in shape with several small bays. Sibbeston Lake was mapped and was shallow with most depths at 2 to 3 m. There were limited areas where depth reached 8 m. Extensive weed beds were evident in the main body of the lake from the air. There also were numerous shallow bays with lush macrophyte growth including yellow lily pads. Tsetso Lake is a small, circular lake with one major inflow. It was visited on a day trip and very poor weather also prevented depth mapping of this lake. However, the lake was shallow with most depths of 2 to 3 m. A deeper area of 5 m also was located in the region where fish are traditionally harvested in winter. As noted in Evans and Lockhart (2000), Cli and Little Doctor lakes are very deep.

At each lake, a standard series of water column measurements were made including temperature, specific conductivity, pH, and water clarity (Table 3). There was an unexpected inverse relationship between surface water temperatures and lake size. Intuitively, shallowest lakes would have the warmest surface water temperatures. However, Tsetso Lake, the smallest and shallowest lake, had the coldest waters while Little Doctor Lake, the deepest lake, had the warmest surface waters. The cooler waters of Sibbeston and Tsetso lakes are suggestive of strong groundwater inputs as has been observed in Cli Lake (see below). In the Bodaly et al. ( 1993) study, higher Hg concentrations in the smaller lakes was related to warmer water temperatures. Methylation rates increase with temperature while demethylation rates decrease. While the temperature differences in our study are small and based on a single observation, they may suggest that low Hg concentrations in whitefish in Tsetso and Sibbeston Lakes are, in part, related to their cooler temperatures which result in lower methylation/demethylation (MID) ratios than in the larger lakes. Little Doctor and Cli Lakes, located in the Nahanni Mountain range, had the highest conductivity, presumably due to the incorporation of dissolved salts in the runoff down the limestone mountain slopes. Tsetso Lake had the lowest conductivity. All five lakes had similar pH values and were slightly basic. These basic conditions were not favourable for high Hg methylation rates: these rates decline with increasing pH and tend to be highest in acidic lakes (Winfrey and Rudd 1990). Low water clarity was, in large measure, associated with humic-stained waters.

A series of water chemistry measurements were made at each lake including nutrients, dissolved organic carbon and total Hg. Plankton samples also were collected. Based on total phosphorus concentration, Cli Lake was the least productive lake. It also had relatively high nitrate concentrations. DOC concentrations were lowest in Cli Lake and highest in Little Doctor and Sibbeston Lakes; concentrations also were high in Tsetso and Willow Lakes. According to Miskimmin et al. ( 1992), Hg methylation (M) rates decrease and demethylation (D) rates increase with increasing DOC concentrations. The largest increase in demethylation rates occurred between 6.7 and 9.1 mg·L-1 DOC. Because Little Doctor Lake has basic waters and high DOC concentrations, the MID ratio is likely to be low in this lake. Watershed inputs of methylmercury (MeHg) may be important (Miskimmin et al. 1992) for Cli and Little Doctor Lakes although high DOC and basic pH also characterize the two primary feeder lakes (Tsetso, Sibbeston) into Little Doctor Lake. Overall, elevated Hg levels in predatory fish in lakes such as Cli and Little Doctor do not appear to be associated with in situ Table 3. Mercury concentrations are not high in the water column of the five study lakes and are remarkably similar to one another (Table 4) . As previously noted, Hg flux rates to Cli Lake, based on a sediment core analysis, are low and comparable to Lac Belot and Great Bear Lake where Hg concentrations are low in lake trout.

As in August 1999, we sampled a series of creeks flowing into Cli Lake for temperature, conductivity, pH, turbidity and Hg (Table 5). Creeks were substantially colder than lake water, indicating that they were fed by cold groundwaters. Creeks also were colder in August 2000 than in August l 999. The three creeks flowing down the mountains had higher conductivity and clearer waters than the humic-stained, lower conductivity waters draining the flatter wetland areas to the east. Nevertheless, all creeks were slightly basic. Total Hg concentrations were low.

Sediment samples were collected from six creeks and these samples, along with a lake sediment sample, were sent to T. Jackson (NWRI, Burlington) for methylation experiments. Two experiments were conducted over a 7-day period and a third over a 14-day period. These data are still being analyzed. However, highest carbon dioxide production was associated with sediments collected from the humic-stained creeks (i.e. creeks 9, 12 and 17) (Table 6). Preliminary MeHg data (not shown) also show the MeHg production rates are highest in the humic-stained creeks. The 2-week experiment, utilizing the lake sediment sample determined that carbon dioxide continued to be produced during the length of the experiment, suggesting that methylation predominated over demethylation. Although methylation rates apparently were lower at the single Cli Lake site examined than the three creek sites, the lake itself may be more important in terms of Hg methylation given its considerably larger surface area.

A broad series of invertebrate samples were collected in the littoral region of each of the study lakes in summer 2000. Where possible, samples were collected in weedy marshy areas and in rocky areas where Hg levels and/or methylation rates possibly may differ. In addition, in Little Doctor Lake, invertebrates were collected in various rocky areas in different reaches of the mountain ranges. Organisms included snails, caddisflies, mayflies, stoneflies, beetles, leeches, amphipods and corixids. Invertebrates have been identified to species. A subset from each lake is being analyzed for total Hg and stable isotopes. Methylmercury analyses will be performed on a subset of these samples.

Mean Hg concentration was the lowest (0.07 μg·g-1). A smaller number of walleye were caught with a mean length of 468 mm, a mean age of 17.2 years and a 15N of 1 1.3%0. Mercury concentration in walleye was the lowest (0.75 μg·g-1) of the three lakes. Walleye approached a Hg concentration of 0.5 μg·g-1 at approximately 15.7 years of age and as 15N approached 1 1 .8%0. Only two pike were captured from Sibbeston Lake during the original study; these fish were relatively small (mean: 631 mm), old (mean: 16.7 years) and with a high 15N (mean: 11.5%0) but a low Hg concentration (0.29 μg·g-1) .

In 2000, we had various community interactions. All of our field sampling was conducted with Ricky Tsetso, our guide during our previous years of sampling. At Willow Lake, an Elder and two community members, including a youth, accompanied us. We also responded to inquiries from Jean Marie River regarding stock assessment and Hg studies in their area. We prepared a draft report on the results of our first 2 years of study and received comments on it during our August field season. This report is being improved and updated.

We had a productive field season in August 2000, conducting new sampling on three lakes and revisiting Cli and Little Doctor Lakes. While ongoing, our study has not shown elevated Hg concentrations in predatory fish in Cli and Little Doctor Lakes to be associated with a combination of low pH and high DOC, as observed in other lakes, nor to high background Hg levels. Nor have our studies suggested that limnological and watershed conditions are such as to favour relatively high Hg methylation and low demethylation rates. Fish age appears to be important because relatively old fish populations dominate many of the lakes; thus fish have been accumulating Hg over many years. Because growth rates are lower than in the more southern regions of their population range, the potential for growth dilution is less. Increased harvesting of larger fish would remove fish with high Hg concentrations from the fish population and may improve growth rates. Fish harvesting has previously been suggested as a means to lower Hg concentrations in fish (Verta 1 990).

Stern and Lyle Lockhart, Freshwater Institute, DFO, Winnipeg, MB; George Low, DFO, Hay River, NT; Maurice Boucher, Akaitcho Territory Tribal Council, Fort Resolution, NT; Brenda Parlee, Lutsel K'e Dene Band, Lutsel K'e, NT; Tim Heron, South Slave Metis Tribal Council, Fort Smith, NT This study is the second year of a long~term monitoring program of contaminant trends (PCBs, DDT, toxaphene, mercury, etc.) in lake trout, burbot (loche, maria) and pike (jack) from two regions of Great Slave Lake. The West Basin is strongly affected by inputs from the Slave River while the East Arm is influenced more by atmospheric inputs. In 2000, burbot from the Slave River were added to the study design. In the West Basin, a community fisherman collected pike and burbot near the Slave River inflow and lake trout in the Simpson Island area. In the East Arm, a community member at Lutsel K'e collected these species of fish in the vicinity of the community. Finally, a community member from Fort Smith collected burbot in the Slave River. Ten specimens of the approx~ imately 20 collected of each species from each location were submitted for analyses, which are ongoing, while the remainder is archived. A presentation was given at Lutsel K'e on previous studies conducted from 1994 to 1998, including preliminary 1999 results. Data from 1999 have been received and initial interpretations are presented in this report.

1. Lake trout, pike, and burbot were collected from the West Basin and the East Arm in 2000 with the support of community members from Fort Resolution and Lutsel K'e. Burbot were collected from the Slave River with support from Fort Smith.
Contaminant analysis of fish collected in 2000 is ongoing.
3. Fish collected in 1 999 have been analyzed for contaminants.
Metals, such as mercury (Hg), occurred in relatively low concentrations in lake trout, burbot and pike from the two locations in Great Slave Lake in 1999.

5. Organochlorine (OC) concentrations also were low in fish from these two locations. Lower OC concentrations were observed in lake trout and burbot caught from the East Arm in 1 999 than in 1993. Continuing research will investigate whether this is a real time trend and the reasons for it.

Organochlorine concentrations in fish collected in the West Basin in 1 999 are similar to concentrations observed in earlier years. Continuing research will investigate why OC concentrations in fish in the West Basin are similar to those observed in earlier years while declining concentrations may be occurring in fish from the East Arm.

Develop a cost-effective, long-term monitoring strategy for assessing temporal trends in persistent organic contaminant concentrations (including PCBs, DDT, toxaphene, coplanar PCBs and Hg) in key predatory fish species inhabiting the Great Slave Lake ecosystem, including the Slave River.
2. Assess spatial patterns in contaminant trends and investigate possible causal factors for these patterns, including sources (long-range atmospheric and the Slave River) and food web pathways.

3. Integrate this monitoring program with research and monitoring programs being conducted in the Peace and Athabasca River drainage systems (supported under the Northern River Ecosystem Initiative) and G.A. Stem's Northern Contaminants Program (NCP)- supported burbot monitoring program on the Mackenzie River at Fort Good Hope, Northwest Territories.

The NCP has noted that the lack of temporal trend data for contaminants in biota is a significant knowledge gap. Accordingly, it has called for the creation of a long-term biomonitoring program to establish time trends in contaminant concentrations. By establishing monitoring sites, useful information will be provided on whether or not contaminant concentrations are decreasing with reduced use of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) worldwide. For time trends in freshwater environments, fish have been identified as the best organism for biomonitoring of contaminant trends. Several sites are being investigated - including the Mackenzie River at Fort Good Hope, various Yukon lakes and Great Slave Lake, the focus of this study. Great Slave Lake was selected as one of the sites for the long-term biomonitoring of contaminant trends in freshwater fish for the reasons described below.

First, in the mid- l 990s, the NCP supported various studies of POPs in Great Slave Lake, including food web biomagnification studies. Biological research was focused at two sites - Fort Resolution, near the Slave River mouth, and Lutsel K'e, in the East Arm and well-removed from a direct Slave River influence (Evans 1994, 1995). Contaminant concentrations tended to be higher in the East Arm than West Basin, possibly because suspended sediments in the Slave River reduce the bioavailability of POPs to biota. Fish collected during these NCP-supported studies are archived; therefore, it is possible to re-examine these archived samples for compounds that were not analyzed or to compare differences between current analytical methods and older methods. Such studies are highly useful and provide for a greater confidence in using older data (Huestis et al. 1996).

Second, Great Slave Lake is strongly influenced by the Slave River, formed by the confluence of the Peace and Athabasca rivers. Increased development in the Peace Athabasca drainage basins (oil sands, pulp and paper mills, agriculture, urban areas, etc.) may potentially affect an increase in contaminant loading to Great Slave Lake. Because of this, it is of vital importance that a long-term monitoring program be established to assess the changing condition of contaminants in the Great Slave Lake ecosystem. An even larger long-term data set for POPs and metal concentrations exists for the Slave River (Sanderson et al. 1997, McCarthy et al. 1997). Fish samples and/or sample extracts are archived from these collections. The addition of a Slave River site to our monitoring program in 2000 will help to assess whether or not contaminant concentrations in burbot in the river are decreasing.

Third, studies conducted in the early 1990s as part of the Northern River Basins Study (Pastershank and Muir I 996) showed elevated concentrations of PCBs in burbot M. Evans and D. Muir liver along several reaches of the Peace and Athabasca rivers. Levels approached or exceeded those observed in the Slave River and Great Slave Lake. These higher concentrations may have been related to trophic feeding and/or to local PCB inputs. The Northern Rivers Ecosystem Initiative is supporting research to elucidate these issues, including possible declines in contaminant body burdens in burbot in Peace and Athabasca River systems. Our monitoring study, especially in the Slave River and Fort Resolution area, will allow for a further assessment of the contaminant status of the Peace and Athabasca Rivers including how changing contaminant trends may affect the Great Slave Lake ecosystem.

Fourth, Great Slave Lake is a major population centre in the Northwest Territories. Yellowknife is the territorial capital while Hay River is an important transportation hub with road and rail links to the south, and is a port serving the Mackenzie River, the outflow from Great Slave Lake. Fort Resolution and Lutsel K'e are two major communities located on the Great Slave Lake shoreline that make extensive use of its fish populations. Both communities are concerned about contaminant concentrations in their fish and have supported other and our NCP studies for many years. Fort Smith also is concerned about contaminant concentrations in fish in the Slave River.

Fifth, in contrast to most aquatic systems in the Northwest Territories, the Great Slave Lake is well-studied with the major features of its limnology and fisheries ecology well understood. Classic limnological and fisheries studies were conducted by Rawson ( 1950, 1951, 1953, 1956). More modern research studies include Fee et al. ( 1985), Patalas and Patalas ( 1978) and Evans et al.

Sixth, the Great Slave Lake commercial fishery has been in existence since the early 1950s. It is a highly regulated fishery with fishing quotas established for some areas of the lake while other areas are closed to commercial fishing. While long-term records have been maintained on the Great Slave Lake fisheries, few studies have investigated contaminant concentrations in the fisheries. In contrast, there are extensive long-term data sets for contaminant trends in Great Lakes fish (Hesselberg et al. 1990, Suns et al. 1993, Huestis et al. 1996). Thus it is timely that similar such data sets are beginning to be generated for important Great Slave Lake fish.

The Great Slave Lake long-term biomonitoring program began in 1999 with the collection of pike, lake trout and burbot at Lutsel K'e and at Fort Resolution. In the West Basin, lake trout were collected near Slave Point at the lake outflow. In 2000, the same species were collected in the same general locations although lake trout were collected in the Simpson Island region, which is much closer to the Slave River plume. In February 200 I , burbot were collected in the Slave River, near Fort Smith.

Intact fish were shipped to DFO (Burlington) for initial examination (final length determinations, sex,% moisture, % lipid), tissue preparation and extraction. Some of this work is ongoing for fish caught in 2000-200 I. Most of the analyses for the fish caught in 1999-2000 have been completed while analyses of fish caught in 2000-200 I continue. Burbot liver and lake trout and pike muscle are being analyzed for POPs including PCBs, DDT, dieldrin and toxaphene. A subset also is being examined for coplanar PCBs and being prepared for possible future dioxin/furan analyses. Muscle is also being analyzed for metals (Hg, arsenic and selenium), and carbon and nitrogen isotope analyses. The latter analyses may provide information on carbon sources and trophic feeding.

Following the removal of the appropriate tissues from the individual fish, the remaining fish samples are homogenized and homegenates placed in several 500-mL containers for archiving. These samples are shipped back to NWRI (Saskatoon) . Because relatively small amounts of tissue were removed from most fish (the exception is the smaller burbot from Lutsel K'e), these homogenates represent "whole body." and whole body (of interest in the biomagnification of contaminants from one organism to another).

Fish collected from different regions of Great Slave Lake in the 2000-200 I study year were similar in mean length and weight (Table I). Lake trout from Lutsel K'e and the Simpson Islands were particularly similar in size. Burbot caught from Resolution Bay were larger than burbot caught from Lutsel K'e, as was observed in 1999-2000 (Evans and Muir 2000). Fort Smith burbot were intermediate in size to burbot caught from the two locations in Great Slave Lake. Lake trout and burbot were similar in size in 1999-2000 and 2000-200 l; somewhat larger pike were collected at Lutsel K'e in 2000 than in 1999 (666 ± 158 mm) . The Fort Resolution pike and burbot populations were strongly dominated by males. This was not observed in I 999.

Stable isotope analyses have been completed for fish collected in 1999-2000. These data are shown (Table 2), along with data collected in earlier years. Lipid values in lake trout from Lutsel K'e varied markedly between the three collection periods with highest values in fish caught in 1995. Lake trout had somewhat higher 15N in 1995. Lake trout from the West Basin tended to have higher % lipid and 15N values than the East Arm lake trout for the 1999 collections year, suggesting a richer diet more strongly dominated by fish . Rawson ( 195 1) reported that lake trout from the West Basin consumed proportionately more fish than lake trout from the East Arm . 13C values were also higher for West Basin lake trout suggesting closer trophic links with plankton rather than periphyton. Analyses of samples collected in 1999 for metals have been completed (Table 3). These data can be compared to the limited metals data from earlier sampling in Great Slave Lake. Highest Hg concentrations were found in pike muscle, although mean concentrations were well below the 0.5 μ g·g-1 guideline for the commercial sale of fish . Mercury concentrations also were lower than in many of the smaller lakes investigated by Lockhart et al. (2000) north of Great Slav@ Lake, although similar to concentrations observed ih Belot and Colville Lakes, which are relatively large lakes located north of Great Bear Lake. The lowest Hg concentrations in the Great Slave Lake fish sampled in I 999-2000 were in burbot. Arsenic concentrations were highest in lake trout muscle. Selenium concentrations were slightly higher and somewhat more variable in the East Arm than West Basin fish . No time trends were evident from these limited data sets. A stronger data set for investigating time trends in Hg will be obtained once the burbot caught from the Slave River in 2000 are analyzed since burbot were sampled over a greater number of years during the Slave River Study and metal analyses were routinely run . The Great Slave Lake metals data will be added to the data sets for our project investigating the factors affecting elevated Hg levels in predatory fish in the Mackenzie River Basin.

Lake trout and pike muscle and burbot liver are being analyzed for a wide variety of POPs. These data have been received recently and so the full interpretation of the data is ongoing. In brief, the initial observations are as follows.

First, in earlier research, we noted that OC contaminants tended to occur in higher concentrations in fish (and invertebrates) collected from the East Arm (Lutsel K'e region) than the West Basin (Fort Resolution region). However, with the 1999 data, we are observing the converse trend (Figures I and 2); higher concentrations of dieldrin, chlordane, DDT (burbot only), PCBs and toxaphene were found in lake trout and burbot collected from the West Basin rather than the East Arm. The reasons for these differences are unclear. While% lipid and 15N was slightly higher in the West Basin versus the East Arm fish in 1 999, this also was observed over the period 1 993 to I 996.

Second, dieldrin, chlordane, DDT, PCBs and toxaphene data are suggestive of a trend of declining concentrations in the Lutsel K'e region between 1993 and 1999. This trend also is evident for burbot liver collected from Lutsel K'e. Such differences do not appear to be lipid-related for lake trout nor to trophic feeding. Age data have not yet been received and so further comparisons based on age will be made at a later date. With a relatively small number of years of study, it is difficult to be certain that there is a real trend in the data. However, because other monitoring programs are in place in other lakes in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, these evaluations can be strengthened as more of the studies report their results.

There is no evidence of a decline in POPs concentrations for lake trout collected from the West Basin (Figure I ). POPs concentrations are consistently higher in 1 999 than in 1993 although % lipid values are lower. There is a larger data set for burbot liver from the West Basin. Concentrations are similar to those observed in earlier years and no time trend is evident for any compound. Again, the analyses of these data will continue to investigate the reasons for similar POPs concentrations in 1993 when compared to earlier years of collection .

PCB data for burbot collected in 1993 and 1999 from the West Basin and the East Arm were examined to investigate possible temporal and spatial differences in homologue concentration and composition. For East Arm burbot liver, concentrations (and% composition) of penta- and hexa-PCBs were lower in 1993 than 1999 while slightly higher concentrations of mono/di-PCBs were observed (Table 4) . Burbot liver from the West Basin in 1993 was similar in homologue composition to burbot liver from the East Arm in 1993, although PCB concentrations were lower. However, in 1999, West Basin burbot liver had a greater predominance of hexa- and hepta-PCBs and a lower predominance of mono/di-PCBs than burbot from the East Arm. Overall, burbot from the West Basin tended to have a high average PCB chlorine number than burbot from the East Arm both in 1993 (6.0 versus 5.5) and 1999 (4.5 versus 5.0).

Organochlorine contaminants occurred in higher concentrations in pike muscle collected from the West Basin than the East Arm in summer 1999 (Table 5) . Lipid composition was similar between the two locations and so spatial differences do not appear to be directly related to lipids. Pike collected from the West Basin in 1996 had similar POPs concentrations to pike collected in 1999. Again, with only 2 years of observation, the detection of time trends is problematic.

There were a number of formal and informal communications over the last year of study. Informal communications involved telephone calls regarding sample collection and general questions. In March 200 I, M. Evans visited Lutsel K'e and discussed the results of the previous and ongoing Great Slave Lake studies with a number of community representatives.

Data generated from the original Great Slave Lake study have been compiled into master data files and the majority of error checking completed. Fish data from the 1999-2000 sampling season will be placed into a brief report that will summarize these earlier data and contaminant data from the 1999-2000 studies. In addition, comparisons will be provided with contaminant levels in 189 similar fish from the Laurentian Great Lakes. By providing brief reports, we hope to streamline the rate at which contaminant data become available to the communities and for health assessments.

The second year of this study was successful, with pike, lake trout and burbot collected from the East Arm and West Basin of Great Slave Lake and burbot from the Slave River. Community support for these studies has been very good. As in 1999~2000, fish collected from the various sampling sites are similar to one another in length and weight. Burbot, however, appear to be more variable from location to location than the other two species.

The results of the metals studies have determined that Hg concentrations are relatively low in all three fish species, with highest values observed in pike. However, mean Hg concentration is well below the 0.5 μg·g- 1 guideline for the commercial sale of fish. Organochlorine data have been received recently and the analyses of these data are ongoing. POPs concentrations are lower in lake trout Figure 1. -o 30 en .s M. Evans and D. Muir muscle and burbot liver from the East Arm in I 999 than in 1993, but the data sets are relatively small for inferring time trends. In contrast, POPs concentrations in fish collected in the West Basin are similar to concentrations observed in earlier years.

Further analyses, including adjustments for lipid content, fish age, etc. may help explain these spatial and temporal differences. In addition, comparison of our results with the results of studies at other ongoing NCP monitoring studies will help to resolve what time trends are occurring.

The results of this study and early studies are of interest to the communities and communications are good. The publication of a brief report summarizing the major features of the fish data will improve these communications and help streamline the consumption assessments.

This is an ongoing monitoring study. Annual sampling is projected until winter 2002 and analysis of collected fish until 2003. It is further anticipated that monitoring will continue after NCP Phase 2 is completed.

Ron Allen, DFO, Yellowknife, NT; Gail Boila, DFO, Winnipeg, MB; Joanne DeLaronde, DFO, Winnipeg, MB; Robert Garrett, Geological Survey of Canada, Ottawa, ON; Glen Stephens, Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Yellowknife, NT Surveys of lakes from the Northwest Territories and Nunavut have consistently indicated that fish from these lakes often have muscle mercury levels above those recommended for human consumption. The questions arising from these observations relate to the geographic extent of the problem of high mercury levels, the sources of the mercury, whether the problem is entirely natural or whether there is an anthropogenic component, and whether the magnitude of the problem is changing. For several years, fish sampled in Northern Contaminants Program (NCP) projects have been analyzed for mercury. More recently fish taken in stock surveys carried out at the request of Renewable Resource Councils have also been analyzed. The result is a growing database of mercury in fish from lakes chosen either by other NCP projects or by local communities. The data reveals that different species generally contain different levels of mercury with predators such as lake trout, walleye and northern pike usually containing more mercury than forage feeders such as cisco and whitefish. Some of the levels in predators have been found to exceed levels considered safe for unrestricted consumption and a number of consumption advisories have been issued. The reasons why levels of a given species are higher in one lake than another are not yet clear and are the subject of ongoing investigations. Mercury (Hg) levels in muscle from whitefish and Arctic char are generally quite low and are thus safe to eat.

Under the terms of land claims settlements, DFO is responsible for the conduct of studies on fish populations at the request of the Renewable Resource Councils in order to assess the existing or proposed harvest of stocks for subsistence, commercial or tourist uses. Historical DFO Inspection Service data indicate that muscle Hg levels in some of the larger fish from a number of lakes in the NWf exceed levels deemed safe by Health Canada for human consumption. However, the sample sizes are small and samples were generally biased to size classes typical of commercial catches.

Fish from a number of lakes have been surveyed over the past several years. The levels of Hg in the fish differ from lake to lake and conclusions drawn from one lake do not necessarily apply to another lake. Fish that feed near the base of the food chain (whitefish, cisco, sucker) consistently contain less Hg those that feed near the top of the food chain (walleye, pike, lake trout) . In a number of instances, the predators contained levels high enough to require consumption advisories (Lockhart et al. 1999a, I999b). We have begun to investigate the form of Hg found in the fish and results to date indicate that most of it is methylmercury.

Several factors can influence the level of Hg in fish tissues including fish age (or length), the structure of the supporting food chain, water chemistry, lake temperature, microbiological processes in the sediments, fish biochemistry, the supply of Hg to the lake and the nature of the drainage (e.g. rocks, uplands, wetlands, etc.) . The supply of Hg is a mixture of natural geological contributions with human-related Hg appearing as additions to the natural supply. There is no doubt that gaseous Hg moves with air masses because concentrations in air have been measured at Alert (Schroeder et al. 1998) and further that Hg is found in snow falling in the Arctic (Lu et al. 200 I). These studies, however, do not answer the question about the relative importance of natural and anthropogenic sources of Hg. To a surprising extent, the answer to this question remains unknown although lake sediment core studies suggest that, in some locations, anthropogenic inputs may be as large as natural inputs. While several Hg isotopes exist, the analytical precision necessary to discriminate among sources is not yet available.

Several independent lines of evidence suggest that Hg inputs to northern Canada have increased over preindustrial levels. Mercury in Arctic seals and whales has increased since the 1970s (Wagemann et al. 1996). Sediment core data from a number of lakes in the NWT have suggested that recent Hg inputs are substantially above pre-industrial levels (Lockhart et al. 1998). Recently, Braune ( 1999) reported that Hg levels have also increased in seabirds. Given these considerations, it is important to assess Hg levels in stocks of fish being used now or being assessed for potential harvest in the near future.

The problem with Hg in fish from lakes in northern Canada is relatively specific to predator species like walleye, northern pike and lake trout. Species that feed lower in the food chain like lake whitefish have low levels of Hg. Arctic char generally have low levels of Hg also, notably anadromous populations; some collections of char had high levels, probably as a result of non-migratory habits. The problem with predator species is extensive geographically; fish from the Yukon to northern Nunavut have been found to contain high levels of Hg. Lake trout from Nunavut had an unusually high proportion of means over the limit for marketing.

This project has produced the first relatively large samples from NWT and Nunavut lakes. These will facilitate the identification of temporal trends with high statistical rigour in future studies.

Freshwater organisms are exposed to atmospheric contaminants deposited on snow or directly onto lake surfaces or lake watersheds. Fish accumulate contaminants, metals and organometallics as they pass water over their gills as well as from their diet. It has been shown that rising water temperatures lead to increased metabolic rates and thus pumping of higher volumes of water across the gills, which in turn results in increased uptake of metals from the water. Unlike mammals, fish have limited capacity to degrade most POPs and metals, and excrete many of these chemicals very slowly. Fish are, therefore, good indicators of freshwater contamination by POPs and metals.

Small lakes in the high Arctic are replenished annually with snowmelt runoff and direct precipitation, which represent significant fractions of their water budgets. Declining concentrations of POPs, or increasing levels of previously unstudied POPs, in air and precipitation should be reflected relatively quickly in changes in levels in food webs and top predator fishes, compared to the vast marine environment. We know this to be the case from the sedimentary record of POPs and Hg in small Arctic lakes (Muir et al. 1996, Lockhart et al. 1998).

The value of long-term annual sampling of fish for measurement of temporal trends of contaminants was well illustrated by studies in Sweden. Arctic char have been collected since 1980 in Lake Abiskojaure, 200 km north of the Arctic Circle, and northern pike have been collected from Lake Storvindeln, a forest lake in northern Sweden, since 1978. Samples were collected annually and were selected for consistency in sex, age, size and sampling season. Each annual sample at a given location was represented by 10 to 25 specimens, thus within-year variation could be estimated. Declines in levels of IDDT (DDT + ODD + DOE), PCBs and hexachlorobenzene (HCBz) were noted in fish from the Arctic locations (Olsson and Reutergardh 1986, DeMarch et al. 1998). The Arctic char data provided a more accurate temporal trend than pike muscle because char has a higher concentration of fat. Hexachlorocyclohexane (HCH) isomers showed no significant declines in fish muscle over a 24-year period. Because of annual sampling, the Swedish program was also able to detect increases in DDT inputs due to the use of DDT in East Germany in 1984 (Bignert et al. 1993).

Lakes near Oausuittuq (Resolute) are ideal sites for a study of temporal trends of POPs and metals in fishes. Many of the lakes (e.g. Char, Resolute, Meretta) are well studied limnologically and the food chain in Char Lake has been well documented (Hobson and Welch 1995) . Char from Char Lake collected by H. Welch in 1993 have been previously analyzed for organochlorine contaminants and metals (Muir and Lockhart 1996, Muir et al. 1997). Levels of PCBs and total DDT in char muscle (plus skin) were relatively high compared to other landlocked or sea run char (Muir et al. 1997). Other persistent organochlorines (e.g. chlordane, toxaphene) in Char Lake char were at levels similar to other Canadian Arctic locations. The higher levels of DDT and PCBs may represent local contamination but could also be due to trophic position of the char that were sampled.

The assessment of co,htaminants conducted by the Northern Contaminants Program (NCP) (Jensen et al. 1997, Muir et al. 1997) found that there was limited information on temporal trends in fish, especially in the eastern and high Arctic. This study is designed to help fil l that knowledge gap.

Arctic char were collected from Char and Resolute lakes in August 2000 by Dr. Kock and research team, working with Debbie Iqaluk of Oausuittuq, using either hand methods or gill netting; char were also collected from North Lake (about I O km northwest of Oausuittuq). These added to previous collections of landlocked char from Resolute Lake ( 1997, 1998, 1999), Char Lake ( 1999), Boomerang Lake on Somerset Island ( 1999) and Sapphire Lake on Devon Island ( 1999). Samples (skin on fillets) were frozen in Resolute, shipped to NWRI (Burlington) and stored at -20 °C until analysis. Subsamples were also shipped to J. Reist (DFO, Winnipeg). Aging of the char was done by J. Babaluk (DFO, Winnipeg).

Arctic char muscle was subsampled and acid-digested using high pressure microwave. The digest was then analyzed for Hg by cold vapour atomic absorption spectrometry and for 22 elements using inductively coupled plasma-low resolution mass spectrometry.

Char (muscle plus skin) samples were homogenized, mixed with pre-cleaned Na 2SO4 and Soxhlet extracted with dichloromethane:hexane ( 1: 1 ). Organochlorines were isolated by gel permeation chromatography, followed by silica gel clean-up. The chromatography on silica gel was used to separate PCBs and p,p' -DOE from more chlordane and toxaphene components, p,p'-DDT and HCH isomers. The two fractions from the silica gel column were then analyzed by gas chromatography with electron-capture detection. Separation was accomplished on a HP 6890 GC using a 30 m DB-5 column with H2 carrier gas. IPCBs represented the sum of 103 congeners. Toxaphene was analyzed by low resolution CC-negative ion MS using a HP 5973 MSD in negative ion mode.

Quality assurance steps included the analysis of certified reference materials for heavy metals and organochlorines, reagent blanks and duplicate samples. The National Laboratory for Environmental Testing (NLET) organics and metals labs are participants in the NCP Quality Assurance Program. The NLET organics lab is a participant in the Quality Assurance for Marine Environmental Monitoring in Europe (OUASIMEME) programs for PCBs and toxaphene. NLET is certified by the Canadian Environmental Analytical Laboratory program of the Canadian Standards Association.

Mean concentrations of metals and organochlorines in char from Resolute Lake were compared among years using the General Linear Models procedure in Systat (Ver 9) (SPSS 1999). The analysis of covariance (AN COVA) model included year, sex and length, and their interactions. Results were first tested for normality using skewness and kurtosis tests. Length adjusted least square means from the ANCOVA were calculated and compared using Tukey's (Post-hoe) Test.

The effect of diet and trophic level on Hg and organochlorine levels was investigated using stable isotopes of carbon and nitrogen (Figure 2). The char from Resolute Lake had a narrow range of 813C, which indicates that they are feeding on similar diets. A few fish have 815N values that were up to 3 .8 parts per thousand (%0) higher than others. Differences in 815N of this magnitude are associated with a change of trophic level because concentrations of the heavier isotope of nitrogen, 15N, are progressively enriched from prey to predator an average of 3 to 5%o (Peterson and Fry 1987). The 815N values suggests that these char were feeding one trophic level higher than others, probably on other char. Landlocked char popula~ tions are known to develop a behavioural dichotomy wherein some individuals at a certain "escape size" adapt to a cannibalistic feeding habit, while other individuals may not. In Char Lake, a system containing only char, Hobson and Welch ( 1995) associated 815N values of 13. 7%o with piscivory in char. They also found a significant increase in the 815N of these fish with size which they attributed to cannibalism within the population. There Table 2. Both Hg and I:PCB were significantly correlated with 815N in char from Resolute Lake collected in 1997 and 1999 (Figure 3) . This trend, which was also observed for I:DDT and I:CHL but not for other metals or OC groups, suggests that biomagnification of Hg and organochlorines is occurring within the char population due to the presence of piscivorous char. These results support the hypothesis that the reason for higher levels seen in char sampled in 1993 in Char Lake (see Muir et al. 2000) was that piscivorous char were analyzed.

This is a long-term study of contaminant levels in landlocked Arctic char in the area of Oausuittuq. The results for Hg in char muscle from Resolute Lake suggest no significant change in concentrations of Hg over an 8-year period, 1992 to 2000. Mean concentrations in char from 1999 and 2000 in Resolute Lake were 1 5% to 20% lower than those from 1992 and 1997, however, if a slow decline is occurring it will take additional annual sampling to confirm this. Results also show that levels of Hg and metallic elements in landlocked char muscle in three other lakes (North, Sapphire, Boomerang) in the region are similar to those in Char and Resolute lakes. PCB levels in char from Resolute Lake in 1 997 were higher than those in 1999 after adjusting for length. Further sampling and analysis will be needed to determine if this observation is part of a declining trend of PCB inputs. Levels of PCBs and DDT-related compounds were much Figure 3.
