The ringed seal is the most abundant Arctic pinniped with a circumpolar distribution, making this species an ideal candidate for examining spatial trends of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) in the Arctic. It is identified as a key species for monitoring by the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme and for temporal trends monitoring by the Northern Contaminants Program (NCP l 999) . As a top predator in near-shore pelagic food webs, the ringed seal prefers land-fast ice or multi-year ice. The ringed seal diet consists of fish, mainly Arctic cod (Boreogadus saida) and polar cod (Arctocadus glacialis), and crustaceans (amphipods, mysids, and euphausids) (Holst et al. Ringed seals are relatively sedentary, and males may occupy the same under-ice habitat for up to 9 months (Smith 1987). Ringed seals are hunted in virtually all coastal communities in the Canadian Arctic and it is, therefore, relatively easy to obtain samples with the help of local hunters and trappers committees.

Until this project began, NCP was funding work on temporal trends in seals only at Holman, NWT, in the western Canadian Arctic (Stern and Addison 1 999). Addison and Smith ( 1998) have recently published time trends of PCB, DOE and DDT in ringed seals from 19721990 at Holman. There are uncertainties in the pre-1981 Holman trends, because archived samples are not available from l 972 and analytical methodologies have changed (packed columns to capillary gas chromatography [GC] columns) . Nevertheless, through reanalysis of l 981 samples by both packed column and capillary column GC, the authors have been able to compare results over the l 8-year period.

The rationale for this project is that with only one site for temporal trends, there are significant geographical gaps in temporal trend coverage. Previous work on POPs and metals in ringed seals from the 1 980s and 1 990s at locations in the high Arctic and in Hudson Bay had not been followed up. There could be differences in the trends of POPs and Hg in the eastern and western Arctic. It is now clear from recent seawater measurements that there are large spatial differences of HCH, toxaphene and PCBs in seawater between the Beaufort Sea and Baffin Bay, and between those areas and Hudson Bay (Hoekstra et al. Presumably this reflects the influence of Atlantic water in Baffin Bay and freshwater inputs, which are also relatively low in HCH, in Hudson Bay.

These differences in seawater levels may give rise to differences in contaminant levels in marine food webs and ultimately in marine mammals. For example, in the case of HCH, much higher levels are found in ringed seal blubber from the central high Arctic (Eureka, Resolute, Arctic Bay) than in waters influenced by the Atlantic Ocean (Baffin Bay [Grise Fiord], Cumberland Sound Hudson Bay populations (Arviat, Inukjuaq) have similar levels to those in the central high Arctic, a trend that is not consistent with levels in water. PCB l 53 shows fewer regional differences after adjusting for the effects of age and sex using analysis of covariance (Muir et al. 2000), but levels of PCBs are generally higher in seals in the eastern Arctic (Muir et al. 1997).

Regional differences in concentrations are even more pronounced for Hg than for POPs in seals with higher levels in the western Arctic (Muir et al. 1 997, Wagemann et al. 1996). This may be due to greater sources of natural Hg in the sedimentary rocks of the western Arctic. Temporal trends in Hg show increasing levels with time in seals, beluga, narwhal and seabird eggs (Wagemann et al. 1996, Braune 1999) but the rates do not seem to be the same in the eastern and western Arctic, at least for beluga. In the case of seals, results for Hg in liver are available for several communities in the eastern Arctic (Resolute, Pangnirtung, Inukjuaq, Wakeham) and western Arctic (Holman, Sachs Harbour) from the l 970s to 1990s, although they have been presented only on a regional basis (Wagemann et al.

This is a new project. However, the principal investigators have access to samples, have published on older results and are custodians of the data from the I 970s, I980s and 1990s. Ringed seal blubber and liver samples collected from Pangnirtung in May 1999 were provided by Dr. Kunito with the research group of S. Tanabe (Ehime University, Japan). Ringed seal blubber samples were obtained from Jones Sound near Grise Fiord as part of the North Water Study (Fisk et al. 2001) and at Arviat as part of studies by I. Stirling and N. Lund (Canadian Wildlife Service) in 1998.

In 2000-2001 ringed seal samples were successfully collected with the help of Hunters and Trappers Committee partner organizations in Resolute, Arctic Bay and Pond Inlet as part of the spring/summer hunt. Hunters were provided with a kit and video prepared in lnuktitut and English by the Nunavik Research Centre (NvRC). Collections consisted of blubber, liver, muscle, kidney and tooth/lower jaw (foraging) from 25 seals; most were adults and about one-half were female. Essential data on length, girth, blubber thickness at the sternum and sex was provided for the Resolute and Arctic Bay animals. All samples were shipped to the NvRC for processing. Large subsamples of all tissues were archived in walk-in freezers at -35°C in sealed plastic bags (double bagged). Aging was performed on tooth sections at NvRC.

For 2000-2001, samples from Pangnirtung, Arviat, Grise Fiord and Pond Inlet were analyzed. Ringed seal blubber samples from Grise Fiord and Pangnirtung were analyzed for organochlorines at NWRC, Hull, and samples from Arviat were analyzed at the National Laboratory for Environmental Testing (NLET) at NWRI. A subset from Pangnirtung was analyzed at both laboratories. Procedures were similar to those used for previous NCP work on marine mammals (Fisk et al. 2001, Muir et al. 1999). At NWRC, seal blubber was homogenized with sodium sulfate. This mixture was placed in a glass column and organochlorines were eluted with dichloromethane:hexane ( 1: 1 ). Organochlorines were isolated by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) followed by chromatography on Florisil. PCBs and organochlorine pesticides were determined by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) on an HP-5973 MSD using selective ion monitoring. At NWRI, seal blubber was homogenized with sodium sulfate and Soxhlet extracted with dichloromethane:hexane ( 1: 1 ). Following GPC cleanup, organochlorines were fractionated on a silica gel column, then analyzed by gas chromatography with electron-capture detection (GC-ECD). Separation was accomplished on a HP 6890 GC using a 30 m DB-5 column with H2 carrier gas. Toxaphene was analyzed at NLET by low resolution CC-negative ion MS using a HP 5973 MSD in negative ion mode.
Liver and kidney samples were analyzed for heavy metals (cadmium, Hg, lead, selenium and arsenic) at NvRC (Kuujjuaq) using atomic absorption spectrometry (MS).

Quality assurance steps included the analysis of reference materials for heavy metals and organochlorines, reagent blanks and duplicate samples. The NvRC, NWRC and NLET organics laboratories are participants in the NCP Quality Assurance Program and in Quality Assurance for Marine Environmental Monitoring in Europe (QUASIMEME) programs for heavy metals and PCBs, respectively. The NLET and NWRC are certified by the Canadian Environmental Analytical Laboratory program of the Canadian Standards Association.

Organochlorine concentrations in ringed seals were normalized to 100% lipid. Results for both Hg and organochlorines were first tested for normality using skewness and kurtosis tests. Data were log10 transformed to give coefficients of skewness and kurtosis < 2. Mean concentrations of organochlorines in blubber of female ringed seals were compared among years using the general linear models procedure in Systat (Version 9) (SPSS 1999). The analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model included age, and age* year interaction. Comparisons of least squares means from the ANCOVA were made using Tukey's (Post-hoe) Test. Geometric means (back transformed log data) and arithmetic means were calculated for Hg in liver. For Hg, the ANCOVA model included age, sex, and age* year and sex* year interaction.

Samples from female seals only were selected for analysis in order to minimize age-related effects on organochlorine levels (Addison and Smith 1974). Results are available for seal blubber samples from Grise Fiord and for a subset of samples from Pangnirtung. Concentrations of Hg in ringed seal liver from the four locations (sampled 1998-2000) are shown in Table 1. Results for both males and female ringed seals were used for Hg in liver because ANCOVA showed no effect of gender on Hg concentrations. In other words, mean concentrations in males and females were not significantly different. Mercury concentrations ranged widely in adult seals and were highly skewed. However, log transformation reduced skewness and yielded normally distributed data (skewness coefficient < 2). There were also age*location interactions, i.e. different relationships of Hg with age at the four locations, thus no comparisons between locations were attempted at this stage.

Arithmetic mean concentrations of Hg in adult seals from Pond Inlet (2000) were three-fold higher than results reported by Smith and Armstrong ( 1978) for the same average aged animals. Results for Arviat and Pangnirtung could not be compared with previous data as there are no published results to our knowledge.

Stern and Addison ( 1 999) conducted a temporal trend study on PCBs and other POPs in beluga from Cumberland Sound using archived blubber for four sampling times from the mid- 1980s to late 1990s. Their results showed a small but significant decline in PCBs, DDT group and a-HCH, but none for~- and y-HCH over the 15-year period (Stern and Addison 1999). The seals, collected from the same area, do not show the same trends for PCBs and DDT, nor for HCH isomers. Analyses of additional Pangnirtung samples from 1999 will help address the question. However, the preliminary results illustrate differences due to species feeding behaviour and migratory pattern. Adult ringed seals are more likely full time residents of Cumberland Sound- while beluga are migratory, spending winter on offshore ice of Baffin Bay and the Davis Strait.

In the case of Hg in ringed seal liver, there was a threefold increase in concentrations at Pond Inlet over the 24-year period from 1976 to 2000. However, this conclusion is based on results from Smith and Armstrong ( 1978) who appear to have reported arithmetic means.

Statistical comparison using ANCOVA with the data from 2000 is problematic because results are probably not normally distributed. Without the raw data from the 1976 Pond Inlet samples, there will be great uncertainty in the conclusion regarding the size of the increase. On the other hand, the two groups of seals were comparable in age, which is an important co-variate for Hg in adult seals. Also, the Hg measurements in seal tissues have been conducted using the same analytical methodology (cold vapour atomic absorption spectroscopy); therefore, analytical differences are not likely to be an issue.

Females were chosen because they exhibit little influence of age on residue levels. No significant trends were found for total chlordanes, total DDT, dieldrin and J3-HCH. Significant declines, in the order of 20% over the 9 years, were found for total chlorobenzenes, a-HCH and total PCBs. Rates of declines in individual PCB congeners appeared to be faster as the number of chlorines increased (DB99 < CBI 53 < CB1 80). However, it is not known how much of this apparent decline was due to other factors, such as condition of the bears. Analysis of trends in chiral signatures of a-HCH, oxychlordane and heptachlor epoxide in these samples is underway in an attempt to determine if the 'age' of these residues has changed over time.

Preliminary analysis of results from immunotoxicology studies carried out in collaboration with the Norwegian School of Veterinary Science in I 999-2000 demonstrated that high PCB exposures of polar bears impair lympho- cyte function, IgG concentration and the ability to produce antibodies following immunization of the bears with certain microbes. It is reasonable to assume that PCB exposure is associated with decreased resistance to infections of the polar bears. Furthermore, a negative correlation was found between individual PCBs, oxychlordane and testosterone concentrations and between I:PCB and testosterone, indicating that PCB and chlordane exposure in polar bears is associated with a decrease in male testosterone concentrations. At the time of writing this report, Norwegian scientists have not completed statistical analysis of the data.

Preliminary data were obtained for in vitro metabolism of four model tetrachlorobiphenyl congeners, J3-HCH, a-HCH and trans-chlordane. Chlorine substitution pattern had a quantitative effect on rate and extent of in vitro biotransformation of the four PCB congeners. However, the relative rates of in vitro metabolism of the PCBs and other organochlorines did not agree with the relative bioaccumulation potential of these organochlorine compounds in polar bears. The ability of in vitro metabolism studies to mimic those in vivo requires further research .
PCBs, and possibly chlordanes, affect the immune system of polar bears, which may result in decreased resistance to infections.

In collaboration with the Canadian Wildlife Service (CWS), Prairie and Northern Region, the Norwegian Polar Institute and the Norwegian Veterinary Institute, determine the immunotoxic effects of PCBs and other organochlorines in polar bears throughout a gradient of exposure (i.e. Hudson Bay, low; Svalbard, high).

The study of organochlorine contaminants in polar bears has a long history. One of the first reports of PCBs in wild mammals was in polar bears in the Canadian Arctic (Bowes and Jonke! 1975). In 1982, the CWS began an investigation to identify the whole range of organochlorines that may be accumulating in polar bears. At the time, very little was being done to look at these contaminants in the Arctic environment. The finding of significant concentrations of several chlordane compounds, HCHs and dieldrin in polar bears, as well as the previously known DDTs and PCBs was one of the primary catalysts that resulted in renewed interest by scientists at Environment Canada and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans in research on the presence and significance of organochlorines in the Arctic. This early group formed the nucleus that eventually resulted in the Northern Contaminants Program (NCP), coordinated under the aegis of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The identification of organochlorines, their geographical distribution in Canadian polar bears and bioaccumulation in the polar bear food chain were documented in a series of publications in 1988 (Norstrom 1988, Norstrom and Muir 1988, Norstrom et al. 1988, Muir et al. 1988). PCBs and chlordanes, principally the metabolite oxychlordane, were shown to be the organochlorines with the highest concentration in polar bears.

A more ambitious study of the circumpolar distribution of organochlorines in polar bears was undertaken a few years later (Norstrom et al. 1998). The latter study showed that PCBs were lowest in the Bering and Chukchi Seas, fairly uniform in Canada (except for one anomalously high area at the mouth of Viscount Melville Sound), and highest in east Greenland and Svalbard. Chlordanes and chlorobenzenes were fairly evenly distributed throughout the Arctic. HCH concentrations tended to be highest in the Bering and Chukchi Seas, decreasing slightly further east. These results are consistent with anticipated distribution in the atmosphere of organochlorines from principal origins: Asia for HCHs, North America and Europe for PCBs.

In the early 1990s, emphasis shifted to the study of organochlorine metabolites and their potential toxicity in polar bears, because some metabolites were suspected of being involved in reproductive failure of seals in the Baltic Sea in the early 1970s. A number of methylsulfone- PCB metabolites were found to be present in polar bear tissues at 5% to 10% the concentration of PCBs (Letcher R. Norstrom et al. 1995). Geographical distribution was found to be similar to that of PCBs. The source of methylsulfone-PCBs was determined to be partly biotransformation of ingested PCBs, but a significant proportion of the methylsulfone- PCBs was bioaccumulated directly from ringed seals (Letcher et al.

The profile of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes in liver responsible for metabolism of organochlorines in mammals was partially characterized in the male polar bear (Bandiera et al. 1995). The activity of CYP enzymes EROD (ethoxyresorufin O-deethylation) for CYPIA and BROD (7-benzyloxyresorufin O-deethylase) for CYP2B, was determined, along with immunoquantitated CYPIA and CYP2B protein concentrations and chemical residues levels (Letcher et al. CYPIA is induced by dioxinlike compounds, and CYP2B by a variety of organochlorines as well as drugs and other xenobiotics. CYPIA protein concentrations were found to correlate with dioxin toxic equivalent concentrations (TEOs) . Most of the TEOs were due to CBI 56 and CB I 57, because the bear was found to easily biotransform the normally recalcitrant CB 126 and the mono-ortho PCBs, CB 105 and CB 1 18, which usually contribute the most to TEOs in high trophic level mammals and birds. Multiple linear regression showed that CYP2B protein concentrations were correlated with a combination of chlordanes and PCBs, but not with either group individually. This provides strong correlative evidence that these two groups are responsible for CYP2B induction. The possibility of immunoquantitating CYP enzymes in liver stored for several years as homogenates at regular freezer temperatures (- 20° to - 40°) was tested for potential as a biomarker of effects that correlate with CYPIA. It was found that most of the protein was degraded, so this approach could not be used (Bandiera et al. 1996).

Another group of metabolites, the hydroxy-PCBs, were targetted for study because studies with rats and other laboratory animals showed that they bound competitively to thyroid hormone transport proteins (TTR) in blood plasma. Polar bear blood was shown to have very high levels of hydroxy-PCBs, probably because of the bear's superior biotransformation capabilities (Sandau et al. 1998, 2000a). Total hydroxy-PCBs concentration in plasma was twice that of PCBs and ranked as the highest of all the organochlorine classes. The individual organochlorine with the highest concentration in polar bear plasma was 4-hydroxy-CB 187 (Norstrom 2000). During the course of this research, a new metabolite of octachlorostyrene, 4-hydroxyheptachlorostyrene, was discovered in polar bear plasma (Sandau et al. 2000b). Its binding capacity to human TTR was determined to be similar to that of T4 itself. The presence of a protein cross-reacting immunochemically with human TTR was confirmed in polar bear plasma, indicating that this new metabolite was likely present in plasma bound to TTR.

The hypothesis was tested that the hydroxy-PCB compounds were affecting thyroid hormone (T4, T3) and vitamin A (retinol) transport in polar bear by analysis of plasma in populations (i.e. southwest Hudson Bay and Svalbard) with a wide range of PCB concentrations. Principal components analysis was used to analyze the data. Four significant components were found that described 65% of the variance (Norstrom 2000). Contribution of individual chemicals to each component was primarily by chemical class. The first principal component (PC I) classified as persistent PCBs, PC2 as hydroxy-PCBs, PC3 as non-persistent PCBs, and PC4 as chlordanes . Total T4 and T3 were not correlated with any component. Retinol was negatively correlated to PC I (total PCBs), but positively correlated to PC2 (hydroxy-PCBs), in agreement with findings in Norway. This indicated that hydroxy-PCBs were not causing decreased vitamin A co-transport by binding to TTR. The free T4 index was inversely proportional to the residual T4 binding capacity of plasma, and directly proportional to free T4 in fish. Assuming the same is true in polar bears, free T4 would be negatively correlated to hydroxy-PCB concentrations. It is not known what significance this may have for thyroid hormone homeostasis in the bear.

Possible disruption of male sex hormone status in the polar bear was studied by in vitro metabolism of testosterone. Microsomes from 13 male bears prepared in 1993 for the enzyme characterization and activity studies (Bandiera et al. 1995, Letcher et al. 1996) had been archived at liquid nitrogen temperature. After testing for viability, these microsomes were used to characterize the metabolite profile of testosterone in the polar bear and to determine whether the rate of metabolite formation was in any way connected with organochlorine residue levels in liver previously determined (Letcher et al. 1996). The major metabolites were 2~-hydroxytestosterone, androstene- dione and 6~-hydroxytestosterone (Norstrom 2000). In rats, testosterone 2~- and 6~-hydroxylation is catalyzed predominantly by CYP3A enzymes and androstenedione formation is catalyzed by CYP2B enzymes. The profile of testosterone metabolites produced by polar bear is different from that produced by male rats, but is similar to that reported for sheep, goats and cattle. A recent 6~-hydroxytestosterone were also the major metabolites of in vitro testosterone hydroxylation in this species (androstenedione formation was not monitored) (Wolkers et al.

Correlational analysis of testosterone hydroxylase activities with other monooxygenase activities as well as with hepatic organochlorine levels was carried out. There 217 was a reasonably good correlation between all of the testosterone hydroxylase activities and BROD activity (r values of 0.53 to 0.79) . There was a weak correlation between rate of testosterone androstenedione formation and concentrations of the highly persistent CB 156, CB 157, CB 170 and CB 180 levels (r values of O .40 to O .69). A similar correlation was found between testosterone 2P- and 6p-hydroxylase activities with relatively non-persistent CB74, CB85, CBI 54, CBI49 and CBI 18 (r values of 0.33 to 0.65). The significance of these finding is greater now that Norwegian studies have shown circulating testosterone concentrations in males to be inversely correlated to Immunosuppressive effects of organochlorines in polar bears has been shown by Norwegian scientists. Concentrations of IgG in polar bear plasma from Svalbard were strongly negatively correlated to plasma concentrations of PCBs, suggesting a cause-effect relationship (Bernhoft et al. 2000). Immunotoxic effects appear to be the most sensitive endpoint in toxic effects of organochlorines, and warrant thorough investigation.

The effects of high PCB exposure on the immune system were studied by comparing the immune functions in male polar bears having high (Svalbard, 1998) and low (Canada, 1999) PCB exposure using a vaccination model with recapture after immunization. Thirty bears at Svalbard and 30 in Canada were immunized with different herpes, reo and influenza viruses and tetanus toxoid to stimulate the production of protective antibodies such as virus neutralizing antibodies, virus hemagglutination inhibition antibodies and toxin neutralizing antibodies. The immunization also included keyhole limpet hemocyanin (KLH) that together with tetanus toxoid would stimulate cell-mediated immune response. Blood was sampled at immunization and 4 to 6 weeks thereafter for detection of antibodies. In addition, in vitro lymphocyte stimulation was performed with mitogens and specific antigens (phytohemagglutinin, concanavalin A, pokeweed mitogen, PPD, lipopolysackarid). By neutralizing virus infections in cell cultures, inhibition of virus hemaglutination and toxin neutralization, the resistance factor was measured directly. Therefore, the effect of PCBs on the infection resistance was measured without being dependent on infection experiments or doing registration in relation to disease outbreaks. The immunological analyses were done by the Norwegian School of Veterinary Science. All immunotoxicological and chemical analysis data were gathered by mid-2000-2001, but statistical analysis has only begun. Some preliminary conclusions are emerging which will be reported herein.
In addition to immune system function, plasma testosterone concentrations were determined in 123 male bears from Canada and Svalbard.

In 2000-2001, five hypotheses, as presented below, were to be tested to address some of the short term objectives. Temporal trends in contaminant levels in Arctic ecosystems have been identified in the NCP Blueprints as a knowledge gap.

From what information is available, the rate of decrease in POPs appears to have slowed. We hypothesize that levels of POPs in the Arctic marine ecosystem are approaching a steady state influenced mainly by global processes, and that this recent trend can be identified for the Hudson Bay marine ecosystem by analysis of biopsy samples from female polar bears.

Archived biopsy samples from adult (> 5 years) female bears taken in the summer period at Cape Churchill were chosen for each year between 1991 and 1999. Samples were not available for 1996. Sample sizes each year ranged from four to 10 for a total of 53 analyses (average: six per year). Females were used because previous analyses showed that age effects were minimal in females, whereas there was a substantial effect of age on concentration of highly chlorinated PCBs in males. Females come to steady state with their diet faster because of lactational excretion. Females are therefore more likely than males to follow general environmental trends. For comparison with females, biopsies from seven males in 1995 were also chosen. The samples were analyzed for 57 PCB congeners and 28 organochlorines, including tetra-, penta- and hexachlorobenzenes, three HCH isomers, 12 chlordane compounds, dieldrin, mirex, photomirex, octachlorostyrene, DOE, DOD and DDT. Significance of temporal trends was determined by linear regression using Statistica.

Biochemical reactions involving chiral chemicals are highly enantiomer-selective, therefore knowledge of the concentration of the enantiomeric forms of chiral contaminants is important in determining toxic effects of exposure to those contaminants.

Determination of enantiomer fractions (Harner et al. 2000) of a-HCH, heptachlor epoxide and oxychlordane is proceeding on pooled samples from each year from the temporal trend study above. These are the only chiral organochlorines in sufficiently high concentration to measure enantiomers. Changes in enantiomer fractions (EFs) over time will indicate if the 'age' of the residue is changing. This is especially important for oxychlordane, which is a persistent compound formed by metabolism of chlordane and nonachlor compounds in birds and mammals. Oxychlordane is recycled into the food chain by excretion from, or death of, the animal. A sub-group of males are being analyzed to determine if there are differences in EFs between genders.

Fat, blood, brain, testis, liver and muscle tissue samples from four male polar bears from the Barrow Strait area in 1993 (Letcher et al. 1 996) are being analyzed to determine if there are differences in tissue distribution of enantiomers of chiral POPs.

Due to difficulties with instrument sensitivity, the analysis could not be started until a new GC-MSD had been purchased. Consequently, the chiral determinations were begun late in the fiscal year, are still ongoing, and could not be completed in time for this report.

Temporal trends of organochlorines in Hudson Bay polar bears Temporal trends of the major organochlorine groups found in polar bears are presented in Figure l. Probability that a significant trend exists in female bears is also given. There were statistically significant (p < 0.05) downward trends of total chlorobenzenes (LCBz), a-HCH and PCBs. There were no significant (p < 0.05) changes in chlordanes, DDTs (mostly 4,4'-DDE), dieldrin, ~-HCH There were no statistically significant (p < 0.05) increasing trends in female bears over the whole 9 years. However, since 1995 LDDT had a tendency to increase. This is likely part of an unexplained oscillation. LDDT concentrations in polar bears seem to be subject to more variation than other organochlorines. Historical concentrations of LDDT in northern Hudson Bay were 884 ng·g·1 ( 1968), 525 ng·g·1 ( 1984) and 148 ng·g·1 ( 1989) (Muir and Norstrom 2000).
Thus, present concentrations of LDDT in Hudson Bay bears are approximately 25% of those during the period of active DDT use.

The changing composition of LCBz over time is shown in Figure 2. HCBz and 1,2,4,5-TeCBz were each roughly half of the total, with a minor contribution from PnCBz. The proportion of 1,2,4,5-TeCBz peaked at 53% between 1995 and 1997, then decreased to values similar to the pre- 1995 period, 40% to 45%. Most of the decline in LCBz was due to HCBz, which had a half-life of approximately 9 years.

LPCB decreased fairly steadily throughout the l 990s, with a half-life of approximately 18 years. The shift in composition of the PCBs was subtle over the decade, but there was a clear tendency for the proportion of less chlorinated congeners to increase, and the highly chlorinated congeners to decrease. Thus, CB99 increased from approximately 10% to 12% of LPCB, CB 153 was relatively stable at approximately 35% and CB1 80 decreased from 1 7% to 14%. The trends in these three congeners indicates that the half-life of CB 153 ( 1 9 years) was similar to that of LPCB. The half-life of CB 180 ( 13 years) was shorter and that of CB99 (> 50 years, not significant) was longer than LPCB. Thus, the decreasing trend in LPCB is driven by loss of the highly chlorinated congeners. Historical concentrations of PCBs in polar bears from northern Hudson Bay were as follows: 3820 ng·g·' ( 1968), 71 30 ng·g·' ( 1984) and 4600 ng·g-1 ( 1989) (Norstrom and Muir 2000). Thus, PCB levels in the early 1990s in Hudson Bay were similar to those in the late 1960s, in sharp contrast to the situation in areas such as the Great Lakes or the North Atlantic, where PCBs were in the order of I O times higher in the late 1960s and early 1970s than at present. Peak PCB concentrations in Hudson Bay may have occurred earlier than 1984, but there are no data for the 1970s. The rate of decline of PCBs appears to have been faster in the 1980s (half-life of 7 to 9 years) that in the 1990s. This may indicate that Hudson Bay is approaching 219 equilibrium with global distribution of PCBs, and further decreases may be slight.

Methodology for assessment of white blood cell activities under field conditions was developed by the Norwegian School of Veterinary Science. This is important for studies of cell biology, physiology and immunology in polar bears. It further represents the basic methodology for measuring cell~mediated immunity to microbes needed for testing how environmental pollutants, infections, nutritional factors, starvation and stress influence lymphocyte function .

Significantly lower lymphocyte responses to lipopolysac~ charide from E. coli and Mycobacteria were found in polar bears with high PCB 156 concentration in the blood. In vitro exposure to selected PCB congeners of mitogen Figure 2. Composition of ICBz in female polar bear adipose induced lymphocyte cultures was found to suppress the lymphocyte response, with the strongest reduction in cultures from polar bears having the highest plasma concentration of PCBs. The present study confirmed our previous finding of a significant inverse correlation between lgG and PCBs, both IPCB and specific congeners (PCB 99, 118 and 194).

The vaccination study revealed significantly higher plasma concentrations of PCBs 118, 156, 180 and 194 in polar bears from Svalbard as compared to Canada, but significantly higher antibody titres to influenza, reo and herpes viruses in Canada as compared to Svalbard. These results, together with the fact that there was inverse correlation between IgG and PCB 99, 11 8 and 194 in the same material, demonstrate that the effect of PCBs on the lgG concentration is associated with decreased ability to produce antibodies following immunization.

Impaired antibody production following immunization and decreased specific lymphocyte response in polar bears with high PCB exposure indicated decreased resistance to infections. This is supported by the findings that polar bears with high plasma PCB have been more exposed to the Pasteurella bacteria, one of the most common microbes in the environment, which attacks the respiratory system.

The PCB metabolism assay proved difficult to set up due, in part, to the time- and labour-intensive extraction procedure which limited the throughput of the assay. Another problem was that the method of analysis used to determine the rate of metabolism was not very sensitive or reproducible. We used a subtraction method that measures disappearance of the substrate rather than a more sensitive method that measures formation of product(s). The assay was optimized for metabolism of the four tetrachloro PCB congeners at enzyme saturation to enhance the ability to compare rate of metabolism among compounds and activity for a compound among individual animals. Results are presented in Table 1.

For this bioassay to be meaningful, the relative V max values should be proportional to rate of metabolism of the these compounds in vivo. This can be tested indirectly by considering relative biomagnification factors, which should be inversely proportional to V max· This appears to not be the case. Of all the tetrachloro congeners, CB47 has the highest biomagnification potential (Letcher et al. 1998, Muir et al. 1988, The greater resistance of the 2,4 substitution to biotransformation relative to 3 ,4 is demonstrated in vivo by the much higher relative biomagnification factor of CB99 (2,3 to 2,4,5) to CB 105 (3,4 to 2,4,5) (Letcher et al. 1998). Of all the congeners, CB52 is expected to be metabolized the fastest using the biomagnification criterion (Letcher et al. 1998). ( 1996) showed that the relative biomagnification potential of 3 ,4-substituted PCBs was much less than that of 2,4-substituted PCBs. Taken together, the expected order of decreasing ease of metabolism from a knowledge of biomagnification factors is therefore CB52 CB77 > CB66 > CB47, whereas the data in Table 1 suggest CB47 = CB52 > CB66 = CB77.

The reason for the inability of the bioassay to duplicate the order of in vivo biotransformation rates of PCB congeners is unknown. The amount of PCB that had to be added to achieve enzyme saturation was relatively high, although below the solubility limit. It is possible that the apparent V max is lower than the true value due to deactivation of the enzyme by binding of the substrate to the enzyme without metabolism. It is probable that more than one enzyme is involved in the metabolism of these congeners (CYPIA for CB77 and CB66, CYP2B for CB52), and perhaps the relative activities of these enzymes in vitro is different from that in vivo. Another possibility is that enzymes in other tissues, such as the gut endothelium, may be involved in metabolism of some compounds via a constitutive enzyme which is not present in liver microsome preparations. Thus, the microsomal metabolism assay would not be representative of metabolic capability of the intact animal.

The assay conditions were also optimized for metabolism of a-HCH and P-HCH by polar bear microsomes. Rates of metabolism of trans-chlordane, a-HCH and P-HCH at various concentrations in the medium are given in Table 2. Saturation (rate independent of substrate concentration) was achieved for trans-chlordane, approached for a-HCH and not achieved for P-HCH, with initial HCH concentrations up to 22 .6 mM. This concentration is approaching the solubility limit of these compounds in the medium. Nevertheless, the ranking of ease of metabolism in this assay is clearly P-HCH > a-HCH > trans-chlordane. As was the case for the tetrachloro PCB congeners, these results are counter-intuitive to our understanding of relative rates of metabolism based on relative biomagnification factors. The ratio of P-HCH to a-HCH in polar bears during the mid- l 990s (Figure I ) was higher ( 0. 56) than in ringed seal from Hudson Strait (0.26, Braune 200 1 ).

Unmistakably, in vitro microsomal metabolism assays of common organochlorine contaminants by polar bear microsomes as currently designed do not represent what is occurring in vivo, based on biomagnification potential of these compounds from seal to bear. The reasons for this may be several, including extra-hepatic metabolism in vivo, involvement of multiple enzymes in the metabolism with different relative activities in vitro than in vivo and different substrate specificities, and inability to optimize conditions (e.g. lack of a cytosolic factor, solubility of the substrate).

The focus of this project in early years was chemical identification and spatial/temporal trend analysis. This gradually evolved into emphasis on identification and tissue distribution of persistent metabolites of these compounds, principally of PCBs. The effects of metabolites on circulating levels of thyroid hormones and vitamin A were studied. The liver enzyme systems involved in metabolizing organohalogen compounds and their activities were characterized. Induction of xenobiotic metabolizing enzymes was shown to be correlated with exposure to Activity (pmol·min·I. Initial concentration Activity (pmol·min·I. mg protein-I) of t-chlordane (mM) mg protein-I) organochlorine contaminants. In collaboration with Norwegian scientists, the immune system of the bear has been examined, and influence of halogenated organic chemicals on immune function researched. Norwegian scientists have also studied possible effects of organohalogen compounds on circulating male and female hormones. Whole body toxicokinetics of organohalogen compounds (in some cases, by recapturing individual bears) have been documented. The influence of seasonal fasting, transfer to cubs by lactation, gender differences in metabolic capability, effects of age on concentrations are a few other factors that have been documented as well.

Thus, we presently have very good knowledge of the identity, concentrations and spatial distribution of halogenated organic contaminants and their persistent metabolites in various tissues of polar bears (arguably better than any wildlife species), quite solid information on the function of some of the vital systems which may be affected by these chemicals, indications of where some effects may lie, knowledge of whole body toxicokinetics, and good information on feeding ecology and population biology. Much of this wealth of information has not yet been published. Drawing on all sources of information, the following points summarize current state of knowledge of exposure and ecotoxicology of the major halogenated organic compounds in polar bears.

• Organochlorine compounds, principally six PCB congeners (CB99, CB153, CB138, CB180, CB170 and CB 194) and oxychlordane are the major halogenated organic contaminants in polar bear tissues, except blood (hydroxy-PCBs) and brain (a-HCH), because of high biotransformation capability of the bears.
• TCDD, CBl 18, CBl05, CB77 and CBl26 are all readily metabolized by polar bears. Most of the TCDD TEOs in the bear are contributed by the mono-ortfw heptachloro PCBs, CBl 56 and CBI 57.

• More volatile organochlorines, such as chlorobenzenes, HCHs, chlordanes and dieldrin are fairly evenly distributed in polar bears around the Arctic; however, only the chlordanes are biomagnified to any extent and are of toxicological importance.

• PCBs are the least evenly distributed of organochlorines. Lowest levels are found in the Bering and Chukchi Seas. Levels increase westward across Canada, but differences are not large among areas, except at the mouth of Viscount Melville Sound, where PCB levels are inexplicably two or more times higher than other areas in North America . PCB concentrations are similarly higher in east Greenland and Svalbard, probably due to substantial input from Europe. Analysis of blood samples by Norwegian scientists indicates that even higher levels may be found in bears from western Russia. Polar bears from this area of Russia may have PCB concentrations of approximately I 00

• Polar bears metabolize DDT and DOE rapidly; therefore, concentrations are low. However, they may be subjected to greater risk of adrenotoxic effects of methysulfoneDDE metabolites, which have been identified in liver and fat.

• Methylsulfone-PCB metabolites are present in most polar bear tissues at approximately 5% to l 0% of PCB concentrations. A significant proportion of these compounds are probably bioaccumulated from seals.

• Hydroxy-PCB metabolites of PCBs are the group of organochlorine compounds in polar bear plasma with the highest concentrations, presumably because of strong binding to the thyroxine (T4) transporting protein, transthyretin (TTR), but possibly other proteins.
• A protein immunochemically cross-reactive with human TTR has been identified in polar bear plasma.

• Correlative evidence strongly suggests that hydroxy- PCBs, and not PCBs or other organochlorines, are responsible for disruption of some parts of the thyroid hormone transport system, presumably by competitive binding to TTR. There appears to be some inconsistency in findings of Norwegian and Canadian groups. The nature of this disruption, and whether it is of significance to thyroid hormone homeostasis, therefore requires further exploration.

• Plasma Vitamin A concentrations are negatively correlated to PCB concentrations, but not to hydroxyPCBs. Disruption of Vitamin A homeostasis by PCB exposure may therefore be due to mechanisms other than interference with retinal transport in plasma by hydroxy-PCB binding to TTR. PCBs are known to affect retinal storage in liver. Further investigation is required to determine the mechanism and significance.
• Norwegian results suggest that circulating levels of testosterone in males are reduced by PCB or other organochlorine exposure, possibly affecting reproductive function.

• Rate of production of some testosterone metabolites in vitro by male polar bear liver fractions is positively correlated with PCB and other organochlorine concentrations in the livers, indicating that CYP enzyme induction may be a primary toxic effect, rather simply an indication of exposure, by an increasing rate of androgen metabolism.
• Correlative evidence shows that PCBs and oxychlordane are most likely responsible for induction of CYP2B, possibly other liver enzymes, which may metabolize testosterone in the polar bear.

• In vitro metabolism studies of PCBs and organochlorines yields results inconsistent with known biomagnification of these compounds. The usefulness of in vitro metabolism studies to predict in vivo behaviour is questionable until further research is done.

• Females that lost their cubs, between emerging from the den and the following summer/fall in southwest Hudson Bay, had significantly higher organochlorine concentrations than females that kept their cubs. Although the difference in concentrations may be due to lack of lactational transfer as a result of loss of cubs, the possibility exists that high exposure to organochlorines in milk affects cub survival.

• The hypothesis that pseudo-hermaphroditism found in some female polar bear cubs at Svalbard has an organochlorine exposure/endocrine disruption etiology is not strong because of occurrence of the same syndrome in black bears.

• Exposure to PCBs and other organochlorines suppresses circulating concentrations of IgG, antibodies to influenza, reo and herpes viruses, and lymphocyte responses. Incidence of Pasteurella bacteria exposure is higher in high PCB bears. Impaired resistance to infection is indicated in bears with high organochlorine exposure. These results confirm that immune system R. Norstrom impairment is one of the most sensitive measures of organochlorine toxic effects.

This project was completed in 2000~200 I . There is still a lot of work to do, especially in polar bear ecotoxicology. As outlined in the Introduction, polar bear investigations have been in the forefront of identifying, scoping and tracking problems associated with persistent organic contaminants in Arctic ecosystems. The circumpolar distribution of the species, simplicity of the food chain, high trophic level, penchant for eating seal fat, relative ease of non~destructive (but costly) sampling of tissues (subcutaneous fat, plasma, hair), good knowledge of its biology, most~aHisk species categorization and emerging evidence of toxic effects, call for continuing this research. If not through the NCP, other means should be sought. The major stumbling block in polar bear ecotoxicology in Canada at present is as much a lack of leadership as a lack of funding. However, this project has been an excellent training ground for environmental toxicologists and chemists over the years (two Ph.D.s at Carleton University and one at University of Saskatchewan), and it is to be hoped that the next generation of scientists will take up the challenge.

Sampling of fish in Lake Laberge in 1991 resulted in the issuing of a food consumption advisory on lake trout flesh and burbot livers, which is still in place. The Yukon Contaminants Committee (YCC) then began a systematic evaluation of all traditional/country foods consumed by First Nations and the general public. The investigation was conducted over several years and evaluated by Health Canada and the Centre for Indigenous Peoples' Nutrition and Environment (CINE).

Over the years, in consultation with these organizations, the YCC has focussed the investigation to several fish species and caribou, collected from consistent locations in the Yukon. Lake trout and burbot are collected from Quiet Lake and Kusawa Lake. The initial investigation had indicated that these two species were the most likely to carry elevated levels of persistent organic pollutants (POPs). The two lakes were selected as having no direct input of POPs, containing both species of fish, having small watersheds, and being accessible. Salmon were originally collected from traditional aboriginal fishing locations, but this has since been changed to existing fish weir locations in the same areas, for ease of sample collection. The salmon species collected are chinook, chum and sockeye.

Salmon were collected in the original regions, but for the first time with the assistance of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) weir facilities. DFO operates a number of salmon monitoring weirs across the Yukon and their staff generously offered to collect salmon from weirs in the same areas that had been sampled in the past. This coordinated effort of collection has a number of advantages for the program: it is tremendously cost effective to receive salmon from DFO staff who are commuting in and out of these areas already; the salmon collected are from mortalities at the weir, so no salmon are being sacrificed to research; and it allows the sampling to continue without removing this valuable and diminishing resource from traditional food fisheries.

Caribou are collected through a unique hunter submission program operated through the Yukon Government's Department of Renewable Resources. Samples of tissue from these submissions are monitored for heavy metals only, as past research indicated that there were little or no POPs within these mammals' tissues.
All of the past results and those of any future sampling are stored within the Yukon Contaminants Database. This database is available through the YCC.

Samples of trout and burbot were collected from Quiet and Kusawa Lakes to be archived for future analysis. Salmon were collected at DFO weirs on the Klukshu River, Fishing Branch River, and at the Whitehorse fish ladder on the Yukon River, and sent for analysis.
The results for the salmon indicate that the levels of POPs within their tissue remain extremely low and that the fishery continues to be safe for consumption.

Past and present sampling indicates that the majority of traditional/country foods continue to be a safe and healthy component in the diet of Yukon people. The example of Lake Laberge reminds us that this may not always be the case and that annual monitoring of selected indicator species is essential to maintain confidence in Yukon traditional/country foods. The Northern Contaminants Program continues to identify emerging contaminants and, as this knowledge progresses, an archive of samples is being collected to help answer questions that may arise from this new information.

The monitoring program continues to be a cost-effective way of maintaining confidence in the consumption of traditional/country foods enjoyed by all Yukon peoples. The efficiency of this program continues to grow through the adjustment of collection strategies and the emphasis on linkages with government agencies involved in the management of the wildlife resource. Through the direction of the YCC, what had begun as a scientific survey, has evolved to be a showcase monitoring program for contaminants in the North. The program will be able to adapt to emerging issues through the maintenance of a sample archive which allows us to step back in time, and the Yukon Contaminants Database provides a unique communications ability.

These results will also help to test the effectiveness of international controls.

With a few exceptions, minimal or no direct temporal trend information on OCs and heavy metals in fish are available in either the Arctic marine or freshwater environments. Much of the temporal trend data that is available are too limited to be scientifically credible because they are based on two or at most three sampling times. In addition, much of this is confounded by changes in analytical methodology as well as variability due to age/size, or dietary and population shifts (Muir et al. 1996, Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme 1998). By comparison, temporal trend data for contaminants in Lake Ontario lake trout (Borgmann and Whittle 1991) and in pike muscle from Storvindeln, Sweden (Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme 1998) are available over a Very few measurements have been made of the toxic coplanar (or non-ortho substituted) PCBs and other planar OCs in Arctic fish, however, where coplanar PCBs have been measured along with PCDD/PCDFs, PCNs and CDPEs, calculations of TCDD equivalents (TEOs) show that the coplanar PCBs, especially CB 126, account for most of the TEOs (Muir et al. 1996). As a result, one of the priorities outlined in both the Canadian Arctic Contaminants Assessment Report (Jensen 1997) and the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Report (Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme 1998) is for additional measurements of coplanar PCBs in Arctic fish. Measurements of PCDD/PCDF were not recommended unless specific sources are suspected. Because of their toxicological significance, analysis of new chemical contaminants (i.e. those not currently identified in the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution protocols) such as PCAs and BDPEs are essential and will provide a "baseline" against which future measurements can be compared.

Burbot is a predatory, bottom-feeding species of fish. Its sedentary nature and high lipid content of the liver make the species very suitable for monitoring lipophilic contaminants (Muir et al. 1996, Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme 1998). As outlined in the Northern Contaminants Program Phase II Call for Proposals (Blueprint for Monitoring the Health of Arctic Peoples and Ecosystems and the Effectiveness of International Controls (Northern Contaminants Program 2000), some of the most comprehensive temporal trend data that exists is for OCs in burbot liver from Fort Good Hope ( 1986, 1989 and 1994). Annual data also exists for Hg and Se in both burbot muscle and liver for the years between 1985 and 1999 (Wagemann 1985, Lockhart et al. 1 989, Lockhart 1999, Stern et al. 2000a).

In December 2000, 36 burbot were collected from the Mackenzie River at Fort Good Hope (Rampart Rapids) by community residents. The heavy metal analyses have been completed and OC analyses are underway. The burbot were not shipped to the Freshwater Institute until late January, 2001 .

Organochlorine contaminants data from 1986 and December 1993 (Muir et al. 1996) were not included in the temporal trend analysis presented in this report because of anomalous results which must first be checked (possibly by re-running the analysis, if the samples can be located) .

Stern, Freshwater Institute, Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO), Winnipeg, MB R3T 2N6; Phone: (204) 984-6761; Fax: (204) 984-2403; E-mail: SternG@dfo-mpo.gc.ca; Michael lkonomou, Institute of Ocean Sciences, DFO, Sidney, BC V8L 4B2; Phone: (250) 363-6804; Fax: (250) 363-6808; E-mail: lkonomouM@dfo.mpo.gc.ca Krystyna Koczanski and Thor Holldorson, DFO, Freshwater Institute, Winnipeg MB; Tim He and Maike Fischer, DFO, Institute of Ocean Sciences, Sidney BC; Derek Muir, Environment Canada, National Water Research Institute, Burlington, ON Archived blubber samples from male western Arctic beluga (Eskimo Lakes 1989, Hendrickson Island 1995 were analyzed for nPCBs and PBDEs (polybrominated diphenyl ethers). In comparison, I PBDE and PBDE47 levels increased by 1.8- and 1.9-fold, respectively, in Holman Island ringed seal over the 5-year period from 1991 to 1996, and by 4. 1- and 3. 7-fold over the 6-year period from 1986- 1992 in eastern Arctic beluga from Pangnirtung. These increases reflect the increase in PBDE industrial use world wide. The presence PBDEs in Arctic marine mammals provides additional evidence in support of their ability to be transported long distances through the atmosphere.

Marine mammals are harvested by several Inuit communities. These animals occupy high trophic levels in marine food webs and so accumulate relatively high concentrations of persistent organohalogen contaminants. Documentation of temporal trends in the extent of contamination by these compounds will contribute to an exposure risk assessment.

Brominated flame retardants are used in relatively high concentrations in electronic equipment such as computers and television sets, building materials, carpets, cars, aircraft and in many other applications. Polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs) are used as additive flame retardants (Sellstrom 1996), which are incorporated into the matrix of various plastic materials such as polystyrenes (Zitko 1993). Over the last 2 decades, the use of brominated flame retardants has increased substantially. In Japan, the annual consumption of brominated organic compounds increased from 2500 tonnes in 1975 to 22 100 tonnes in 1987 (Watanabe and Tatssukawa 1989) . From 1984 to 1992, the total consumption of PBDEs world-wide doubled from approximately 20 000 to 40 000 tonnes per year. Presently, the word-wide consumption of brominated flame retardant is estimated to be 1 50 000 tonnes per year (Sellstrom and Jansson 1995, Jansson et al 1993, Sellstrom 1996, Zitko 1993). As a result, PBDEs have been released into the environment to such an extent that they are now ubiquitous environmental contaminants.

PBDEs are similar in behaviour and toxicity to well-known environmental contaminants such as polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and DDT, but have not been banned to date. Because of their high lipophilicity (log Kaw > 5, where Kaw is the octanol-water partition coefficient) and resistance to degradative processes, PBDEs are expected to bioaccumulate easily (Pijnenburg et al. 1995, de Boer et al. 1998, de Boer et al. 2000). PBDEs have been detected at the parts per billion levels (lipid wt) in fish, fish-eating birds and marine mammals from remote areas (Pijnenburg et al. 1995, Jansson et al. 1987, Watanabe et al. 1987, de Boer 1989, de Boer et al. 1998, de Boer et al. 2000, Kuehl et al. 1991 , Sellstrom et al. 1993, Loganathan et al. 1995, Haglund et al. 1997), but limited information is available in Arctic marine mammals. Recently, Stern et al. (2000a, 2000b) and lkonomou et al. (2000) reported 6.8- and 5.7-fold increases of IPBDEs in blubber samples from Pangnirtung beluga ( 1982-1997) and Holman Island ringed seal ( 1981-1996), respectively.

Archived blubber samples from male western Arctic beluga (Eskimo Lakes 1989, Hendrickson Island 1995) were analyzed for nPCBs and PBDEs. In addition, all Eskimo Lake samples and 10 archived samples of blubbers from male beluga collected at East Whitefish ( 1993), were analyzed for organochlorine pesticides (OCs) and PCBs. OC and PCB data for the Hendrickson Island animals was provided by D. Muir.

Blubber samples from 24 male Hendrickson Island beluga were collected in July 2000. Unfortunately, as a result of a storm of unprecedented strength, which hit on August 7, all the jaws from the collection were lost. Because of the high cost of analysis, and the importance of the age data, it was decided that we should not proceed any further and that the collection should be repeated in 2001 .

All samples were obtained by Department of Fisheries and Oceans personnel (Winnipeg, MB) with the cooperation of local hunters. Blubber, kidney, liver, ovaries and uterus, muscle and the lower jaw, as well as morphometric data, were collected for each animal. All samples were shipped frozen to the Freshwater Institute and stored at - 30°C until analysis. Animals were aged by thin sectioning a canine tooth from the rear of the lower jaw and counting growth layer groups in the dentine using transmitted light (Heide-Jrrgensen et al. 1994).

Samples of beluga blubber were analyzed for 130 individual OC contaminants (90 PCB congeners and 40 other OC pesticides) as described by Muir et al. In brief, 2 g of each blubber sample was combined with anhydrous sodium sulfate (heated at 600°C) for 16 hours prior to use. The mixture was then extracted twice with 50 mL of hexane using a ball mill, centrifuging and decanting the hexane between extractions. Surrogate recovery standards of CB30 and octachloronaphthalene were added prior to extraction . Extractable lipids were determined gravimetrically on one-tenth of the extract. A portion of the extract equivalent to approximately G. Stern and M. lkonomou l 00 mg was then separated into three fractions of increasing polarity on a Florisil column (8 g, 1.2% H2o deactivated) . The first fraction was eluted with hexane and contained PCBs, p,p' -DOE, chlorobenzenes, mirex, and a small portion of CHBs (toxaphene), most notably T2/B8-l 4 l 3 (Stern et al. Fraction two was eluted with hexane:DCM (85: l 5) and contained HCHs, chlordanes, and the remainder of the DDT and CHB congeners. The final fraction was eluted with a 1: 1 mixture of hexane:DCM. Each of the three fractions were then analyzed by high resolution gas chromatography with electron capture detection using a thickness) with hydrogen carrier gas. Total PCB (IPCB) corresponds to the sum of all congeners. Total chlordane (ICHL) to the sum of all chlordane related compounds and DDT (IDDT) to the sum of p,p'-DDE, o,p'-DDE, p,p'-DDD, o,p'-DDD, p,p'-DDT and o,p'-DDT. Toxaphene (ECHB) was quantified using a single response factor based on 27 peaks in the technical mixture. Approximately 75% to 80% of ICHB in beluga blubber is ascribed to two individual congeners, an octa- and nonachlorobornane, referred to as T2 (Parlar#26, B8-l 4 l 3) and Tl 2 (Parlar#50, B9-l 679) (Stern et al. Approximately, 1 g of each sample extract was sent to Institute of Ocean Sciences for nPCB and PBDE analysis. Samples were spiked with a suite of internal standards and processed for GC/HRMS analysis using the methodology described by Ikonomou et al. Ouantitation was based on custom standard solutions prepared by Cambridge Isotope Laboratories.

All univariate analyses were performed with lipid normalized log10 transformed data to adjust for skewness. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was used to assess the effects of year-to-year collections (temporal trends), location (Hendrickson Island and Pangnirtung), age of the animals, age*year and age*location interactions (homogeneity of slope between age and [organohalogen]) using the models where [organohalogen] = log concentration of individual congeners and homologue groups.

Differences between collection years and locations were examined with paired comparisons of age adjusted mean concentrations (SAS Institute 1989- 1996). Only results for animals > 2 years of age were included in the analysis of covariance because of the large variations in concentrations seen in younger animals (Stern et al.

Temporal trends of lipid normalized (age-adjusted) nPCBs, PBDE homologue group and congener concentrations are shown in Table l . Over the 6-year period from 1989 to 1995, the levels of the PeBDE and HxBDE homologue groups and all major congeners in the western Arctic beluga have increased significantly. Increases ranged from 1.5-fold for PBDE47 (2,2',4,4'-TeBDE), the most predominant PBDE congener residue in the beluga blubber, to 5.7-fold for BDEl 53. Overall, IPBDE concentrations increased by 1.3-fold. Coplanar PCB congeners CB80, CBl26 and CB169 declined in concentration by 2.0-, 3.3- and 3.6-fold, respectively. Accordingly, nPCB toxic equivalences (TEOs) have also declined (e.g. CB 126 has declined from 19.09 to 5.76 pg·g-1). No significant differences were observed between the concentrations of major OC groups (e.g. DDT, toxaphene, CHL, PCB homologues) in male blubber samples collected from animals at Eskimo Lakes ( 1989), Hendrickson Island (1993-1995) and EastWhitefish (1993) .

Measured increases of PBDEs in blubber samples from male Holman Island Ringed seal (western Arctic), Pangnirtung beluga (eastern Arctic), Hendrickson and Eskimo Lake beluga (western Arctic) over comparable time periods are shown in Table 2. Similar increases were observed for both the Holman ringed seal and the western Arctic beluga. In the Pangnirtung beluga, the greatest increase in PBDE levels occurred over the 6 years between l 986-1992 . With the exception of congeners BDE99, BDEl 54 and HxBDE, no significant differences were observed between PBDE concentrations in the eastern ( l 997 collection) and western ( 1995 collection) Arctic animals (Table 3).

This report provides additional temporal trend data on PBDEs in Arctic marine mammals. Total PBDEs concentrations in western Arctic beluga, as has recently been reported for ringed seal from Holman Island and Pangnirtung beluga (eastern Arctic), have increased by approximately 32% over the 6-year period from 1989 to 1995.

The presence of this class of flame retardants in Arctic marine mammals provides additional evidence in support of their ability to be transported long distances through the atmosphere. This and the observed increasing trends are of great concern and call for measures to further regulate usage of PBDEs.
